=== PAPER 12e854ac62a4 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum optimization broadly, arguing that practical quantum advantage in optimization should be evaluated beyond formal complexity-theoretic separations and decision-problem formulations, and instead in terms of relational problems that return actual solutions relevant to practice, including finance and energy use cases. In finance, it emphasizes that many models in regulated institutions involve optimization under uncertainty and constraints, such as portfolio selection that is highly sensitive to estimation error and may require robust or regularized formulations. The authors also highlight that multi-period financial models introduce additional layers of complexity through market dynamics and temporal dependence.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper surveys a range of quantum optimization approaches rather than focusing on a single algorithm. For discrete optimization, it discusses Grover-based unstructured search as the best generic exact speedup, adiabatic quantum optimization whose runtime scales with the inverse squared minimum spectral gap, QAOA as a heuristic for QUBO (with warm-start variants), and three main strategies for handling constraints (Grover-based, penalty terms, and state restriction/projection). For convex and nonconvex optimization, it covers quantum SDP methods based on Gibbs-state subroutines, quantum interior-point and central-path methods, and high-dimensional quantum gradient descent with potential polylogarithmic dimension dependence, while noting QRAM and other implementation issues. The discussion also extends to dynamic programming, robust optimization accelerated by quantum sampling, and quantum reinforcement learning where speedups depend on coherent environment access.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-034, C-036, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: As a conceptual survey, the paper mainly reports synthesized and cited results rather than new empirical benchmarks. It highlights that Grover’s algorithm provides at most a quadratic exact speedup for generic unstructured search and thus for discrete optimization, and that this is essentially best possible in that setting. For QAOA on QUBO, the authors report that warm-started variants can significantly outperform standard QAOA on certain instances, inheriting some guarantees from the classical warm-start. They also note that quantum central-path interior-point methods can achieve a speedup while avoiding QRAM, block-encodings, QLSAs, and tomography, and that dynamic programming admits quantum speedups for many problems but at most quadratic improvement in the generic case. In the application sections, they observe that some energy-retailing-with-storage formulations are convex under simplifying assumptions, and that classical preprocessing in optimization can, in some cases, eliminate up to 95% of variables.
    [codes: C-008, C-015, C-024, C-031, C-036, C-037, C-049, C-061]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors repeatedly situate quantum methods relative to classical baselines, emphasizing both theoretical and practical comparisons. They note that worst-case complexity results such as NP-hardness and APX-hardness for QUBO limit the possibility of exponential quantum speedups and that for some convex and nonconvex settings, quantum lower bounds match classical ones, meaning no asymptotic improvement is possible in black-box models. Quantum interior-point methods can improve dependence on problem dimension but may not deliver an overall speedup once all numerical and implementation factors are considered. For dynamic programming and robust optimization, the survey points to at-most quadratic generic speedups and polynomial advantages via quantum sampling, respectively, compared to classical algorithms. The paper also stresses that many real-world mixed-integer problems in finance and other domains are already solvable to sufficient accuracy by mature classical solvers, leaving limited room for practical quantum advantage on those instances.
    [codes: C-007, C-011, C-012, C-022, C-027, C-030, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-052]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper is explicit about numerous theoretical, algorithmic, hardware, and application-level limitations. On the theory side, it stresses that we lack proofs of strict separations between BQP and classical randomized classes, that NP-hard problems are unlikely to admit exponential quantum speedups and even approximation can remain as hard as exact optimization, and that improving classical inapproximability ratios via quantum methods would unrealistically imply efficient solutions to NP-hard problems. It further notes that worst-case complexity may not reflect typical practical instances, that many nonconvex variants are undecidable and that quantum lower bounds can match classical in such settings. For heuristic and variational methods, the authors emphasize the absence of performance and runtime guarantees and identify barren plateaus as a central scaling bottleneck, while QAOA for general QUBO remains a heuristic without guarantees. Algorithmically, adiabatic optimization can require exponential runtimes due to exponentially closing gaps, QPE needs good initial overlap with the ground state, and quantum Gibbs sampling is believed to be at least QMA-hard. For convex optimization, QRAM dependence is a major practical issue and even improved quantum interior-point methods may not yield end-to-end advantage. In reinforcement learning, quantum speedups often assume coherent access to the environment, a strong conceptual limitation. On the hardware and benchmarking side, the authors highlight that dense encodings reduce readout quality, current hardware metrics such as QV, EPLG, and CLOPS are only proxies for true utility, and that many experimental demonstrations should be viewed as capability or hardware benchmarks rather than evidence of performance advantage. They additionally caution that many financial portfolio models are highly sensitive to estimation error and that real-world mixed-integer problems are often already solvable by classical solvers, making it easy to overstate quantum impact; they explicitly urge readers not to misinterpret or exaggerate the paper’s results.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-037, C-039, C-041, C-043, C-050, C-052, C-053, C-055, C-062]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors identify several avenues for future work. They advocate for model-independent, problem-centric benchmarks that place minimal restrictions on admissible solution strategies as a promising way to expose genuine quantum advantage in optimization, provided the instances are chosen to be hard for classical solvers yet still compatible with near-term hardware. At the methodological level, they suggest moving from static to dynamic and multi-period financial optimization, which introduces market dynamics and temporal dependence, and extending deterministic optimization formulations in energy and EV-charging to stochastic settings that may require Markov decision process models. They also point to multi-objective optimization as an area where better performance metrics are needed, and more broadly, call for continued development of responsible benchmarking practices and richer application models in finance and sustainable energy.
    [codes: C-048, C-051, C-057, C-060, C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s contribution is primarily conceptual and synthetic: it proposes that practical quantum advantage in optimization should be assessed through a broader lens than traditional complexity-theoretic separations, incorporating relational and heuristic problem formulations, hardware constraints, and realistic benchmarking practices. It organizes constraint-handling strategies into three main families, articulates a stack-aware view of running optimization on noisy hardware, and emphasizes responsible, non-hyped interpretation of quantum optimization results, particularly in sensitive application domains like finance and energy. Within finance, the authors contribute a layered modeling perspective on portfolio optimization under uncertainty and robustness, and they highlight concrete optimization formulations in the sustainable energy transition as socially meaningful targets for future quantum work.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-025, C-042, C-046, C-047, C-054, C-056, C-058, C-062]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper emphasizes rigorous and transparent benchmarking and implementation practices rather than presenting new experiments. It argues that benchmarking for quantum optimization should be problem-centric and fair, with the community agreeing on shared benchmarks, and that each study must clearly specify model selection, preprocessing steps, computational platform, target metrics, and chosen algorithms to ensure reproducibility and replicability. The authors note that preprocessing can dramatically simplify some instances by removing the majority of variables, which must be reported to contextualize any observed speedups. They distinguish between hardware capability demonstrations and true performance benchmarks, and recommend stack-aware method choices on noisy devices, including limited circuit depth, careful encoding trade-offs, and the use of error-mitigation techniques that extend device reach, particularly for sampling-based optimization tasks where the goal is to obtain good solution samples rather than only accurate expectation values.
    [codes: C-042, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-049, C-051, C-053]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: A few codes reflect broader contextual points rather than direct methodological or result-focused content. The observation that parameterization can turn otherwise NP-hard instances into tractable ones connects to fixed-parameter tractability as a general strategy. The paper also notes that dynamic programming and optimal control suffer from curse-of-dimensionality effects and that the sustainable energy transition offers optimization problems with societal benefit, positioning these as important but challenging domains for future quantum optimization research.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets portfolio optimization in a mean–variance framework, emphasizing the combinatorial explosion of binary inclusion decisions (2^n configurations) and the NP-hardness of cardinality-constrained variants, and highlights an operationalization gap: turning live market data into parameterized circuits, selecting backends, and managing end-to-end workflows is still largely manual. The authors frame their contribution as addressing this operational complexity layer between quantum portfolio algorithms and practical deployment in financial settings.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-017, C-058]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core quantum method is a QAOA-based portfolio optimizer where all qubits are initialized in uniform superposition, and the cost Hamiltonian encodes a QUBO mapping of the mean–variance objective, with single-qubit rotations parameterized by empirical annualized returns and ZZ interactions by pairwise covariances, using analytically specified layer-wise schedules for cost and mixer angles. Circuits are regenerated from live Yahoo Finance data on each run and executed via a backend-agnostic flow through QBraid, with equal-weight decoding of measured bitstrings for financial evaluation.
    [codes: C-003, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Experimentally, the authors show that their pipeline can be executed across multiple cloud simulators via QBraid with highly consistent normalized measurement means (~0.6712–0.6713) and identical distributional behavior between local and cloud runs, including full support over all 32 bitstrings and a strong top-5 concentration of probability mass. The dominant measured portfolio bitstring (01011, AAPL+XOM+JNJ) appears at 23.55% frequency—around 7.6× the uniform baseline—and exhibits interpretable selection patterns explained by the encoded covariance structure, while execution-time profiling indicates that more than 70% of runtime is dominated by cloud job waiting, with the agentic orchestration contributing well under 2% of total execution time. Additional analyses detail how empirical return and covariance structures shape circuit parameters and asset inclusion/exclusion, and quantify potential cost ranges at production-scale job volumes to motivate the governance layer.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-023, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-059]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors compare portfolios emerging from the QAOA measurement distribution with simple classical baselines such as equal-weighting across all assets, best and worst single-asset picks, random 3-asset portfolios, and a minimum-variance classical strategy, reporting that one QAOA-sampled portfolio (XOM+JPM+JNJ) attains the highest Sharpe ratio among all evaluated strategies. They also note that higher-Sharpe portfolios tend to be sampled less frequently than the dominant bitstring because QAOA is optimizing a mean–variance cost, not Sharpe directly, and suggest that this explains observed discrepancies between sampling frequency and risk-adjusted performance.
    [codes: C-051, C-053, C-025]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several limitations: the demonstration uses only 5 assets (5 qubits), making the instance classically trivial; the QAOA parameters are not learned variationally but set analytically; all executions are on simulators with no physical QPU runs; the reported findings are based on single pipeline executions without statistical repetition; and the financial evaluation assumes equal-weight allocations for selected assets, which simplifies real-world portfolio construction.
    [codes: C-060, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064]

    [codes: C-065, C-066, C-067, C-068, C-069]

    [codes: C-001, C-012, C-013, C-058]

Robustness mechanisms include local pre-validation with a three-tier simulator/random-fallback sandbox, backend enumeration and submission via QBraid with fallback to local bitstring simulation on failure, a polling agent with explicit timeout policy, a simple normalized-mean-based quality gate, structured remediation suggestions on result rejection, and provenance-tracked JSON artifacts capturing full job and data context. It situates QAOA within the broader family of hybrid algorithms like VQE—which uses a parameterized quantum ansatz, a classical optimization loop, and variational principles—and discusses enhancements such as Divide‑and‑Conquer QAOA for large graphs, L‑VQE, and QUBO-based formulations for routing and power network problems, alongside Bayesian optimization with Gaussian process surrogates as a classical optimizer for noisy black-box objective functions.

Across reviewed studies, they highlight that higher QAOA depth generally improves approximation quality, that noise impacts VRP minimum energy costs nonlinearly, that COBYLA performs best among tested optimizers for VRP, that QAOA achieved success on a toy JSSP instance, that L‑VQE shows better approximation ratios and robustness to finite-sample errors, that QAOA works better with many samples while VQE is more viable with fewer, and that a quantum approach to power network optimization outperformed classical solvers. They also note that QAOA performance is commonly evaluated via depth, approximation ratio, and qubit count, with approximation ratio used to quantify proximity to the optimal solution.

In a specific power network optimization study, the authors report that the quantum QUBO-based approach outperformed classical solvers, and they also describe QAOA as working better with a high number of samples whereas VQE is viable with fewer samples, implicitly contrasting behavior with classical optimization settings.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames finance as fundamentally concerned with uncertainty, volatility and the trade‑off between risk and return, highlighting portfolio optimization, option pricing and risk estimation as core problems often cast as optimization or Monte Carlo estimation tasks. It notes that many financial tasks, including portfolio construction and dynamic portfolio selection, can be expressed as optimization over portfolios for a given risk/return profile, while derivatives and risk measures like VaR/CVaR often rely on computationally costly Monte Carlo simulation. The authors also emphasize that machine‑learning style pattern discovery in past data underpins applications such as credit scoring and fraud detection, but stress that widely accepted models may fail in qualitatively new market conditions.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-037, C-040, C-049]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors survey both gate‑model and quantum‑annealing hardware families and describe how finance problems are mapped into quantum form, e.g., encoding optimization as QUBO Hamiltonians for adiabatic optimization/quantum annealing and using amplitude encoding plus reversible quantum circuits for Monte Carlo and machine‑learning tasks. They outline generic quantum algorithm structure relying on superposition, entanglement and reversibility, and discuss specific subroutines such as Grover‑based search, quantum Fourier transform, HHL‑style linear‑system solvers, quantum PCA, and amplitude amplification/estimation that underlie quantum Monte Carlo, regression and classification methods. Quantum classification and SVM approaches focus on efficient projection operations and amplitude‑encoded inner products, while adiabatic/annealing methods attempt to find ground states corresponding to combinatorial minima under adiabatic conditions, albeit only approximately realized in current annealers.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-035, C-038, C-042, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The review reports several conceptual and proof‑of‑principle results: summarized speedups for various quantum machine‑learning subroutines, including Grover‑based O(√N) search and exponential scaling claims for quantum SVMs and quantum PCA, and quadratic speedups for amplitude amplification and quantum amplitude estimation leading to quantum Monte Carlo with quadratically reduced sample complexity. On the empirical side, the authors describe D‑Wave annealing experiments for optimal trading trajectory and arbitrage detection where the annealer matched classical optimal solutions on small instances, a Boltzmann machine trained on a present‑day D‑Wave device, and quantum risk‑analysis experiments on IBM hardware that estimated VaR and CVaR with excellent accuracy and theoretically quadratic speedup. They also note that neural networks have already proved highly successful in financial prediction classically and that small IBM experiments could already show quantum speedups in limited settings.
    [codes: C-017, C-018, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-039, C-043, C-045, C-047, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Comparisons to classical methods are mostly at the level of asymptotic complexity and small‑scale benchmarks. For optimization on annealers, the trading‑trajectory experiments on 512‑ and 1152‑qubit D‑Wave chips showed performance similar to classical hardware, and in the arbitrage example the annealer recovered the same optimal solutions as an exhaustive classical solver on a five‑asset graph. For sampling‑based methods, the authors argue that amplitude amplification and quantum amplitude estimation provide quadratic improvements over classical Monte Carlo in terms of required samples for a given accuracy, which translates into faster pricing and risk‑metric estimation, though the review does not report detailed runtime benchmarks. For machine learning, they highlight theoretical exponential or polynomial‑in‑log‑N scaling advantages for quantum SVMs and quantum PCA relative to classical counterparts, while noting that classical neural networks and related models are already highly successful in finance.
    [codes: C-032, C-034, C-039, C-043, C-045, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-055]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper is explicit about multiple limitations. On the modelling side, it cautions that even widely accepted financial models may make erroneous predictions in qualitatively new situations, and that least‑squares regression can be computationally expensive in classical settings. On the quantum side, decoherence is said to destroy quantum behavior and any potential advantage, while fault‑tolerant error correction demands thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit and practical qRAM capable of efficient data loading does not yet exist. The authors stress that quantum annealing is only an approximate realization of adiabatic computing, and that quantum hidden Markov models and related ideas for quantum AI are still in their infancy with their power not yet well understood. They further emphasize that numerous experimental breakthroughs are still required before universal quantum processors can surpass present‑day supercomputers, making most of the claimed speedups contingent and largely theoretical at this stage.
    [codes: C-005, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-030, C-041, C-048, C-057]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that near‑term efforts should concentrate on algorithms for Noisy Intermediate‑Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, exploring how faulty quantum computers might still deliver useful financial applications before full fault tolerance is available. They highlight quantum‑accelerated Monte Carlo for derivative pricing and the use of quantum amplitude estimation for broader risk‑metric computation as promising directions, as well as deploying quantum annealers for optimal feature selection in credit analysis and potentially speeding up neural‑network training. They also remark that many financial applications remain unexplored in the paper, explicitly mentioning blockchain and cryptocurrencies as areas where quantum technologies could become relevant in future work.

=== PAPER 1bad58b8e8e7 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses an environmental portfolio optimization problem for carbon credit allocation in Brazil’s Cerrado, framed as a multi-objective territorial planning task involving carbon sequestration, biodiversity connectivity, and social impact, with concerns about greenwashing conceptualized as an allocation failure in a knapsack-type NP-hard problem. This is mathematically formulated as a cardinality-constrained multi-objective QUBO with quadratic spatial interaction terms over 88 municipalities, where the search space is explicitly noted as computationally prohibitive. The case is motivated by the urgency of Cerrado conservation, where more than half the biome has already been converted and very little private land is protected.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs a QAOA-based approach as the operational core for solving the QUBO portfolio selection, implemented on IBM NISQ hardware with a shallow depth p=1, an XY-mixer to preserve cardinality, and warm-start initialization from a greedy classical solution. To handle hardware noise, the authors apply Zero Noise Extrapolation using gate folding to generate multiple noise-scaled expectation values and fit three extrapolation models, with ZNE yielding mitigated expectation values of the portfolio objective (rather than discrete bitstrings) and uncertainty quantified via nonparametric bootstrap. Circuit parameters and penalty weights are tuned via grid search on a noisy simulator, with global scaling of QUBO coefficients to respect gate amplitude limits.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-018, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-038, C-039, C-005]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across seven independent hardware runs on IBM backends, the QAOA+ZNE method achieved a mean portfolio score of 58.47 ± 6.98, consistently exceeding the greedy baseline score of 44.42 with a 100% success rate and large statistical effect (t(6) = 5.33, p = 0.0009, Cohen’s d = 2.01). Mitigation substantially boosts performance relative to raw hardware results, raising the mean score from 43.55 (unmitigated) to 58.47 (quadratic ZNE extrapolation), while even a conservative linear ZNE fit yields a mean of 49.12 with a 95% confidence interval [46.13, 52.14]. The authors also report temporal stability of their methodology: a validation run 13 days after the main experiments confirms robustness against calibration drift, and analysis of selected municipalities suggests that QAOA portfolios emphasize territorial synergies, e.g., repeatedly selecting Chapadão do Céu, which is absent from the greedy solution.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-034, C-035, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-007]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum approach is benchmarked against three classical methods: a deterministic greedy heuristic, simulated annealing, and random search; the greedy method, with score 44.42, is treated as the primary baseline. Raw QAOA hardware results and simulated annealing both underperform relative to greedy on average, with raw QAOA reaching about 98% of the greedy score and not consistently surpassing it, whereas QAOA+ZNE outperforms all baselines in every run. Simulation-based ablations show that random and warm-start initializations converge to statistically indistinguishable scores near the greedy value, supporting the authors’ claim that warm-start does not simply transfer performance but seeds a region from which quantum exploration yields distinct portfolios.
    [codes: C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly state that their results do not demonstrate formal quantum advantage in the computational complexity sense; such a claim would require comparisons against optimal solver-grade classical methods like Gurobi or CPLEX, which they do not provide. They emphasize that the demonstrated instance size (88 variables, k=28) does not establish scalability to industrial-scale problems with thousands of variables. They also note that Zero Noise Extrapolation introduces additional uncertainty because ideal performance is inferred rather than directly observed, and that ZNE delivers extrapolated expectation values of the portfolio objective instead of an actual noise-free discrete solution. Moreover, hardware noise and measurement errors, exacerbated by gate folding at higher noise scales, cause leakage from the intended cardinality-constrained subspace, and timing comparisons are caveated because quantum wall-clock times include transpilation and queue latency, limiting direct runtime comparisons to classical methods.
    [codes: C-005, C-021, C-027, C-037, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper proposes exploring deeper or alternative QAOA ansätze to increase circuit expressivity, alongside more advanced error mitigation and suppression techniques beyond the ZNE scheme used here. It also suggests extending the methodology to larger-scale national and international conservation networks, implying tests on more complex and realistic environmental planning instances.
    [codes: C-054, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim to establish empirical quantum utility for an environmental sustainability application, positioning QAOA as a potential operational core for environmental governance rather than asserting formal quantum advantage. They present what they state is the first application of Zero Noise Extrapolation to multi-objective environmental sustainability problems and emphasize that they address a gap in the literature, where most prior studies rely on simulators or simplified instances, by executing and statistically validating a real-hardware experiment on intermediate-scale IBM devices.
    [codes: C-007, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study constructs a domain-informed dataset by filtering an initial pool of 246 Goiás municipalities down to a robust subset of 88 high-potential candidates, choosing a cardinality k=28 to balance portfolio diversification against QAOA depth within the effective ZNE regime, and defining three 88×88 synergy matrices (spatial, biodiversity, social) to encode interactions. The cardinality constraint is implemented as a quadratic penalty, with global scaling of QUBO coefficients to respect NISQ gate amplitude limits, and key hyperparameters (penalty weight, QAOA depth) are tuned via grid search on a noisy simulator, leading to the selection of p=1 for hardware runs. Experimental rigor is supported by seven independent runs (8,192 shots per noise scale factor) across two IBM backends over roughly two weeks, use of nonparametric bootstrap (both at shot level and run level) to quantify uncertainty and robustness, and clearly specified statistical hypotheses testing QAOA+ZNE mean performance against the greedy baseline. The authors also document hardware and execution windows, backend allocation, and reproducibility details, including Qiskit Runtime usage and calibration-based design choices like XY mixers and warm-starting from greedy solutions.
    [codes: C-002, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-045]

=== PAPER 1caec67a4a64 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum variational optimization for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems, motivated by the prospect of solving large-scale optimization tasks faster than classical methods. QUBOs are formulated as graph optimization problems on undirected graphs characterized by size and density, and are further mapped to Ising Hamiltonians to enable treatment with VQE-style algorithms, with a focus on frustrated instances believed to be harder.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for QUBO/Ising Hamiltonians, using parameterized circuits whose quality is certified by the variational principle and estimated via finite-shot stochastic measurements. They introduce a CVaR-based cost function that selectively averages over the lowest-energy measurement outcomes, and systematically vary the entanglement structure (linear, random, problem-compatible, and product-state/no-entanglement) while defining success in terms of exceeding a probability-overlap threshold with the optimal solution; simulations are implemented with an ideal classical simulator and both gradient-based and gradient-free classical optimizers are benchmarked.
    [codes: C-003, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-031]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: CVaR-VQE is reported to outperform standard VQE across problem sizes, densities, and entanglement structures, both in success rate and convergence speed, and to yield quantum superpositions that are more useful for sampling optimal or near-optimal solutions than the classical states to which standard VQE typically collapses. Tailoring entanglement to the problem topology gives only a marginal advantage, mainly for low-density graphs, and increasing circuit depth yields saturated success rates while incurring higher evaluation costs; under finite-shot conditions, entanglement offers only modest success-rate gains and product-state ansätze can be advantageous when cost-function estimates are highly uncertain. The study also finds that gradient-based optimizers perform best under noiseless wavefunction simulations, whereas gradient-free methods are more robust under stochastic objective evaluations, and that problem hardness—manifested as reduced success and slower convergence—is strongly correlated with the Hamming distance between ground and first-excited states, with Hamming distance a clearer hardness indicator than graph density.
    [codes: C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Within the variational loop, several classical optimizers are compared: gradient-based methods (SLSQP, BFGS, L-BFGS-B) are found to perform very well in exact wavefunction simulations, while gradient-free optimizers (SPSA, COBYLA, Powell, Nelder–Mead) are preferred when the cost-function evaluation is stochastic due to finite shots. The authors further argue that CVaR-based techniques also enhance product-state (non-entangled) ansätze that can be classically simulated, suggesting that in regimes with significant measurement uncertainty a purely classical optimization strategy built on product-state CVaR may match or outperform NISQ-style entangled VQE approaches.
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-025, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The study is restricted to frustrated QUBO/Ising systems where the coupling matrices contain both positive and negative coefficients, which the authors note may be harder but limits generality to that subclass of problems. Moreover, all performance claims are based on classical simulations of ideal quantum hardware (with finite shots as the only source of stochasticity in some experiments), so hardware noise, connectivity constraints, and scaling beyond the tested sizes are not empirically addressed, and the modest benefits of entanglement observed under finite shots highlight that NISQ architectures may not deliver strong practical gains in the studied regimes.
    [codes: C-011, C-022, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Based on the finding that CVaR with product-state ansätze can rival or surpass entangled VQE, the authors propose exploring new classical optimization methods built around such product-state CVaR formulations as a promising direction. They also explicitly call for further investigation of alternative quantum optimization algorithms, including the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), to understand whether other approaches can avoid the limitations observed for the VQE-style methods studied here.
    [codes: C-006, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims a systematic study of how entanglement structure, circuit architecture, and problem structure jointly affect the success and efficiency of variational quantum optimization on random-graph QUBO instances, introducing a CVaR-type objective that empirically improves overlap with optimal solutions relative to standard VQE. It further contributes an analysis linking problem hardness to the Hamming distance between ground and first-excited states, and argues that appropriately leveraged CVaR on product states may enable classical strategies competitive with, or better than, current NISQ entangled ansätze in certain regimes.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-007, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The methodology is based on a structured QUBO-as-graph formulation where instance difficulty is parameterized by graph size and density and hardness is further characterized via ground-to-first-excited-state Hamming distance. The authors define a clear variational objective justified by the variational principle, use a finite-shot stochastic estimator and a CVaR modification that focuses on the lowest-energy samples, and benchmark across multiple circuit entanglement topologies and a product-state baseline using an ideal classical simulator. Success is operationalized via a fixed overlap threshold with the optimal solution, and the study includes a broad comparison of seven classical optimizers and explicit consideration of how finite-shot sampling necessitates switching to SPSA, providing a reasonably systematic though simulator-based assessment.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-031, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Not addressed in this paper
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 1d715e0cd1aa (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets an end-to-end financial risk–decision pipeline that links joint forecasting of asset returns and volatility to discrete portfolio optimization and verifiable audit trails in enterprise settings. It frames the core finance problem as constrained mean–variance portfolio allocation driven by learned risk signals that must be tightly coupled to decisions and realistic constraints, addressing instability and slowness in traditional split prediction-then-optimization workflows. The formulation explicitly maps the risk–return objective with constraints into a QUBO suitable for quantum annealing while preserving a coherent flow from forecast to allocation to signed, traceable outputs.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-027]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum component comprises a variational quantum circuit (VQC) front-end that embeds preprocessed time-series features as differentiable quantum features trained via the parameter-shift rule, jointly predicting next-step returns and a volatility proxy with a small classical head. Downstream, the portfolio optimization is cast as a QUBO by binary-encoding asset weights into B bits per asset, enforcing budget via normalization, and incorporating constraints through penalty terms in the QUBO objective; this QUBO is designed to run on quantum annealing hardware when available but can also be solved by classical QUBO heuristics without changing the pipeline. The method also integrates a post-quantum signature layer that cryptographically signs each rebalance output, enabling later verification of allocations against the exact model state and time using a public key, while incurring minimal latency and storage overhead.
    [codes: C-002, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-041, C-042, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that HQFS reduces return prediction error by 7.8% and volatility prediction error by 6.1% relative to a tuned classical baseline, achieving the best joint accuracy and return-direction signal among compared models. At the portfolio level, HQFS is claimed to improve out-of-sample Sharpe ratio by 9.4%, lower maximum drawdown by 11.7%, and deliver the best risk-adjusted performance with lower drawdown and turnover than a classical mean–variance projected-gradient approach, while maintaining strong returns. For optimization speed, the QUBO stage reportedly cuts average solve time by 28% compared to a mixed-integer baseline under the same constraints, and the audit layer adds only a small constant per-rebalance latency (under 5 ms) with compact per-rebalance records measured in kilobytes.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares HQFS against several classical forecasting baselines (ARIMA, LSTM, GRU, TCN, and a small Transformer encoder) and reports that HQFS attains the strongest joint return–volatility accuracy and return-direction signal. For allocation, it benchmarks against equal-weight portfolios, classical mean–variance optimization via projected gradient on the same forecasted inputs, and a classical mixed-integer heuristic, where HQFS is said to yield superior risk-adjusted performance with lower drawdown and turnover. An ablation study further contrasts the full hybrid pipeline with variants that replace the VQC with a fully classical encoder or swap the QUBO step for continuous mean–variance projected gradient, finding that removing the VQC worsens volatility correlation and Sharpe ratio, while replacing QUBO with continuous optimization increases turnover and drawdown, highlighting the contribution of both quantum-inspired blocks relative to classical designs.
    [codes: C-035, C-036, C-038, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that traditional pipelines where forecasting and optimization are disconnected can yield unstable decisions when markets shift, when discrete constraints like lot sizes and caps are imposed, or when optimization becomes slow as the asset universe and constraint set grow, motivating but also implicitly constraining HQFS’s applicability. They explicitly note that decision optimization becomes expensive as the number of assets, constraints, or discrete choices increases, and that existing approaches often fail to expose how uncertainty propagates into downstream decisions, reflecting a trust and auditability gap. At the data level, they handle long stretches of missing data by dropping those time segments to keep labels well-defined, effectively limiting the usable dataset in such cases.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-022]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Planned extensions include evaluating HQFS under explicit stress regimes, such as high-volatility windows, combined with drift-aware retraining to maintain signal stability under changing market conditions. The authors also intend to strengthen covariance estimation via shrinkage and factor-model updates to keep the QUBO well-conditioned at larger scales, and to introduce more trading-realistic constraints—like sector caps, lot sizes, and slippage—to study their impact on QUBO dimension and solve time. Finally, they propose to explore additional post-quantum signature schemes and to generate a more compact audit report format to enhance the compliance and security layer.
    [codes: C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its main novelty the design of HQFS as an end-to-end risk–decision pipeline that tightly couples joint return–volatility forecasting to a constrained optimization objective, with an explicit mapping of discrete portfolio allocation into a deployable QUBO compatible with both quantum annealing and classical solvers. Additional contributions include a joint predictor that supplies consistent moments to the optimizer rather than mixing sources, an audit layer that cryptographically signs each rebalance and links allocations to precise model states and time windows for compliance, and an evaluation protocol that emphasizes both predictive and decision quality under realistic temporal splits and stress windows so the system is judged by operational outcomes rather than isolated metrics.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study enforces a strict chronological train/validation/test split and applies the same time-aware protocol across all experiments to approximate future-time generalization. Data preprocessing includes winsorization of extreme returns based on training quantiles and standardization of features using training statistics, along with explicit sequence target construction and rules for handling missing data by dropping long gaps, which are documented to preserve label definition. The learning setup defines a VQC feature embedding chosen for differentiability via parameter-shift, a joint loss over return and volatility with L2 regularization to stabilize and prevent overfitting, and a clear mean–variance allocation objective formulated as a QUBO with binary encoding, budget normalization, and penalty-based constraints, plus a top-M asset filter to keep problem size predictable. Evaluation covers linked forecasting and allocation outputs, uses a consistent protocol with transaction costs to report net performance, and includes ablations on the VQC and QUBO blocks and measurements of the audit layer’s computational and storage overhead, enhancing transparency and reproducibility claims.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper emphasizes enterprise and regulatory contexts by highlighting the requirement for traceable outputs that tie each allocation to the specific model version and rationale, and notes that audit signing provides verifiable records without altering forecasting or allocation decisions themselves. It also reiterates the broader trust and auditability gap in existing financial pipelines, where uncertainty propagation into decisions is opaque, further motivating the integrated audit layer.
    [codes: C-010, C-012, C-032, C-048]

=== PAPER 21e9746e62c2 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses discrete Markowitz financial portfolio optimisation with long/short/no-position choices, which the authors note becomes an NP-hard combinatorial optimisation problem when discrete asset constraints are included. They formulate this as a discrete mean–variance objective with a signed net investment constraint that must be satisfied by valid portfolios, and they focus on finding high‑quality (possibly near‑optimal) solutions suited to near‑term NISQ devices.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-008, C-009, C-005]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study compares three hybrid variational quantum approaches—standard QAOA with a soft penalty, constraint-preserving QAOAz with a dual-parity ring mixer, and a new Quantum Walk Optimisation Algorithm (QWOA). QWOA is based on a generalisation of the QAOA mixer to a continuous-time quantum walk over a circulant (in practice, complete) graph on the valid solution set, using two-qubit-per-asset basis encoding and an efficiently computable bijective indexing between valid portfolio encodings and integers, with recursive ranking/unranking achieving O(n²) overall mixing/indexing complexity. All three methods start from structured initial states (equal superpositions over their respective search spaces), differ in how they encode and preserve constraints, and are benchmarked across varying circuit depths p.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that QWOA substantially improves performance over the QAOA and QAOAz baselines in terms of objective value and convergence, especially at low depth p. Combinatorially, they derive exact counts for non-degenerate valid portfolios and for all valid (including degenerate) encodings, showing that QWOA’s search space is on average less than half that of comparable QAOA-based methods and, for n=8, A=4, is only 0.406% of QAOA’s and 14.61% of QAOAz’s search spaces. In simulations on two real ASX datasets, QAOA performs poorly with large variability, QAOAz plateaus above the optimum after moderate depth, while QWOA rapidly amplifies the optimal portfolio (to about 40% probability on Data Set A and 20% on Data Set B) and consistently finds the best expected solution quality and annual return; the authors attribute these gains to reduced search space, reduced bias, and global-symmetry mixing, and conclude that QWOA yields higher-quality portfolios in fewer iterations.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-013, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-042, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical brute-force enumeration is used to obtain the exact optimal portfolio for each instance, against which the quantum heuristics’ objective values and ground-state probabilities are compared; QWOA and QAOAz can match the optimum objective while QAOA often does not. Additionally, the authors’ explanation for QWOA’s advantage rests partly on reducing the effective search space and classical optimisation complexity relative to QAOA and QAOAz, rather than on a proven asymptotic quantum speedup over classical optimisation algorithms in general.
    [codes: C-024, C-027, C-029, C-031, C-036, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper highlights several limitations of the compared approaches. For QAOAz, the dual-parity ring mixer makes the parity bands disconnected, limiting exploration of the feasible space, and the efficiently prepared initial state is biased because probability amplitude is binomially distributed across these bands, which can hinder amplification of the true optimum. More generally for hybrid variational schemes, the authors note that the classical optimisation component suffers from the curse of dimensionality as the number of variational parameters grows, making rapid convergence at low circuit depth p practically essential. While QWOA mitigates some of these issues by design, the work does not address hardware noise or full-stack resource constraints.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest extending QWOA to other combinatorial optimisation problems where the number of valid solutions is not a power of two, arguing that its constraint-respecting indexing and mixing would confer similar advantages whenever classical encodings produce degenerate or non-binary feasible sets. They specifically mention the Travelling Salesman Problem on n cities as an example of a real-world application where their quantum walk–based approach may be applicable.
    [codes: C-043, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core claimed contribution is the introduction of the Quantum Walk Optimisation Algorithm (QWOA), which combines an efficient indexing of valid discrete Markowitz portfolios with a continuous-time quantum walk mixer on a complete graph over the non-degenerate feasible set, thereby reducing search space and eliminating encoding bias in constraint handling. The authors argue that this design yields substantially better performance and faster low‑depth convergence than existing QAOA-based methods for portfolio optimisation, and potentially for broader classes of non-binary combinatorial problems, due to its global-symmetry mixer and hard enforcement of constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-032, C-043, C-044, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper formulates a discrete Markowitz objective with a signed net investment constraint and uses a two-qubit-per-asset encoding to represent long, short, and no-position choices, then carefully counts and indexes valid portfolios (including distinguishing degenerate from non-degenerate encodings via lattice-path combinatorics). The authors implement three algorithms (QAOA, QAOAz, QWOA) under a common protocol: all use the same objective and constraint structure, are run on real historical ASX stock price datasets with n=8 assets, and their results are reported as means and standard deviations over 15 independent optimisation repeats for each depth p and dataset, with separate analyses of search-space structure, bias, and constraint preservation. They also provide asymptotic gate-complexity estimates for the indexing and mixing subcircuits, which supports assessment of scalability at the algorithmic level, though code availability and hardware experiments are not discussed.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-033, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Not addressed in this paper
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 223ed1df56d0 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies an electric power demand (negawatt) portfolio optimization problem arising in demand response aggregation, where an aggregator bundles consumer-owned energy resources to procure and sell electricity by modifying demand patterns. The operational objective is to select a fixed number of DR participants so that the variance of total negawatt over a trading period is minimized while the time‑averaged total procured negawatt closely matches a target amount, reflecting that negawatt trading is executed with a constant portfolio over a period T.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use and extend fermionic QAOA (FQAOA), originally developed to efficiently solve constrained optimization problems with shallow circuits, by introducing a new variant FQAOA-SCLFM that employs a Hartree–Fock driver Hamiltonian with self-consistent local field modulation (SCLFM). The constrained combinatorial portfolio problem is mapped to finding the ground state of a fermionic problem Hamiltonian in a fixed particle-number subspace, and the HF driver is designed to conserve particle number, connect all sites, and have a ground state expressible as a single Slater determinant that approximately encodes the procurement constraint via a self-consistent approximation replacing a quadratic term; standard QAOA variational parameters are then optimized classically and the resulting bitstring distribution measured. Implementation-wise, the new scheme adds only a linear gate overhead in p compared to previous FQAOA and is simulated using the qulacs statevector simulator with BFGS optimization, using historical residential usage data to set negawatt parameters and a normalized cost scale for comparisons.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In noiseless simulations on a 20‑residence dataset, the authors report that FQAOA‑SCLFM procures negawatt more stably than both XY‑QAOA and their previous FQAOA, with the total negawatt approaching the target procurement as QAOA depth p increases and the variance of total negawatt significantly decreasing for harder evening periods (e.g., T = 18 and 21). They further observe that FQAOA‑SCLFM starts from an initial state whose expected total negawatt is already close to the target at p = 0, and that across all time periods its expected cost—defined from the bitstring cost distribution—is lowest among the compared methods, with the HF energy reduction and HF driver yielding a more stable initial state that better respects the soft penalty. They also note practically that HF iterations can be numerically stabilized by choosing a mixing parameter α ≤ 0.6.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The coded evidence only discusses comparisons among quantum optimizers (XY‑QAOA, prior FQAOA, and FQAOA‑SCLFM), with the authors stating that the proposed FQAOA‑SCLFM performs better than the widely used XY‑QAOA and their previous FQAOA in all studied instances and has the lowest expected cost for any given time period T and finite depth p. No explicit comparison to classical optimization algorithms is described in the available codes.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-021, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the underlying DR portfolio optimization is an integer programming problem whose difficulty is expected to grow as more renewable options and DR participants are added, motivating but not resolving scalability concerns. To stay within the limitations of current quantum hardware, they replace an inequality procurement constraint with a quadratic penalty, explicitly stating that this alternative cost function may violate the original inequality constraint even though it improves efficiency and feasibility. More broadly, the use of a soft-penalty formulation and approximate constraint handling via the HF driver implies that constraint satisfaction is approximate rather than guaranteed.
    [codes: C-005, C-012]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that their soft-constraint Hartree–Fock–based FQAOA framework could be extended beyond the specific negawatt portfolio problem to other combinatorial optimization problems of the same form, involving mixtures of hard and soft constraints, indicating future work in applying and adapting the method to broader constrained optimization classes.
    [codes: C-035]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in proposing FQAOA with self‑consistent local field modulation (FQAOA‑SCLFM), which introduces a Hartree–Fock driver Hamiltonian and self‑consistent local fields within the existing FQAOA framework to approximately encode the balance between desired procured power and total negawatt directly into the driver. This new driver and initialization are presented as improving negawatt procurement stability and lowering expected cost relative to both XY‑QAOA and the authors’ previous FQAOA, with only linear additional gate overhead in circuit implementation.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-021, C-030, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study formulates the constrained portfolio as a fermionic ground-state problem in a fixed particle-number subspace and designs a HF driver meeting specific conditions (particle-number conservation, site connectivity, Slater-determinant ground state), which is then approximated via a self-consistent procedure. Variational parameters are optimized classically and the bitstring probability distribution is used to define expected cost; simulations are performed noiselessly using the qulacs simulator on a public residential electricity-usage dataset treated as negawatt supply, with cost values normalized to a defined range for fair comparison. The authors also report practical details on HF iteration stability (e.g., effect of the mixing parameter α), which bears on reproducibility of the driver construction, but there is no mention in the codes of open-source code release or noisy hardware experiments.
    [codes: C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all codes were mapped to other dimensions.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 2291b049d70f (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies discrete portfolio selection, framed as minimizing investment risk by choosing a suitable combination of assets in a Markowitz-style setting, and notes that this portfolio selection problem is NP-hard and thus a candidate for quantum optimization. It formulates the problem via a generalized N-asset portfolio, expected return and variance expressions, and a Quantum Markowitz cost function that trades off covariance-based risk and expected return. The formulation assumes risk-averse investors who only invest when expected return exceeds the portfolio average, and encodes portfolio configurations into discrete states and paths on an asset lattice based on pairwise correlations.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-032]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors focus on quantum optimization algorithms with special interest in Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (QWOA) and propose an extended scheme called Quantum Mix Optimization Algorithm (QMOA) that modifies the lattice structure and search subspace. QMOA encodes each portfolio in a quantum register, restricts the search to valid non-degenerate positions defined by parameters (N, A), and introduces an ancillary covariance constraint as well as swap-gate operations to improve minima across cycles, while handling stationary and move cases via specific H-move logic. The paper situates QMOA conceptually alongside QAOA and QAOAz, describing QAOA’s initial state and soft constraints and QAOAz’s Hamming-weight-preserving mixer as baselines, and defines QWOA’s advantages and lattice structure as the starting point from which QMOA’s modified lattice and iteration bounds are derived.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-023, C-026, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the paper derives combinatorial expressions for path counts, cycle partitions, and iteration counts on the proposed lattice, including formulas for the number of paths between states, the number of cycle partitions CN, and the optimized iteration count I*N, and shows that for certain parity conditions the cycle-count formula simplifies. From these derivations the authors conjecture that the total number of brute-force calculations Ttt exceeds the optimized iteration count I*N, and argue that QMOA contracts the valid solution subspace by half and requires p ≥ 2 iterations for the initial state compared to QWOA’s p > 2. They further state bounds on the iteration ranges for QWOA (2 < p ≤ Ttt) and QMOA (2 ≤ p ≤ I*p), and provide an example where the ‘natural’ number of calculations (e.g., 2304) is much larger than the optimized computation implied by their principle-of-optimality-based reduction.
    [codes: C-005, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-038, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present an explicit empirical comparison against classical optimization algorithms; instead, it motivates quantum methods by labeling portfolio selection as NP-hard and suggesting that quantum computing may be a better candidate than classical techniques. Its comparisons are primarily intra-quantum: it recalls prior work where QWOA outperforms QAOA and QAOAz at higher p and then claims analytically that QMOA improves QWOA by reducing search space and gate complexity, as summarized in a comparison table.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-035, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that QMOA has no numerical or experimental results in the paper, stating that it remains unknown how its empirical performance compares with other algorithms. They attribute this absence of numerical analysis to the practical limitation of not having access to a quantum or hybrid (quantum-classical) laboratory capable of running the QMOA algorithm, and thus defer any validation of their theoretical claims to future work.
    [codes: C-046, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the paper recommends implementing and testing QMOA using the same kind of software environments that have been used for QAOA, QAOAz, and QWOA, implying a need for simulation or hardware-backed studies to generate numerical benchmarks.
    [codes: C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main novelty claimed is the proposal of a new quantum algorithm for discrete portfolio optimization, the Quantum Mix Optimization Algorithm (QMOA), which extends QWOA by redesigning the lattice network and exploiting the principle of optimality to contract the solution space and reduce the required number of iterations for a high-quality solution. The authors also present new analytical derivations for path counts, cycle partitions, efficiency relations, and iteration bounds that they argue show QMOA to be more efficient than QWOA and related quantum schemes in terms of search space and gate complexity. They emphasize that QMOA sets p ≥ 2 for initial state computations (versus p > 2 in QWOA) and claims an exponential-in-time halving of the valid subspace as part of its contribution.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is conceptual and analytical rather than experimental: it builds a generalized Markowitz-style N-asset model and a dynamic discrete asset lattice, then applies the principle of optimality to derive combinatorial and efficiency formulas for quantum iterations, without implementing or benchmarking the algorithms. The paper specifies modeling assumptions such as known initial and final states, correlation-driven asset paths, and risk-averse investor behavior, and provides a stepwise high-level description of the QMOA algorithm including encoding, constraints, swap gate operations, and output format. However, due to the lack of numerical experiments or implementation details (e.g., datasets, noise models, hardware constraints), reproducibility in a computational sense is limited, and the authors themselves note that experimental evaluation is left for future work.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Some additional content characterizes QWOA’s lattice as an open, tree-like network whose complexity grows with the number of assets and notes a concrete example of path counting between specific states (e.g., from S13 to S4), which primarily serve to motivate the redesign in QMOA rather than introduce separate findings.
    [codes: C-010, C-024]

=== PAPER 23e03dc57b20 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles a real-life investment analytics problem by formulating portfolio construction as a graph-cut / partitioning task over large universes of equities, with two specific objectives: selecting portfolio constituents via binary indicator vectors for assets and choosing factors with at most one selected from each factor subset. It frames the challenge as a combinatorial explosion in possible asset partitions that becomes intractable for large universes such as the S&P 500, and links the resulting optimization to normalized graph cuts and MAXCUT-type problems suitable for quantum formulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-015, C-021, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a "quantumized" variant of a portfolio graph-cut algorithm, mapping the portfolio-cut problem to a MAXCUT-like formulation with known quantum analogs, and then relying on quantum sampling of the problem Hamiltonian via IBM Qiskit’s Max-Cut tools on a quantum simulator. They describe reducing the effective combinatorial search space (e.g., to (5 choose 3)^16 combinations) and emphasize quantum generation of correlated random vectors to avoid classical matrix inversion bottlenecks in sampling, along with a spectral compression strategy (eigenvalue decomposition to a low-dimensional subspace) to fit within available qubit/resources.
    [codes: C-010, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Key results include quantification of the combinatorial search burden for large universes and demonstration, on a real equity dataset, of how their graph-cut method behaves as the mixing parameter between sector and correlation information is varied, with lower κ leading to more correlation-driven cuts. They report that their quantumized variant dramatically shrinks the number of portfolio combinations to be examined (e.g., to around 10^16), which they regard as computationally tractable on modern hardware, and present runtime growth measurements for the Hamiltonian evaluation step on a QASM simulator, showing rapidly increasing times as problem size grows and identifying a regime where simulated quantum runtimes begin to approach brute-force runtimes. They also fit a rough growth model for quantum speedup in terms of ln(speed/base) and argue that, after spectral compression, problems with m ≈ 25 can be handled, with the resulting 2^m search still deemed tractable.
    [codes: C-007, C-014, C-019, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study explicitly compares three approaches on subuniverses of assets: a classical brute-force search, a classical eigensolver-based graph-cut method, and a quantum-simulator implementation using Qiskit’s graph-cut algorithm. The authors observe that the eigensolver’s runtime growth is not a major improvement over brute force and that, based on their timing data, the quantum simulator’s runtime begins to catch up to brute force around n = 24 assets, leading them to argue that the scalability/growth behaviour is more important than absolute runtimes in assessing potential quantum benefit.
    [codes: C-003, C-026, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations and caveats. On the data and modelling side, it warns that sector definitions based only on fundamental taxonomies may be poorly defined, and stresses that AI components should be trained on expert-system-consistent data rather than generic sources. In the portfolio-cut design, the authors note the need to avoid or correct "orphan" cuts with only one or two assets, indicating this as a structural weakness that must be handled. Computationally, they identify classical bottlenecks in generating correlated random vectors due to time-consuming matrix inversion/Cholesky decompositions, and recount practical issues in their experiments: the statevector backend ran out of memory, forcing a switch to the QASM simulator, and even then their tests hit a hardware-imposed ceiling at n = 25 assets. They further report compatibility issues between Nvidia’s cuQuantum library and the supported TensorFlow version, limiting exploration of GPU-based alternatives. For future deployment on real quantum hardware, they explicitly state the need for access to devices with a high number of qubits, implying that current hardware is inadequate for their full-scale industrial use case.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-017, C-022, C-027, C-030, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include migrating from quantum simulators to real quantum computers, where the authors expect dramatic reductions in computational time (potentially by thousands to millions of times), contingent on access to high-qubit hardware. Methodologically, they propose further development of their spectral subspace compression approach and emphasise deriving formal error bounds for their approximate methods, analogous to known approximation guarantees like Christofides’ for TSP. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies a mean–variance portfolio optimization problem that balances expected return and risk and is known to be NP-hard when cardinality constraints are imposed, specifically extending it to a ternary setting where each asset can be held long, not held, or sold short. This ternary structure is used to better capture real-market strategies with short positions and is formulated for QAOA-based quantum computation as a constrained optimization over discrete asset states.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-009, C-010, C-012]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors apply QAOA to the ternary portfolio optimization problem, encoding each ternary asset variable using two qubits per asset with a specific mapping from long, short, and no-position states to qubit pairs, and introduce a scaling factor in the cost Hamiltonian to stabilize parameter optimization. They compare five mixer operators—Standard, XY Ring, XY Parity Ring, XY Full, and QAMPA—where XY-type mixers enforce the cardinality constraint as a hard constraint via subspace-preserving evolution, while the Standard mixer handles it via a penalty term in the cost function; simulations are run on real DAX30-based data and include a depolarizing-channel noise model applied after every gate to probe robustness.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In noiseless simulations, XY mixers, particularly the XY Full mixer and QAMPA, converge most rapidly, restricting the search to feasible portfolios and achieving approximation ratios above 99% with optimal-solution probabilities around 0.6 for the smaller instances. However, as problem size grows the number of feasible portfolios increases sharply, making optimization harder, and under realistic conditions sampling noise slows convergence relative to statevector simulations. When explicit depolarizing noise is added after each gate, XY mixers’ initial superiority degrades, with the Standard mixer overtaking them beyond depth- and noise–dependent crossover thresholds, reflecting the cumulative effect of XY mixers’ larger gate counts and showing that shallower XY Ring and XY Parity Ring variants are relatively more noise tolerant; additionally, depolarizing noise monotonically reduces the probability of remaining in the feasible subspace, driving the system out of the constraint-satisfying subspace.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper motivates quantum approaches by noting that cardinality-constrained mean–variance portfolio optimization is NP-hard but does not present any explicit empirical comparison of QAOA performance against classical optimization algorithms or heuristics.
    [codes: C-010]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight that the initial Dicke-state used by XY mixers is fragile under noise, so decoherence during state preparation and evolution undermines the hard-constraint advantage in realistic settings. They also note that Dicke-state preparation introduces significant overhead, with circuit depth and CNOT counts growing with system size, in contrast to the Standard mixer’s very shallow uniform-superposition initialization, and they show that depolarizing noise systematically pushes probability mass out of the feasible constraint-satisfying subspace, eroding the supposed hard-constraint enforcement.
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The work positions itself as filling a gap by providing a systematic comparison of different mixer operators—including several XY-type mixers and QAMPA—for ternary portfolio optimization with short-selling, and by assessing their robustness under depolarizing noise, in a setting where prior QAOA portfolio studies have predominantly used binary formulations and emphasized the importance of mixer design for constrained problems.
    [codes: C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses real-market data derived from the German DAX30 index for simulations, formulates the constraint either as a hard subspace restriction via XY mixers or as a soft penalty via the Standard mixer, and explicitly introduces a scaling factor in the Hamiltonian to improve numerical stability of QAOA parameter optimization.
