=== PAPER 374d8058ad85 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets tail-risk management in finance by focusing on Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) as a central risk measure for regulatory and portfolio-optimization purposes, and formulates CVaR minimization as a convex optimization problem requiring efficient estimation of subgradients for first-order methods such as projected stochastic gradient descent. The authors identify a specific gap in prior quantum finance work: the lack of a rigorous complexity analysis for CVaR optimization and, in particular, for the subgradient estimation needed for tail-risk minimization. This is anchored in the Rockafellar–Uryasev convex representation of CVaR, which underpins their gradient-based optimization formulation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-031]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum subgradient oracle for CVaR minimization built around Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE), which leverages its quadratic improvement in expectation-estimation sample complexity to potentially accelerate tail-risk optimization. The oracle prepares a superposition over return scenarios, computes the loss reversibly, compares it to a VaR-like threshold to mark tail events, and then uses controlled rotations and payload amplitudes (after affine rescaling of returns) so that QAE can recover both tail probabilities and tail-weighted expectations whose ratio yields conditional expectations and hence CVaR subgradient coordinates. The implementation is QRAM-free, relying instead on basis-state sampling via a distribution-preparation unitary, fixed-point arithmetic for computing losses, simple comparators, and single-qubit controlled rotations, with VaR itself estimated via a QAE-powered bisection routine before being integrated into a staged oracle interface that combines VaR, tail probability, and payload estimation.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-009, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the theoretical side, the paper proves that CVaR subgradients in d dimensions can be estimated with O(d/ε log(1/η)) quantum queries, achieving an ℓ2-accurate subgradient with error at most ε and success probability at least 1−η, compared to a classical Monte Carlo complexity of O(d/ε²); the authors describe this as a near-quadratic improvement in query complexity. They analytically quantify how approximation error in the VaR threshold induces only a linear bias in the estimated CVaR subgradient and show that the full oracle’s estimation error can be bounded by a combination of threshold error and amplitude-estimation error terms. For optimization, they prove that projected stochastic subgradient descent using their noisy quantum oracle achieves a convergence guarantee of O(1/√T + ε) and that attaining an ε-optimal CVaR solution requires O(d/ε³) quantum queries end-to-end. Empirically, noiseless simulations show gradient-estimation errors decaying as O(1/M) for the QAE-style estimator versus O(1/√N) for Monte Carlo, with tabulated results indicating lower mean gradient error for the QAE-style method; optimization trajectories in simulated CVaR minimization are similar per iteration across methods, but when plotted against cumulative queries the QAE-style method reaches comparable CVaR reductions using fewer effective queries.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The classical baseline is standard Monte Carlo estimation of CVaR and its gradients, which the authors note has sample complexity O(1/ε²) for expectations and O(d/ε²) for d-dimensional subgradients, providing the reference point for their quantum query improvements. In theory, their QAE-based oracle achieves near-quadratic query savings, moving from O(d/ε²) to O(d/ε log(1/η)) for gradient estimation, and from classical MC’s O(1/√N) error scaling to QAE’s O(1/M) error scaling as the effective budget increases. In simulation, they compare a noiseless QAE-style estimator against a Monte Carlo baseline both for isolated gradient estimation and for use within projected stochastic subgradient descent: numerical results show higher mean gradient error for Monte Carlo than for the QAE-style estimator, while optimization trajectories over iterations show similar CVaR improvements for both, with query-normalized plots indicating that the QAE-style method achieves similar CVaR reduction with fewer queries.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that their evaluation is conducted entirely via noiseless simulation because current quantum hardware cannot support the query depth required for large-scale CVaR optimization, and they emphasize that the QAE-style estimator they simulate is idealized in the sense that it assumes quadratic scaling in an effective sample budget without modeling device noise or overhead. They further admit that their resource trade-off analysis is incomplete, calling for a more detailed study of circuit depth, qubit routing and measurement repetition overhead, and error-mitigation trade-offs across problem sizes. On the theoretical side, they highlight that a lower bound tailored to the conditional-expectation structure underlying CVaR gradients remains open, so the optimality of their query complexity is not fully resolved. In supplementary error-correction estimates they report that the physical qubit counts required are very large even for modest portfolio dimension (e.g., d=10 and precision around 10⁻²), leading them to conclude that near-term implementation on fault-tolerant hardware is out of reach, even though these estimates may inform hardware roadmaps.
    [codes: C-032, C-033, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper outlines several directions for future work: analyzing the noise-robustness of the quantum subgradient oracle under realistic noise models and potentially within fault-tolerant regimes; extending the framework from basic projected subgradient descent to accelerated methods such as Nesterov acceleration and to mirror-descent or dual-averaging schemes in non-Euclidean geometries; generalizing beyond linear loss functions to handle nonlinear payoffs, such as option portfolios or other derivative instruments; and exploring hybrid heuristics that combine the proposed oracle with variational or sampling-based subroutines to create more practical hybrid quantum–classical schemes.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim that their work provides the first rigorous complexity analysis of quantum subgradient methods for tail-risk minimization, specifically for CVaR optimization, by designing a quantum subgradient oracle and proving its statistical and computational properties. They position this as filling a gap in the existing quantum finance literature, which had not previously delivered a detailed complexity treatment of CVaR subgradient estimation for use in first-order methods.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-009]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the theoretical contribution is organized into three main propositions that formalize bias due to VaR approximation, accuracy and query complexity of the quantum gradient estimator, and convergence rates and overall query complexity of optimization with noisy quantum gradients; this structured approach clarifies the assumptions and guarantees at each stage. The empirical evaluation is explicitly presented as simulated evidence using synthetic correlated Gaussian returns, with results reported in two stages: first assessing gradient-estimation accuracy versus budget, then examining optimization dynamics of projected stochastic subgradient descent with simplex projection enforcing long-only constraints. The authors also stress that their circuits are QRAM-free, which is relevant for implementability, and provide a staged oracle interface that clearly separates VaR estimation, tail-probability estimation, and payload (gradient) estimation, which supports reproducibility of their algorithmic design even though hardware-level resource metrics are not fully specified.
    [codes: C-012, C-018, C-020, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several cross-cutting analytical observations do not neatly fall into the other dimensions: the authors use ratio perturbation bounds to control error when reconstructing subgradients from amplitude-estimated tail probabilities and payload expectations, and they highlight an intuitive explanation for why errors in the VaR threshold introduce only modest bias—namely, that only a thin tail slice of scenarios is misclassified when the threshold is perturbed. These analytic insights help justify the robustness of their estimator construction but are ancillary to the main problem framing, method description, or results.
    [codes: C-024, C-027]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to portfolio_optimization because it directly addresses CVaR-based portfolio selection and rebalancing under long-only constraints, with a quantum oracle designed to estimate CVaR subgradients for first-order optimization. Its main value for this silo is the claimed query-efficiency improvement for tail-risk-aware portfolio optimization, plus the explicit simplex-projection setup used in the optimization experiments.
    [silo_relevance_score: high]
  KEY_POINT 1: CVaR is framed as a central objective for portfolio optimization, not just a generic risk metric.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-031  dim_source: dimension_1]
  KEY_POINT 2: The proposed quantum subgradient oracle targets the exact computational bottleneck in iterative portfolio optimization: estimating CVaR gradients efficiently.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-018, C-019, C-026  dim_source: dimension_2]
  KEY_POINT 3: The optimization setup uses simplex projection, matching long-only portfolio constraints.
    [codes: C-035, C-016  dim_source: dimension_8]
  KEY_POINT 4: The main practical promise is fewer queries for comparable CVaR reduction in portfolio optimization runs.
    [codes: C-015, C-017, C-038, C-037  dim_source: dimension_3]
  KEY_POINT 5: The paper’s limitations and future work are especially relevant for portfolio optimization because they point to the gap between the current linear-loss, simulation-only setup and more realistic portfolio models.
    [codes: C-032, C-033, C-042, C-044, C-048  dim_source: dimension_5]
  PRIMARY_CODES: C-001, C-003, C-007, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-031, C-035, C-038, C-042, C-044, C-048

=== PAPER 378c2a73ea46 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a combined problem of improving financial prediction (market anomaly detection, portfolio optimization, dimensionality reduction for high‑dimensional indicators, and time‑series forecasting) and strengthening transaction security against quantum attacks. It motivates quantum methods by claiming that classical cryptography and ML struggle with high‑dimensional data, complex optimization, and the coming quantum threat to RSA/ECC, and proposes integrating quantum machine learning with quantum‑resistant lattice cryptography for finance. The portfolio problem is explicitly posed as maximizing the Sharpe ratio under risk constraints, while security is posed as protecting financial transactions in a post‑quantum world.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-012, C-013, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use several gate‑based quantum approaches: QSVM with a quantum kernel defined as the overlap of data‑encoded quantum states to accelerate high‑dimensional classification and capture asset correlations via entanglement; QAOA encodes portfolio optimization as an Ising Hamiltonian over asset qubits to search allocations in superposition while targeting a high Sharpe ratio; QPCA represents the covariance matrix as a density matrix and uses phase‑estimation‑style routines to extract principal components; and QBM is used as a probabilistic time‑series model to capture short‑ and long‑run dependencies in financial data. For security, they specify lattice‑based cryptography grounded in SVP and LWE, detailing an LWE‑style encryption c = As + e + m and highlighting homomorphic properties for secure computation on encrypted financial records. All quantum ML components are evaluated in a hybrid quantum‑classical simulator setup.
    [codes: C-010, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-012, C-031, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QSVM improves classification accuracy by up to about 20% and reduces training time by around 50%, including 92.3% accuracy on S&P 500 anomaly detection and detection of 95% of anomalies in their summary. QAOA is claimed to improve portfolio optimization with a 10–15% Sharpe ratio uplift and 25% faster optimization, including a reported Sharpe ratio of 1.45 for a 50‑asset portfolio and an example allocation of 45% equities and 30% bonds. QPCA is reported to reduce dimensionality by ~90% while preserving around 95% variance (e.g., 95.2% variance retained on S&P 500 indicators), and QBM is said to increase forecasting accuracy by about 5–10% with 30% faster convergence, achieving roughly 88–88.5% stock‑price prediction accuracy. For security, lattice‑based cryptography is claimed to provide 99.9% security against classical and quantum attacks with roughly 10–15% extra execution time, yet still securing financial transactions with minimal overhead in their examples. The conclusion summarizes that all quantum‑enhanced components yield substantial gains in computing efficiency, predictive accuracy, and security.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-026, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Throughout, the authors compare their quantum approaches to classical baselines, arguing that classical cryptography (e.g., RSA/ECC) and ML models are inadequate for high‑dimensional financial data and complex optimization. In their review and experiments, they state that QSVM and hybrid quantum–classical models outperform classical SVMs by 10–20% in accuracy and halve training time, QAOA improves Sharpe ratios over classical mean‑variance optimizers by about 10–15% and is claimed to reduce optimization time by 25%, QPCA retains more variance than classical PCA for equivalent dimensionality reduction, and QBM outperforms classical RNNs by 8–10% in prediction accuracy with around 30% faster convergence. For security, they emphasize that lattice‑based schemes resist both classical and quantum attacks, unlike legacy RSA/ECC, though at the cost of 10–15% higher encryption/decryption time versus classical schemes.
    [codes: C-007, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-026, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several technical and organizational limitations. On the quantum side, it notes that current hardware noise and limited qubit coherence can seriously affect the performance and reliability of QSVM, QAOA, QPCA, and QBM, and that scalability to larger datasets remains unresolved because performance may degrade as data size and complexity grow. There is also an explicit admission that lattice‑based cryptography introduces a 10–15% increase in encryption and decryption time relative to classical schemes, and this overhead is reiterated in the comparative analysis. In terms of adoption barriers, the authors highlight a shortage of quantum‑trained professionals in the financial sector and the difficulty of embedding these quantum technologies into existing financial infrastructures, which together constrain near‑term deployment.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-037, C-045, C-061]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose scaling their quantum‑enhanced methods to larger and more diverse datasets, including global assets, emerging markets, cryptocurrencies, and derivatives. They foresee testing these models on actual quantum hardware as devices mature, and emphasize the need to improve robustness of algorithms against noisy quantum environments. Methodologically, they suggest designing a hybrid QBM‑RNN architecture that combines quantum modeling of complex dependencies with the scalability of classical recurrent networks. On the cryptographic side, they point to developing advanced quantum‑resistant schemes enabling efficient secure multiparty computation and analytics on encrypted financial data.
    [codes: C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-060]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper presents its main contribution as an advanced integrated framework that combines quantum machine‑learning techniques (QSVM, QAOA, QPCA, and QBM) with quantum‑resistant lattice‑based cryptography to jointly address financial predictive modeling and cybersecurity. In its literature review and comparative analysis, it claims that, taken together, these quantum‑enhanced methods significantly outperform prior classical approaches in computational efficiency, predictive accuracy, and security, thereby positioning the proposed architecture as a next‑generation solution for financial systems.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-050]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, all quantum models are evaluated in a hybrid quantum–classical setting using quantum simulators coupled with classical processing, rather than on physical quantum hardware. The authors provide mathematical formulations for QSVM kernels, QAOA Hamiltonians, QPCA density‑matrix representations, QBM energy functions, and LWE‑based lattice encryption, and they illustrate behavior with concrete financial examples such as market anomaly detection cases, sample portfolio allocations, dimensionality‑reduction statistics, and secured transaction scenarios. However, the reliance on simulators, the optimistic assumptions about quantum parallelism (e.g., logarithmic‑time kernel and QPCA operations), and the high‑level descriptions of integration into real financial infrastructure suggest that the results are exploratory and require further validation in realistic production environments.
    [codes: C-024, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several cross‑cutting claims recur, including that quantum parallelism and superposition provide a generic computational advantage for financial bottlenecks, enabling QSVM kernels and QAOA portfolio searches to explore many high‑dimensional configurations at once. The paper also reiterates an overall narrative that each quantum‑enhanced component—prediction, optimization, compression, and encryption—could substantially impact efficiency and security in financial systems.
    [codes: C-009, C-026, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-038, C-050]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to portfolio_optimization because it centers QAOA on maximizing the Sharpe ratio under risk constraints and reports portfolio-specific gains over classical optimizers.     [codes: C-003, C-014, C-016, C-042, C-047  dim_source: dimension_3]

=== PAPER 37f43983f4d2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as a potentially important technology for solving high-value computational finance problems, focusing on a general multiperiod portfolio optimization problem with discrete integer holdings, transaction costs, and permanent/temporary market impact. The portfolio manager must choose how much to invest in each of N assets across T time steps, given forecasts of expected returns and risk, while accounting for rebalancing costs, making the problem a hard nonconvex combinatorial optimization that is naturally suited to a quantum annealer via a QUBO formulation. The author emphasizes that this multiperiod, discrete, impact-aware trajectory formulation aims to produce globally better portfolio paths than the common practice of solving a sequence of single-period mean–variance problems and then rounding continuous weights.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-010, C-028, C-030, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-055, C-058]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper uses the quantum annealing paradigm, specifically D-Wave hardware accessed via the 1QBit SDK, to solve the portfolio problem by casting it as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) over binary variables. The author explains that QUBO requires binary decision variables and a general (not necessarily positive definite) Q matrix with no explicit constraints, and that nontrivial encoding and embedding steps are needed to map the real-valued, constrained portfolio problem into this form, including choices of binary encodings that affect the effective problem size and the need to tune annealer parameters. Practically, the quantum annealer is operated at 12–17 mK to reduce noise, problems are solved multiple times (e.g., 200 runs), and the most frequently observed solution is taken as the final heuristic answer, with the SDK abstracting away much of the low-level hardware and physics complexity while exposing heuristics for building "quantum-ready" applications.
    [codes: C-012, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-047, C-049, C-052, C-059]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Using a small illustrative instance, the paper reports that existing quantum annealing technology can produce solutions to the discrete multiperiod portfolio problem that are equal to, or very close to, the optimal solution, despite the annealer being a heuristic solver. The author also claims that, conceptually, quantum annealing can exploit quantum tunneling to escape local minima in nonconvex landscapes and that ill-conditioned or degenerate covariance matrices do not pose numerical problems for the quantum annealer. Beyond the portfolio example, the author cites external work (e.g., Google 2015) indicating up to 10^8× speedup over classical computations for specific optimization problems and notes that, for some specialized problems, quantum hardware has already shown significant speed advantages over classical computers.
    [codes: C-006, C-019, C-031, C-032, C-045, C-051, C-053]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts quantum annealing with classical approaches by arguing that combinatorial optimization problems, such as the multiperiod portfolio construction problem (likened to the traveling salesman problem), are particularly hard for classical exhaustive search, which must check combinations often in series, whereas quantum superposition in principle allows exploration of all combinations simultaneously. Within finance, the paper argues that the naive classical approach of solving a sequence of single-period continuous mean–variance optimizations and then rounding to lot sizes is suboptimal because it ignores rebalancing costs and the nonconvex, discrete nature of the true problem, while the quantum-annealing-based discrete trajectory formulation can find globally better portfolio paths. The author also highlights that quantum annealing is less sensitive to ill-conditioned covariance matrices than classical numerical solvers and cites external empirical work showing large quantum speedups over classical methods for certain specialized optimization tasks.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-053]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several important limitations. On the hardware side, gate-model quantum computers are still extremely small (demonstrated 4-qubit grids) and are not expected to be commercially viable for 5–10 years, while quantum annealers, though larger, suffer from significant noise and require extreme operating conditions (12–17 mK and extensive shielding). The author notes ongoing debate about whether quantum annealers exhibit genuine quantum effects that yield true computational speedup, and emphasizes that the annealer is a heuristic solver that does not guarantee optimality, requiring multiple runs and careful interpretation of results. Usability is limited: using a quantum computer today is likened to classical computing 40+ years ago, with specialized expertise, possible machine-level programming, and nontrivial, time-consuming problem setup and parameter tuning. Methodologically, transforming realistic, constrained, real-valued portfolio optimization problems into QUBO is explicitly described as nontrivial, encoding choices affect the size of solvable problems, and the discrete formulation itself is nonconvex and harder to solve than continuous mean–variance counterparts. Finally, the author stresses that existing quantum annealing technology currently permits only small portfolio problems (few assets, time periods, and investment units) to be solved, and that the concrete portfolio example in the paper is correspondingly small in scale, even though the formulation is intended to be generic.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-018, C-020, C-022, C-024, C-030, C-036, C-044, C-047, C-048, C-050, C-056]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The author anticipates that commercially viable gate-model quantum computers may arrive within 5–10 years and that quantum computing improvements will revolutionize optimization in computational finance. Shorter-term, the paper points to cloud-based access to quantum annealers via SDKs and advocates developing "quantum-ready" algorithms that run on classical hardware today but can later be switched to quantum backends, enabling a smooth transition. It also notes that industry leaders and researchers are beginning to investigate quantum applications for high-value commercial finance problems, particularly in portfolio and risk management, and suggests that the presented multiperiod, impact-aware formulation is designed to scale to generic large problems once hardware permits.
    [codes: C-015, C-027, C-054, C-057, C-059, C-060]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its contribution an accessible overview of fundamental quantum computing concepts and their applicability to high-value computational finance problems, combined with an illustrative formulation of a general multiperiod portfolio optimization problem suitable for existing quantum annealing technology. The author emphasizes that this formulation explicitly incorporates transaction costs and both temporary and permanent market impact, handles discrete lot-size constraints directly rather than via rounding, and is structured as a generic framework that, while presently limited to small instances, is intended for large-scale portfolio and risk-management problems as quantum hardware advances.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-041, C-043, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is primarily conceptual and illustrative rather than a large-scale empirical benchmark: it uses a small synthetic multiperiod portfolio instance and acknowledges that embedding and tuning the QUBO on the annealer are crucial but nontrivial steps. The quantum annealer is treated as a heuristic black box whose variability is managed by running each problem multiple times (e.g., 200 runs) and selecting the most frequently observed solution, without detailed reporting of success rates or error bars. Reproducibility is partially supported through the use of the 1QBit SDK, which abstracts hardware details and provides heuristics, but no code or dataset is released, and the discussion of encoding choices, noise control, and parameter tuning remains high-level, reflecting the early, expert-driven state of the tooling.
    [codes: C-018, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-036, C-037, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-056]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper provides general educational explanations of quantum computing concepts and optimization theory, such as qubit superposition and its role in enabling simultaneous evaluation of combinations, the distinction between quantum annealing and gate-model paradigms (with the gate model described as more general and more similar to classical computers), and intuitive descriptions of optimization landscapes (convex vs. nonconvex). It also includes an analogy between the traveling salesman problem and the multiperiod portfolio construction problem, and notes concrete examples where discrete solutions are required in practice, such as even-lot trading constraints, together reinforcing the motivation for studying discrete, combinatorial portfolio optimization on quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-043, C-052]

=== PAPER 394db2cbf8da (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies a discrete portfolio selection problem where binary decision variables indicate whether each asset is included in the portfolio, motivated by the computational hardness introduced by cardinality and other discrete constraints that make such extensions NP-hard. The continuous Markowitz model with fractional weights is used only as a historical and conceptual motivation, while the actual optimization target is a QUBO-encoded binary asset-selection formulation combining expected return, risk via the covariance matrix, and penalty terms for constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-009, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors formulate the discrete portfolio problem as a QUBO, map it to an Ising Hamiltonian, and then solve it using standard QAOA, which alternates cost and mixer unitaries applied to an initial uniform superposition state. Each binary asset variable is encoded in a single qubit (six in total), with a binary-to-spin transformation to build the cost Hamiltonian; they use the standard mixer Hamiltonian, evaluate shallow depths p=1 and p=2, and run the parameterized circuits in a hybrid classical–quantum optimization loop on a Qiskit Aer statevector simulator with 1024 shots, implemented in Python/Qiskit.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the six-asset synthetic instance, QAOA at depth p=1 attains a QUBO cost of −17.740, which the authors describe as very close to the classical optimum, while p=2 yields −17.630, slightly worse. They observe that different bitstrings can correspond to very similar costs, and interpret their numerical findings as showing that QAOA can effectively approximate the optimal solution of the QUBO model and recover solutions close to the classical optimum for small instances.
    [codes: C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The continuous Markowitz model is used purely as conceptual background and is explicitly not employed as a numerical baseline, because it is not directly comparable to the discrete formulation. Instead, the authors use an exact classical QUBO solver applied to the same discrete model as the main baseline, and interpret the comparison as contextualizing QAOA’s behavior against classical methods that solve the identical QUBO instance, finding that QAOA approximates the classical optimum but does not provide an advantage at this six-asset scale.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-031, C-032, C-039, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper repeatedly stresses that no quantum advantage is expected or observed for the small six-asset instance and that current hardware limitations—restricted depth, noise, limited qubit counts, and the exponential cost of classical simulation—preclude any practical advantage over established classical methods. It notes limited scalability because realistic portfolios with tens or hundreds of assets would require prohibitive numbers of qubits, and current noisy devices also constrain circuit depth due to decoherence and gate errors; deeper QAOA circuits, though potentially more expressive, are more sensitive to noise. The authors further highlight that the QAOA parameter landscape is non-convex with multiple local minima, making classical parameter optimization challenging and explaining why p=2 can perform slightly worse than p=1 in their experiments.
    [codes: C-022, C-032, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors frame as an open research question whether advancing quantum technology will enable QAOA to deliver practical benefits for portfolio optimization or whether mature classical methods will remain sufficient. They suggest that future devices with more qubits, lower noise, and greater circuit depth could allow QAOA to operate on large-scale QUBO models and to encode richer, more realistic financial structures, including complex non-linear interactions, advanced risk measures, stochastic scenarios, and stress tests directly in the problem Hamiltonian; small-scale simulations are positioned as a way to study QAOA’s behavior and assess its potential future impact.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-045, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its main contribution as pedagogical and exploratory rather than as a demonstration of quantum advantage: it aims to provide a clear and detailed exposition of QAOA and its application to a realistic yet small discrete portfolio problem, using small-scale simulations to study the algorithm’s internal workings and behavior. QAOA is presented as an attractive framework for financial optimization aligned with QUBO/Ising formulations, with the study emphasizing understanding and contextualization relative to classical methods rather than outperforming them.
    [codes: C-004, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-013]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work uses a synthetic six-asset portfolio with generated expected returns and covariance matrix designed to mimic realistic correlations, and encodes return, risk, and discrete constraints via a quadratic QUBO cost with penalty terms for cardinality and similar constraints. The experiments are implemented in Python using Qiskit with a Qiskit Aer statevector simulator, six qubits (one per asset), the standard mixer Hamiltonian, and shallow QAOA depths p=1 and p=2 executed with 1024 shots; results are compared against an exact classical QUBO solver on the same model, and the authors provide implementation details including the code repository, enabling reproducibility of their small-scale study.
    [codes: C-009, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors emphasize that classical portfolio methods remain highly mature and efficient, serving primarily as a contextual benchmark in this study rather than as targets to be beaten; this underpins the paper’s balanced framing of quantum approaches as exploratory rather than immediately superior alternatives.

=== PAPER 39e897283cac (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles large-scale portfolio optimization, noting that such problems are generally computationally intractable and that prior quantum portfolio methods scale linearly in qubits with the number of assets (one qubit per asset). It reformulates the portfolio selection task as a relaxed long-only, equal-budget QUBO/Ising problem over N binary asset variables, serving as the target Hamiltonian for the hybrid quantum scheme.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-007]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors build on the LSSA hybrid framework, which decomposes a large Ising portfolio problem into smaller sub-systems solved on a quantum annealer or gate-based chip and then recombines the sub-system ground states via a weighted sum whose coefficients are optimized by VQE. Their key methodological change is a coupling-aware sub-system sampling procedure: they construct a market graph based on pairwise correlations, compute a Maximum Independent Set (MIS) to select representative, diversified assets, and then form possibly overlapping sub-systems from assets connected to each MIS ‘placeholder’ asset, with a second-level division used to keep the MIS QUBO itself within hardware limits. A further variant recursively solves the MIS problem using random sampling in the MIS stage while arguing that, for MIS, any random selection of assets is mathematically similar in approximating the full objective.
    [codes: C-004, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Using real Indian stock market data with up to 64 assets on D‑Wave Advantage plus a VQE simulator, the authors report that their MIS-based LSSA variants achieve approximation ratios comparable to classical Tabu or exact solvers while requiring significantly fewer sub-system samples than the original random LSSA. For N = 64 and Ng = 32, they state that LSSA_random needs 32 samples, whereas LSSA_MIS and LSSA_MIS_random use only 12 and 13 samples respectively, and that the portfolio built from MIS-selected assets shows substantially better return–volatility characteristics than randomly chosen stock combinations. They emphasize that, despite stochasticity, multiple experiments indicate that the proposed methods match the baseline in terms of solution quality and reduce sampling effort, thereby lowering hardware demands.
    [codes: C-025, C-028, C-029, C-022, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: For evaluation, the authors define an approximation ratio between their method’s ground state energy and a classical reference, using exact classical solutions for N < 20 and the D‑Wave Tabu solver for N ≥ 20 as baselines. They report that their MIS-based LSSA methods perform at par with the Tabu solver in this metric while using fewer sub-system samples than the original LSSA_random approach, and that the MIS-selected portfolio dominates randomly composed portfolios in return–volatility space.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The portfolio model is explicitly simplified to a static, long-only, equal-budget setting that ignores changing market conditions and investor preferences, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation of their QUBO formulation. They note that random sub-system sampling in the original LSSA can omit important couplings, and for their own MIS-based scheme they point out that the correlation threshold α critically shapes the market graph: very low α leads to a nearly complete graph that degenerates their sampling back to random selection. They also state that their approach is best suited to instances with genuine diversity in asset correlations, implying reduced effectiveness when diversification grades are weak or absent and underscoring that their method’s advantages are conditional on realistic heterogeneity in market structure.
    [codes: C-008, C-013, C-020, C-021, C-035]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose replacing the current annealing-based or gate-based sub-system solvers with algorithms such as Grover Adaptive Search, suggesting potential performance gains in solving individual QUBOs. They also suggest substituting the VQE-based amplitude optimization step with a Variational non-orthogonal optimization strategy, which they argue might scale better to larger problem instances.
    [codes: C-036, C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is a new coupling-dependent sub-system sampling technique for LSSA that selects groups of assets to maximize captured dependencies, implemented via a market graph and MIS-based selection to obtain a diversified, representative set of assets. They further claim that this MIS-based sampling can drastically reduce the number of required sub-system samples—down to at most N in the worst case—without compromising solution quality, thereby significantly lowering the resource demands of hybrid quantum portfolio optimization on real hardware.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper builds on the LSSA framework that partitions an N-variable Ising portfolio problem into Ns sub-systems of size Ng with guaranteed minimum variable coverage under random sampling, then recombines sub-system ground states via VQE-optimized coefficients to approximate the full-system ground state. In their experiments, they use real Indian stock market data, cap the number of sub-system samples at N/2 after finding little benefit from larger Ns, and employ a correlation-thresholded market graph (with α controlling graph density) as a structured basis for forming sub-systems. The authors also note that their results are stochastic but report consistency across multiple experiments, though detailed run counts or uncertainty measures are not provided in the extracted text.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-020, C-025, C-026, C-033]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all extracted codes map naturally onto the other reporting dimensions.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 3a3ba897009d (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The work addresses Markowitz-style portfolio optimization, seeking the portfolio with the best return for a given risk and measuring portfolio quality via the Sharpe ratio, while modeling risk through the covariance matrix of historical asset returns and mapping a binary asset-selection formulation into a QUBO/Ising form suitable for quantum computation. A practical case study uses real market data from Yahoo Finance (via yfinance) over 2016–2023 to instantiate several small binary portfolio problems. The authors frame this as a finance optimization problem called portfolio optimization to which QAOA is applied.
    [codes: C-004, C-010, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper employs the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), presented as a prominent variational algorithm and practical NISQ application, implemented in a hybrid VQA framework where a parameterized quantum circuit is optimized by a classical routine. The QAOA circuit alternates problem and mixer unitaries with parameters (γ, β) optimized classically (using COBYLA) and is run both in an ideal, noiseless setting (statevector simulator) and with realistic noise models (IBM Manila and Lima via Qiskit), with noise described using quantum channels and Kraus operators. The portfolio problem is encoded via a QUBO-to-Ising mapping, starting from a binary formulation, and implemented using Qiskit and Qiskit Finance.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-011, C-018, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In noiseless simulations, QAOA is reported as converging to the correct portfolio for the 2-asset large-gap case, the 3-asset, and 4-asset problems, while failing in a 2-asset small-gap instance and only partially succeeding in the 5-asset case, where it did not quite converge but still yielded informative output. The authors observe that smaller energy gaps—associated with closer expected returns—correlate with convergence difficulties, and they regard performance for 2–4 qubits as satisfactory within the energy-gap restrictions. Under noisy simulations using IBM device models, QAOA performance degrades as expected: penalized states appear more often, the noisy small-gap 2-asset case can even underperform random guessing, but in other cases (e.g., some 2-qubit and 3-qubit instances) results remain worse than ideal yet still above random, with the Lima noise model performing better than Manila, possibly linked to T2 differences.
    [codes: C-007, C-039, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-061, C-062]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classically, the authors construct an efficient frontier from random portfolios to benchmark portfolio quality and compare QAOA’s performance against a random-guess baseline on the discrete search space. They report that in most small instances, both noiseless and some noisy QAOA runs achieve higher probability of the optimal state than random guessing, while in the noisy small-gap 2-asset case the QAOA-based strategy performs worse than random, with the green QAOA line falling below the cyan random baseline in their plots.
    [codes: C-039, C-053, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper emphasizes several limitations: at the algorithmic level, QAOA’s main restraint is the exponential cost and NP-hardness of optimizing its 2p parameters, and VQAs more broadly suffer from barren plateaus, including those induced by noise, which can make gradients vanish with system size. On the problem side, performance is sensitive to the energy spectrum; small energy gaps—linked to similar asset returns—make convergence harder, and the five-qubit portfolio instance is an unexplained outlier possibly related to the larger state space. Noise further limits performance by populating penalized states, rendering the expectation value of energy a poor performance metric in the noisy setting. Regarding hardware, real IBM devices are deemed non-viable for the study because queueing and calibration constraints would require an impractically large number of queued jobs (e.g., 16,380 queues for a four-qubit case), so the work is restricted to simulators and calibrated noise models. The authors also note that the better performance of the Lima noise model relative to Manila is only tentatively attributed to T2 differences, and they explicitly state that the five-qubit anomaly remains unclear.
    [codes: C-026, C-027, C-032, C-046, C-050, C-058, C-059, C-060, C-062, C-063]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions include testing QAOA modifications such as warm-starting and mixed-Hamiltonian techniques to improve convergence and solution quality, running larger simulations (e.g., six-qubit instances) to shed light on the five-qubit anomaly, and introducing a new evaluation metric based on the probability gap between the optimal and second-most-probable states. The authors also propose richer portfolio encodings by adding more qubits to represent weight probabilities instead of binary inclusion variables, and suggest exploring error-mitigation methods, such as those under development by IBM, to ameliorate noise effects in NISQ devices.
    [codes: C-064, C-065, C-066, C-067, C-068]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The thesis positions its main contribution as applying the QAOA variational algorithm—highlighted as a practical NISQ-era method—to a concrete finance optimization problem, namely portfolio optimization, using real market data, and systematically comparing ideal and noisy simulations under realistic IBM noise models. Within this framing that quantum computing has progressed beyond its earliest stages into an intermediate noisy era without full error correction, the work aims to empirically study whether QAOA can provide satisfactory approximate solutions on small portfolio instances and to characterize how noise and problem structure (e.g., energy gaps) affect performance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-038, C-040, C-051]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is structured across chapters that cover quantum theory (circuit and adiabatic models), finance foundations, implementation, and conclusions, and provides standard definitions of qubits, gates, universal gate sets, adiabatic computation, noise channels, and readout errors to ground the implementation. The VQA framework and parameter-shift gradients are discussed, though the actual optimizer used is gradient-free (COBYLA), and the simulations explicitly distinguish statevector-based ideal runs from noisy QASM-based runs calibrated to IBM Manila and Lima noise models. Risk is measured via covariance matrices from historical prices, portfolio quality by the Sharpe ratio, and binary encoding is justified as making the problem more digestible as a QUBO. The implementation relies on Qiskit and Qiskit Finance, with explicit acknowledgment that real-device execution was impractical due to queueing and calibration constraints, which the authors treat as a methodological limitation of their experimental setup.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-051, C-052, C-059, C-060]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes were integrated into the above dimensions.

=== PAPER 3a533a166c84 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum approaches to portfolio optimization, explicitly formulating three continuous variants—MaxRet (maximize return under a volatility cap), MinVola (minimize volatility under a minimum return), and MultiObj (a weighted combination of both objectives)—over asset weights ωi ∈ [0,1]. It ultimately focuses on the MinVola variant as the hardest to solve classically and therefore the most promising for investigating potential quantum speedups. The MinVola problem is cast into a penalty-based QUBO objective suitable for quantum solvers.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors investigate heuristic quantum algorithms, specifically quantum annealing and QAOA, motivated by their lower resource demands compared to exact quantum methods and structuring them in a hybrid fashion with clearly separated quantum and classical components. Portfolio instances are encoded as a penalty-based QUBO with a heuristic choice of penalty parameters and a discretization with d = 3, which yields 4n binary variables for n assets and is then solved via quantum annealing hardware and QAOA circuits with various parameterizations.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the classical side, all benchmark instances can be solved to proven optimality by a mixed-integer programming solver within seconds. Among approximate methods, a problem-specific heuristic attains the best average approximation ratio and finds feasible solutions for nearly all instances despite objective evaluation being costly on large problems. For quantum methods, default quantum annealing initially performs worst, even below random sampling, and after chain-strength tuning only reaches performance roughly on par with random sampling, while QAOA generally fails to significantly beat random sampling and exhibits degrading feasibility and solution quality as problem size grows. Increasing QAOA depth empirically worsens performance, and overall both quantum approaches lie close to random sampling and are clearly dominated by the tailored classical heuristic, leading the authors to conclude there is only very limited room for quantum advantage in this portfolio optimization setting.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-015, C-025, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-005]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The benchmark explicitly contrasts quantum algorithms with state-of-the-art classical methods on a large, real-world instance set. A mixed-integer programming solver finds optimal solutions for all instances in seconds, and a problem-specific classical heuristic achieves higher feasibility and better approximation ratios than the best-tuned quantum annealing and QAOA configurations under the same 60-second runtime budget. In contrast, both quantum methods perform only at the level of random sampling, with quantum annealing slightly better than QAOA due to producing more, slightly higher-quality feasible samples, reinforcing the conclusion that classical methods currently dominate for this task.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The study highlights several limitations. On the modeling side, the QUBO objective relies on a heuristic penalty approach rather than formally derived penalty weights, and the choice of discretization precision d = 3 embodies a trade-off between QUBO size and discretization error. On the hardware and algorithmic side, embedding overhead on the D-Wave annealer restricts the largest solvable instance to just 25 assets, while for QAOA the circuit depth grows dramatically during transpilation (e.g., from 161 to around 11,000 gates for 20 assets), undermining performance. The authors also emphasize that all heuristic methods, including classical ones, are bottlenecked by expensive objective evaluations on large instances. Finally, they conjecture that the all-to-all connectivity of the portfolio QUBO is a main reason for the poor observed performance of both quantum annealing and QAOA, indicating a structural limitation of current quantum hardware and mappings for this problem.
    [codes: C-018, C-020, C-021, C-028, C-033, C-036, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is implied in several ways: the identification of MinVola as the hardest variant and the structuring of methods with clearly separated quantum and classical parts suggest extending the benchmark to other formulations and hybrid decompositions as quantum hardware improves. The reliance on heuristic penalty parameters and a fixed discretization trade-off points to future research on more principled constraint encoding and alternative QUBO constructions that might mitigate all-to-all connectivity. Moreover, the conjecture that dense connectivity is driving poor quantum performance suggests exploring problem reformulations or hardware with better suited connectivity for portfolio optimization.
    [codes: C-016, C-007, C-018, C-020, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as filling a gap in the literature by providing an extensive benchmark that quantitatively assesses the potential of quantum computers for portfolio optimization, using real-world NASDAQ data and systematically comparing quantum approaches with strong classical baselines. It further contributes by defining and analyzing three portfolio variants, identifying MinVola as the most challenging and thus most relevant for potential quantum speedup, and by designing hybrid methods with a clear separation between quantum and classical contributions to enable fair attribution of performance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-007]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study constructs a large benchmark based on daily prices of 1,978 NASDAQ assets from 2020–2023, generating 10 instances for each portfolio variant and each problem size under study. The authors enforce a uniform 60-second runtime limit across methods and define quantitative evaluation metrics—approximation ratio relative to the optimal objective value and feasibility percentage across the 10 instances per size—to compare algorithms. They also clarify that their quantum–classical methods have well-defined partitions, which helps in fairly attributing performance to quantum versus classical components. The need to balance discretization error against QUBO size is explicitly discussed when choosing d = 3, and the study reports practical issues like objective-evaluation bottlenecks for heuristics and embedding or transpilation overheads for quantum methods, supporting transparency and reproducibility.

=== PAPER 3adb18321a79 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets high-frequency statistical arbitrage, arguing that existing classical statistical methods become too computationally expensive at realistic market scales (e.g., N up to 10^7 leading to complexity around 10^15) and cannot meet strict speed requirements in HFT environments. To address this, the authors formulate the task as identifying multicollinear, cointegrated stock portfolios via matrix-based condition number screening and cointegration testing over very large historical time series.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed quantum approach decomposes the trading pipeline into two main subroutines: a Variable Time Preselection Algorithm (VTPA) that uses a Quantum Condition Number Comparison Algorithm to screen portfolios based on condition number thresholds, and a Quantum Cointegration Test Algorithm (QCTA) that employs Quantum Linear Regression for cointegration verification. Both subroutines assume data are stored and accessed via qRAM, use threshold-based stopping mechanisms (including fixed and progressive κ-threshold variants), and exploit the link between large condition numbers and multicollinearity; the QCTA is implemented as a hybrid quantum–classical procedure where residuals and some arithmetic are computed classically.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim a reduction in algorithmic complexity for high-frequency statistical arbitrage from a classical benchmark of O(N^2 d) to a lower quantum complexity, with the abstract stating that their algorithm "has been reduced" from O(N^2 d), and Theorem 1 giving an average query complexity for the preselection routine. Correctness of VTPA is argued by partitioning condition-number ranges into intervals [κ_j, 2κ_j] or greater than a base threshold κ_0, and in the realistic case analysis they estimate that with a condition-number bound κ_0 = 1000, their average complexity is dominated by the first preselection subroutine and provide concrete parameter-based complexity examples. They also state that the total complexity of the cointegration test follows by a direct sum of its subcomponents.
    [codes: C-002, C-015, C-016, C-022, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classically, the preselection of portfolios via matrix factorization is described as having complexity O(N^3), and the overall statistical arbitrage pipeline is benchmarked at O(N^2 d); the authors repeatedly use these as baselines for their quantum complexity claims. They note that problem sizes in realistic HFT settings can reach N ≈ 10^7, yielding classical computational costs on the order of 10^15 operations, and in the realistic-case section explicitly compare this to their proposed algorithm where the average complexity is mainly determined by the quantum preselection step.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-024, C-025, C-027]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several important limitations and assumptions. First, the complexity analysis for the condition-number comparison and preselection relies on distributional assumptions about the spectrum: they discuss a uniform eigenvalue distribution case and explicitly assume that log κ follows a uniform distribution when deriving average query complexity, which constrains the generality of their speedup claims. Second, the quantum algorithms require data to be stored in qRAM and operate in the standard oracle model, which is a strong architectural assumption not yet met in current hardware. Third, their realistic resource estimates indicate that more than 50 qubits are needed, which the authors state is already difficult for them to simulate, implying that they have not performed full-scale numerical experiments. These points collectively highlight that their results are theoretical and contingent on idealized hardware and spectral assumptions.
    [codes: C-009, C-013, C-017, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors indicate that future work will relax and extend their modelling assumptions by considering many other statistical models and different distributions beyond those analyzed in the current complexity derivations. They also plan to simplify and simulate the proposed quantum circuits, suggesting that more detailed implementation-level optimization and empirical validation are left for subsequent research.
    [codes: C-031, C-032]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to contribute quantum algorithms specifically tailored for high-frequency statistical arbitrage, including a two-stage structure that first preselects portfolios using condition-number-based multicollinearity screening and then verifies cointegration, along with two auxiliary "tool" algorithms for condition number estimation and cointegration testing. They present this as a way to reduce algorithmic complexity compared to classical benchmarks for large-scale HFT applications.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-007]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is primarily theoretical: the correctness and complexity of the Variable Time Preselection Algorithm are argued through interval-based reasoning over condition-number ranges, and the average query complexity result depends on explicit probabilistic assumptions about log κ. The cointegration testing procedure is designed as a hybrid algorithm where quantum linear regression produces coefficients while classical routines handle matrix multiplications, subtractions, and residual construction, reflecting a conscious choice to offload numerically simpler tasks to classical computation for efficiency. The realistic-case analysis provides concrete market-scale parameter estimates (number of intraday observations and annual data length) and uses them to motivate that multicollinear portfolios form a tiny proportion of the search space, but the authors also note that circuit sizes beyond ~50 qubits are hard for them to simulate, underscoring that no end-to-end empirical experiments are reported.
    [codes: C-011, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-030]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes add contextual detail: threshold-based stopping mechanisms are central to the design of the preselection algorithm, including the use of clock registers to discard matrices with small condition numbers starting from a small κ_0; and the authors give a concrete example of choosing κ_0 = 1000 when estimating complexity in a realistic market scenario. These details further illustrate how their thresholding strategy is parameterized and justified in practice.
    [codes: C-010, C-012, C-014, C-028]

=== PAPER 3c1b7774da65 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles discrete Black–Litterman (BL) portfolio optimization, where selecting a fixed number of assets under constraints turns the task into an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with an exponentially growing search space. The authors frame BL as more practically appealing than classic Markowitz mean–variance (MPT) and cast the discrete, budget-constrained BL portfolio selection as a QUBO/Ising problem amenable to quantum optimization subroutines. They also formalize investor views as a classification problem that can be handled with quantum machine learning.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-009, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a hybrid quantum pipeline: quantum machine learning (QML), specifically QSVM and a QNN classifier, is used to predict investor views, and a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) then solves the resulting BL combinatorial optimization problem. The authors implement a 12‑qubit proof-of-concept instance selecting 6 assets from 12, with heuristic VQE and QAOA ansätze compared, and emphasize using very few final measurement shots after variational optimization because the optimized heuristic ansatz yields a probability distribution concentrated on high-quality eigenstates. They also execute the optimized 12‑qubit heuristic VQE circuits on the IBM Auckland device using only 5 hardware shots for final sampling.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that VQE solutions achieve high approximation ratios and that even near-optimal solutions (high AR) perform about as well as exact optima in backtesting. Backtests indicate that the BL model with quantum-generated views consistently outperforms several common portfolio models, including MPT, in terms of pure return and mean certainty-equivalent return (CER) over a long walk-forward period from 2008–2021. For the view-prediction stage, QSVM with a simple, non-entangling embedding is found to deliver higher testing accuracy than alternatives such as a Pauli feature map, leading the authors to adopt QSVM-predicted views in their main backtests. Real-device runs on IBM Auckland reproduce the simulator’s best solution within only 5 shots in 6 out of 9 cases, supporting the claim that few final samples suffice when the ansatz distribution is well concentrated.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-012, C-021, C-022, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares its quantum-enhanced BL approach against classical baselines on both the machine learning and portfolio performance sides. For investor views, QSVM was chosen over other methods because its quantum kernel achieved higher accuracy than classical alternatives, and simple feature maps outperformed more complex entangling Pauli maps. In portfolio backtests, the BL model (including the quantum-generated views and approximate quantum optimizer) is reported to outperform the classical MPT model and several other portfolio constructions in terms of pure return and mean CER over a long continuous period.
    [codes: C-005, C-012, C-021, C-022, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight several limitations and practical caveats. Penalty parameter tuning is delicate: λ must be large enough to enforce discrete constraints but not so large that it dominates the Hamiltonian, which can hurt solution precision. QAOA is reported as more difficult to work with in this setting: it requires fully connected entanglement reflecting the fully connected problem structure, its optimization results vary tremendously with the choice of initial parameters, and the resulting circuits tend to be much deeper and still spread probability mass over many eigenstates, making them ill-suited to current noisy hardware. These issues motivate the preference for shallower heuristic VQE ansätze in the NISQ regime.
    [codes: C-024, C-027, C-031, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that larger problem instances may better reveal the potential of quantum computing for BL portfolio optimization, arguing that the required qubit resources grow only linearly with problem size, in contrast to the exponential growth of the classical search space. This scaling argument underpins their expectation that quantum methods could become more advantageous as asset universes grow.
    [codes: C-007, C-008]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper presents itself as a practical demonstration of integrating NISQ algorithms into the Black–Litterman framework by enhancing subroutines with quantum components: using QML (QSVM) to generate investor views and VQE-based quantum optimization to solve the discrete BL allocation problem. It also advances the idea that, with an appropriately chosen heuristic ansatz producing a highly concentrated solution distribution, one can—and should—use only a minimal number of final measurement shots to obtain high-approximation-ratio portfolios in a realistic backtesting setting.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-006, C-012, C-013, C-030, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study specifies several financial-modeling and data-processing choices: it uses log returns, arguing they are preferable for optimizing buy-and-hold strategies; defines market-implied returns via reverse optimization to make the market-cap-weighted portfolio optimal in the BL prior; and sets view uncertainty proportional to each asset’s variance. The risk-aversion parameter γ is adjusted via an effective γeff = γ/B to account for the discrete budget constraint. For QML, the authors describe a structured feature preprocessing pipeline (including labeling, moving averages, normalization, PCA, and label-based filtering of ambiguous feature vectors) and note that simple embedding maps without entanglement suffice for good performance. They design a walk-forward backtest from 2008–2021 with a 260-week training and 52-week testing window, and empirically choose the penalty λ = 1.0 based on inspection of Hamiltonian eigenvalues, while emphasizing that λ must balance constraint enforcement and objective fidelity.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: No additional relevant content beyond what is already captured in dimensions 1–8.
    [codes: —]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to portfolio_optimization because it directly addresses discrete asset selection under budget constraints and evaluates a quantum-enhanced Black–Litterman pipeline on backtested portfolio performance. Its main value for this silo is the combination of portfolio construction, optimization, and empirical comparison against classical portfolio models.
    [silo_relevance_score: high]
  KEY_POINT 1: Discrete Black–Litterman portfolio selection is framed as an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem, making it directly aligned with asset-selection and allocation tasks.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-001  dim_source: dimension_1]

=== PAPER 3c79c53d5d90 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets a discrete single‑period mean‑variance portfolio optimization problem, framed as an unconstrained budget‑return‑risk trade‑off with a penalty term enforcing the budget constraint. The authors map this finance problem into a QUBO and then an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal portfolio, with a granularity parameter controlling how finely the total budget can be sliced across assets.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work uses digitized adiabatic quantum computing enhanced with approximate counterdiabatic (CD) driving, in both non‑variational and variational (QAOA‑style) forms. They define an initial Hamiltonian with an easily prepared uniform superposition ground state and an interpolating adiabatic Hamiltonian, then add local CD terms of the form ∑i αi(t)σy_i whose coefficients are obtained by variational action minimization and scheduled so the CD term vanishes at the boundaries; evolution is digitized via first‑order Trotterization, and higher‑order approximate CD terms are also constructed using a nested‑commutator ansatz. For the hybrid variational setting (DC‑QAOA), they introduce an extra CD unitary drawn from an operator pool derived from the nested‑commutator CD construction and optimize all variational parameters with a stochastic gradient‑based Adagrad optimizer.
    [codes: C-009, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across simulated portfolio instances, the inclusion of local and approximate CD terms yields a drastic improvement in ground‑state success probabilities relative to naive digitized adiabatic evolution, especially for small numbers of time slices, and substantial enhancement persists across evolution times. For larger granularity (more slices), the benefit of simple local CD terms decreases due to a higher density of low‑lying states, but approximate CD terms from the nested‑commutator ansatz restore improved success probabilities, with an enhancement ratio of 1 indicating CD terms are always advantageous in the tested g=2 setting and that the enhancement appears to grow with system size. In the variational regime, DC‑QAOA consistently achieves higher success probabilities than standard QAOA on small portfolio instances, with authors attributing this to increased ansatz expressibility, and they summarize that approximate CD terms substantially improve success probability in both finite‑time evolution and hybrid algorithms.
    [codes: C-002, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-040, C-041, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not report any empirical or theoretical comparison against classical portfolio optimization or classical heuristics; all comparisons are between different quantum algorithms (adiabatic vs. CD‑enhanced, and QAOA vs. DC‑QAOA) rather than against classical methods.
    [codes: C-003, C-036, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight several limitations related to NISQ hardware and their algorithms: current devices’ noise and limited coherence times prevent relying on fully adiabatic evolution, motivating shortcuts but also constraining performance. Digitization via Trotterization requires many gates, which can reduce fidelity, and their use of only first‑order Trotterization introduces O(Δt²) errors. Hardware connectivity constraints may necessitate additional SWAP gates to implement the all‑to‑all Ising couplings. For variational approaches like QAOA and DC‑QAOA, classical parameter optimization is problematic: optimizers can get stuck in local minima or barren plateaus, and as system size grows, the Hilbert space and energy landscape complexity make finding global minima increasingly challenging; they note that random initialization in such landscapes remains a difficult open issue and leads to large variance across runs.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-042, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that their CD‑enhanced algorithms could be promising for a broader class of financial optimization problems beyond the specific portfolio model studied. Methodologically, they propose extending their approximate CD construction to higher‑order terms, expecting further performance enhancement, and they outline the development of digital‑analog quantum computing encodings as a future direction.
    [codes: C-044, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as applying digitized counterdiabatic quantum algorithms—including both local and nested‑commutator‑based approximate CD terms—to a discrete mean‑variance portfolio optimization problem, and demonstrating enhanced success probabilities and performance over baseline variational quantum algorithms such as QAOA and DC‑QAOA without CD. They also emphasize that their approximate local CD terms are experimentally attractive because they only require local operators, are easy to implement, and do not need knowledge of instantaneous eigenstates.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-009, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: All experiments are performed on simulated, randomly generated portfolio data intended to mimic real‑world trends, with explicit choices of objective weights that prioritize satisfying the budget constraint. The study systematically varies problem parameters—number of assets, budget granularity, and evolution time—and defines quantitative metrics such as success probability and an enhancement ratio to compare with and without CD terms. However, the work remains fully simulator‑based without hardware noise, and while it carefully analyzes quantum baselines and parameter choices, it does not include classical optimization baselines or real market datasets, which limits external validation against realistic financial performance.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-031, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that as the number of budget slices increases, the density of states close to the ground state grows, which they use to qualitatively explain why simple local CD control becomes less effective and motivates the use of higher‑order or approximate CD constructions in those regimes.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-030]

Penalty dephasing and Zeno show lower feasibility ratios than QUBO, and in depth-scaling experiments penalty dephasing tends to improve with more QAOA layers while QUBO and Zeno often worsen; Zeno also has significantly longer runtime than penalty dephasing due to mixed‑state simulation.

    [codes: C-027, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is implied in exploring post-selection for the Zeno-based method, investigating strategies to mitigate barren plateaus at higher QAOA depths, and further tailoring the choice of constraint-encoding method to specific problem characteristics and resource regimes such as problem size and desired accuracy.

The authors design explicit metrics for quantum resource utilization and numerical performance, and discuss how landscape ruggedness and barren plateaus may affect optimization, emphasizing that method selection should account for problem size, desired accuracy, and available quantum resources.
