[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum runtime scaling for several combinatorial optimization problems relevant to finance and data analytics—specifically portfolio optimization, feature selection, clustering, and weighted MaxCut—by reformulating all of them as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) instances, with portfolio constraints incorporated via penalty terms in the cost function.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ a linear-ramp variant of QAOA in which the optimal parameters exhibit smooth increasing/decreasing patterns and are compressed into a schedule with only two free parameters, implemented as a specific parametrized quantum state. To circumvent costly high-dimensional variational optimization, they propose an extrapolation-based parameter estimation strategy that learns these two parameters on small random subinstances via grid search (with a log-scale parameter grid and a multivariate skew-Gaussian fit) and extrapolates them on a log–log scale to larger instances, then choose the QAOA depth p by minimizing a total-depth runtime metric.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the extrapolated linear-ramp parameters agree well with those obtained from direct optimization on larger instances, supporting the validity of the extrapolation scheme. For portfolio optimization, the authors report that the quantum runtime scaling exponent is smaller than the classical one and interpret this as an indication of potential quantum scaling advantage, while for feature selection the results suggest a quantum disadvantage relative to classical methods. In clustering, they observe instability with outliers exhibiting extremely large total depths, but show that using universal parameter scaling across instances both improves scaling coefficients and keeps success probabilities for the optimal solution on average above 0.1, which they argue would, if constant, imply algebraic (subexponential) median quantum runtime.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Quantum runtime scaling is explicitly compared against several classical optimization baselines, including commercial solvers (CPLEX and GUROBI), the MQLib/Burer2002 heuristic, and the Goemans–Williamson algorithm, with classical scaling quantified via the slope of fitted models. The authors ultimately select the MQLib/Burer2002 algorithm as the main classical reference for detailed comparison, against which they report superior scaling for portfolio optimization and inferior performance for feature selection.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors caution that their runtime comparisons implicitly assume that suitable LR-QAOA circuit parameters are already known or can be efficiently found, even though the computational effort for their parameter-search and extrapolation procedure itself grows with problem size. They also highlight instability in some applications—notably clustering—where outliers with extremely large total depth values appear, indicating that the extrapolation and parameter-scaling strategies may not behave uniformly well across problem instances.
    [codes: C-031, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors argue that to substantiate or refute the observed scaling indications, future studies must cover a broader range of problem sizes beyond N = 28. They additionally call for more elaborate statistical analyses that go beyond median runtime and examine the scaling behavior of multiple runtime percentiles to better characterize performance variability.
    [codes: C-036, C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its core contribution an extrapolation-based method that estimates suitable linear-ramp QAOA parameters for larger problem sizes using only optimizations on smaller subproblems, thereby reducing the parameter-search burden while leveraging a two-parameter linear schedule informed by observed parameter patterns. It further positions the work as providing an evaluation of quantum runtime scaling on a simulator across four QUBO-formulated applications and as demonstrating, in the portfolio case, empirically superior scaling compared to classical runtimes, albeit as a potential rather than definitive quantum advantage.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study standardizes all considered problems via QUBO reformulations, including explicit handling of portfolio constraints through penalty terms, and models clustering as a MaxCut problem, which supports comparability across domains. Classical baselines are carefully selected and their scaling quantified by fitting slopes to runtime data, while on the quantum side the authors define runtime in terms of total circuit depth D and empirically validate their parameter extrapolation by comparing predicted parameters to optima from direct grid search on larger instances. They also introduce a universal parameter-scaling scheme and report success probabilities and median runtime implications, indicating attention to both optimization landscapes and performance metrics, though all evidence is obtained on a simulator rather than hardware.

=== PAPER 3fb78ea9b31b (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the constrained portfolio selection problem, defined as allocating budget across stocks to maximize expected mean return while minimizing risk, i.e., a risk–return tradeoff formulation of portfolio optimization. The authors highlight that the problem is NP‑hard and that classical mean–variance formulations often neglect practical constraints such as cardinality bounds, class and round-lot constraints, and local-minima avoidance, motivating the use of meta-heuristics and interest in quantum-inspired approaches.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce Quantum Beetle Antennae Search (QBAS), a quantum-inspired meta-heuristic that extends the single-particle beetle antennae search (BAS) by modeling the beetle as a quantum particle evolving under a chosen potential. Specifically, they derive a quantum update rule for the beetle position by applying quantum mechanics principles and assuming a delta potential, which they state is chosen because of its convergence speed and propensity to avoid local minima; the resulting algorithm uses this quantum update equation within the BAS framework.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Theoretical analysis in the paper claims that QBAS has monotonic improvement in its objective function across iterations, is stable, converges to the optimal solution as iterations go to infinity, and has polynomial time and space complexity. Empirically, QBAS converges rapidly on standard benchmark functions (e.g., Ackley, Rastrigin, Beale, Levi N.13) within about 120 iterations with very small variation across runs, and on real stock portfolio problems (20, 50, 75, and 100 assets) it consistently attains the highest objective values and Sharpe ratios among the tested methods, with fast convergence in the 20‑stock case.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: QBAS is empirically compared against classical meta-heuristics—particle swarm optimization (PSO), genetic algorithms (GA), and the original BAS—and the authors report that QBAS outperforms these swarm algorithms in terms of optimized objective value and Sharpe ratio across portfolio sizes. They also note that PSO can slightly miss satisfying equality constraints in the 20‑stock case, whereas QBAS achieves both high objective values and near-perfect feasibility, and converges in fewer iterations (around 40 for the 20‑stock problem) than the baselines.
    [codes: C-003, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that although QBAS has a higher probability than gradient methods to avoid local minima, it does not guarantee local-minima avoidance, and its single-particle nature limits its search ability and makes it prone to local minima. They also point out a computational drawback: due to its virtual-particle principle, QBAS evaluates the objective function three times per iteration, increasing computational cost. More broadly, they note that standard portfolio formulations commonly omit several real-world constraints (cardinality, bounds, class, round-lots, pre-assignment, and computational resource limits), which their current QBAS instantiation has yet to fully incorporate.
    [codes: C-005, C-023, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Planned extensions include designing a QBAS variant that requires only a single objective evaluation per iteration to reduce computational cost, and developing a swarm-based version of QBAS to enhance search ability and mitigate local-minima issues. The authors also propose to extend their portfolio model by explicitly incorporating additional real-world constraints such as cardinality limits, upper and lower bounds, class constraints, round-lot constraints, and pre-assignment constraints.
    [codes: C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty by formulating a quantum variant of the BAS algorithm, termed QBAS, and explicitly states that this is the first quantum version of BAS. They further claim theoretical contributions in showing that this QBAS is stable, convergent, and polynomial in time and space complexity, and that it can be successfully applied to constrained portfolio optimization on real stock data.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-042]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the portfolio optimization is cast into a single unconstrained objective via penalty terms, combining a Sharpe-ratio-based objective with equality and bound constraints, which are penalized when violated. The optimization model is built on standard mean–variance and efficient frontier formulations, where risk is treated as the objective to be minimized and expected mean return as a constraint, with a trade-off parameter to navigate the efficient frontier. Experiments use real stock data from the Shanghai Stock Exchange 50 Index (and selected US tech firms) across multiple portfolio sizes, and the authors benchmark QBAS on four standard single-objective test functions, reporting small variation across repeated runs as evidence of robustness; however, the paper does not describe any actual quantum hardware implementation, and QBAS remains a quantum-inspired classical algorithm.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-026, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper provides additional conceptual framing by motivating the work through recent interest in quantum computing applied to portfolio selection and by describing the biological inspiration of BAS, which models beetle antennae-based exploration to guide the search process.
    [codes: C-007, C-018]

=== PAPER 40e4c7fdd4ac (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies dynamic portfolio optimization with transaction costs and other constraints, formulating it as a multi-period problem where portfolios are rebalanced over time under a risk–return trade-off. The continuous formulation is analytically solvable in a special case without transaction costs, but the discrete version—obtained via a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian over binary decision variables—is NP-hard in generic cases, motivating the use of quantum and quantum‑inspired methods. The Hamiltonian structure is such that it decomposes by time step, enabling per-period optimization within the overall dynamic setting.
    [codes: C-006, C-011, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-007]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study benchmarks several quantum and quantum-inspired approaches on the QUBO-encoded dynamic portfolio problem, including D‑Wave’s hybrid quantum annealing, gate-based VQE on IBM-Q with a custom strongly entangling-layer ansatz up to 12 qubits, and a quantum-inspired tensor-network optimizer based on Matrix Product States. The D‑Wave Hybrid algorithm uses a classical–quantum decomposition strategy to overcome raw processor size limits, VQE and a VQE-Constrained variant generate low-energy candidate states which are classically recombined, and tensor networks compress the state representation to a polynomial number of parameters to search for low-energy configurations. Hybrid quantum–classical strategies are a central design choice across these methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-037]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across real-data experiments, the authors compare solutions in terms of Sharpe ratios, profits, and computing times, finding that D‑Wave Hybrid and the tensor-network method can handle the largest problem sizes—up to 1272 fully connected binary variables—while achieving competitive risk–return profiles. D‑Wave Hybrid solves the largest instance in about 171 seconds, and the tensor-network optimizer, though slower, reaches similar scale. However, they observe that minimizing the encoded energy (Hamiltonian) does not always coincide with maximizing realized profit or Sharpe ratio, and no single algorithm or hardware platform emerges as clearly best across all metrics or system sizes.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-029, C-032, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical optimization methods, implemented explicitly as baselines, sometimes outperform quantum and quantum-inspired approaches on certain financial metrics; in particular, the Gekko solver is reported as having remarkably strong performance, occasionally exceeding the quantum methods depending on the Sharpe or return metric. At the same time, Gekko faces a scalability limitation, hitting a memory wall around 500 binary variables, whereas D‑Wave Hybrid and tensor networks scale further to 1272 variables, highlighting a trade-off between solution quality and problem size among classical versus quantum(-inspired) solvers.
    [codes: C-014, C-030, C-031, C-005, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize several limitations: the discrete dynamic portfolio problem is NP-hard in generic cases, constraining exact optimality for large instances even with advanced solvers. Gate-based VQE on current universal quantum processors like IBM-Q is described as struggling to handle optimization problems of commercially relevant dimensionality, necessitating aggressive dimensionality reduction, and the need for clustering-based preprocessing is explicitly limited to methods and hardware that cannot handle the full problem. Classical solvers such as Gekko encounter a memory wall at around 500 qubits/variables, limiting their scalability. More conceptually, the authors note that the Hamiltonian energy minimum does not always align with maximized profit or Sharpe ratio, indicating an intrinsic misalignment between the mathematical objective and practical financial performance.
    [codes: C-013, C-033, C-025, C-031, C-029, C-007]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors suggest that their tensor-network optimizer could be made substantially faster, estimating at least a ~100× runtime improvement with better implementation and hardware. They also propose that hybrid combinations of quantum processors with tensor-network techniques could be particularly effective for many complex problems, indicating a direction toward even more tightly integrated quantum–classical and quantum-inspired workflows.
    [codes: C-035, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to provide the first open, systematic comparison of multiple quantum and quantum-inspired optimizers, implemented on different hardware platforms, on a realistic dynamic portfolio optimization task using multi-year real market data. Within this benchmark, they state that, for the first time in this financial context, a tensor-network-based optimizer is applied, expanding the toolbox beyond standard quantum and classical approaches.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-009]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a real dataset of daily prices for 52 assets over 8 years, preferring log returns to raw returns and applying filtering to discard assets with both below-average variance and returns, reducing the universe to 28 assets. They apply hierarchical clustering of asset return series, choosing around 6–8 clusters, and only use this dimensionality reduction for methods and hardware that cannot handle the full problem, later unfolding clustered positions back to assets. The dynamic setup uses monthly rebalancing with covariance matrices estimated over a 20‑day window, and experiments are conducted at multiple problem scales (XS–XXL) with a fixed risk-aversion parameter γ=1. Structural properties of the Hamiltonian—being diagonal in time—enable optimization at each rebalancing step independently, and the discrete problem is cast as a classical Hamiltonian/QUBO instance, aligning with standard quantum-optimization formulations.
    [codes: C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010, C-012]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors motivate their work by noting that dynamic portfolio optimization is in practice intractable in generic instances and that recent developments suggest quantum and quantum-inspired computing may help address such hard financial problems. They further observe that hybrid quantum–classical solutions, both in hardware and software, appear especially promising in terms of operational performance, even though they find no universally best algorithm or platform for large-scale dynamic portfolio optimization.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-037, C-036]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles portfolio optimization when assets are discrete or indivisible, noting that including such large, indivisible assets (e.g., real estate, NFTs, machinery) turns the task into an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem for classical computers, and that there is a pressing need for algorithms that can handle these complex COPs in financial computing. The formulation is based on the classical Markowitz mean‑variance model, converted into a QUBO representation that can handle multiple discrete decision variables and multiple asset types with different discretization schemes.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-012, C-013, C-014]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum‑classical hybrid annealing (QCHA) framework that is compatible with both quantum and classical paradigms, formulating the multiple‑discretization portfolio problem as a QUBO that includes budget and cardinality constraints via penalty and slack-variable encodings. QCHA operates by decomposing the large QUBO master problem into several subproblems, thereby leveraging quantum devices without being constrained by available qubit counts, and is implemented alongside D‑Wave quantum annealing and various classical solvers on two real‑market datasets. Assets are encoded using binary expansions for fungible continuous positions, discrete encodings for fungible discrete assets, and binary on/off variables for non‑fungible assets, with penalty coefficients tuned to balance feasibility with risk‑return optimization.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across backtests on two real‑world datasets, the QCHA hybrid algorithm is reported to outperform both classical methods and quantum annealing in terms of returns and risk metrics such as accumulated return (ACC), Sharpe ratio, and downside protection. On Dataset‑1 (stocks only), QCHA consistently leads other methods over the entire evaluation horizon and shows superior ACC and Sharpe ratio, while on Dataset‑2 (mixed assets), QCHA and Gurobi jointly dominate overall, with QCHA highlighted for its robust downside risk control and competitive returns. Scaling experiments indicate that increasing the number of qubits (i.e., binary variables) improves allocation precision and outcomes, with QCHA surpassing Gurobi already at a 40‑qubit setting and showing roughly linear performance gains with qubits on Dataset‑2, though all methods experience slight deterioration in performance when cardinality constraints are imposed, with QCHA degrading the least.

In Dataset‑1 backtests, QCHA’s net asset value trajectory (solid red line) is described as consistently superior to all other algorithms, and it attains better ACC and Sharpe ratio at the end of the period. For Dataset‑2, the narrative emphasizes that both QCHA and Gurobi dominate the other classical heuristics over time and that QCHA offers particularly strong downside risk protection, especially once constraints on the number of invested assets are enforced, where its performance drop is significantly smaller than that of tabu search and Gurobi.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations: hardware constraints on current quantum annealers mean that the pure QA approach is not applicable to the larger mixed‑asset Dataset‑2 because it exceeds the D‑Wave system’s qubit capacity, motivating the hybrid decomposition scheme instead. The authors also note that increasing the number of qubits, while beneficial for precision, poses challenges for present‑day quantum hardware and makes convergence harder. Methodologically, they recognize that adding cardinality constraints increases the complexity of the solution space by introducing more variables and structural limitations, which slightly reduces performance across all algorithms. Looking ahead, the authors stress that quantum hardware still requires substantial improvement in gate fidelity and qubit count before larger portfolios can be handled more directly and robustly.
    [codes: C-041, C-042, C-043, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose extending their framework to dynamic portfolio optimization that incorporates real‑time market data, which would require a dedicated time‑series modeling framework tailored to multiple discretization levels. They also argue that further advances in quantum hardware—especially higher qubit counts and improved gate fidelity—are necessary to handle larger, more realistic portfolios, and suggest that integrating machine learning techniques with quantum computing for portfolio problems is a compelling avenue for subsequent research.
    [codes: C-004, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047]

Within this framework, the authors show how to encode fungible continuous, fungible discrete, and non‑fungible assets, and to incorporate both budget and cardinality constraints in an integer‑coefficient QUBO. The experimental design uses two real‑market datasets—a short‑horizon Chinese stock set and a mixed‑asset set including private equity, mutual funds, and stocks—with asset‑type‑specific discretization schemes, and compares QCHA against a suite of classical and quantum baselines. === PAPER 470b798927ef (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum optimization for three combinatorial problems reformulated as QUBOs: a constrained portfolio optimization problem with the budget constraint enforced via a quadratic penalty term, a feature selection task that balances feature–target relevance against inter-feature redundancy, and a clustering task reduced to a Max-Cut problem on a dense graph (including applications to financial/credit data). The overarching framing is to understand how QAOA runtime scales with problem size on these QUBO-encoded tasks, with portfolio optimization as the main finance use case.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a linear-ramp variant of QAOA (LR-QAOA) where the many variational parameters of standard QAOA are reduced to two global parameters Δγ and Δβ that define linearly ramped angles across layers, motivated by observed smooth patterns in optimal QAOA parameters and an interpretation of QAOA as a discrete adiabatic schedule. They define the LR-QAOA quantum state and parameterization explicitly, and avoid full variational optimization by fixing these ramp schedules and then optimizing only the circuit depth p via minimizing an estimated total circuit depth D. A key methodological contribution is an extrapolation scheme that learns suitable Δγ, Δβ from optimized solutions on small random sub-instances, iteratively refining them via grid search and skew-Gaussian fitting and then extrapolating their scaling with N under an assumed linear log–log relation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For portfolio optimization, the authors report that LR-QAOA with extrapolated parameters achieves a smaller fitted exponential runtime scaling exponent (α ≈ 0.22) in total circuit depth than the chosen classical heuristic baseline, and that the success probability of obtaining the optimal solution remains approximately independent of problem size within the studied range, consistent with an earlier conjecture. In contrast, for feature selection the quantum runtime scales worse than classical (≈ 2^0.46N vs ≈ 2^0.2N), and for clustering LR-QAOA also fails to outperform classical baselines (α ≈ 0.25 vs α = 0.061), though the extrapolated parameters generally match those found by full grid search except for some outliers at particular sizes. The paper thus finds problem-dependent behavior, with an indicative scaling advantage only for portfolio optimization in the simulated regime.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-031, C-035, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Quantum runtime is explicitly benchmarked against several classical solvers whose runtimes on the same QUBO instances are empirically fitted to exponential models, with MQLib/Burer2002 chosen as the main comparison baseline because other solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Goemans–Williamson) exhibit heterogeneous scaling, discontinuities, or frequent failures to find the optimum. The authors find that different classical methods have markedly different scaling behaviors across portfolio optimization, feature selection, and clustering, and they emphasize that for feature selection and clustering the tested classical methods still scale better than LR-QAOA, whereas for portfolio optimization LR-QAOA’s fitted exponent beats the MQLib/Burer2002 baseline but not all commercial solvers in all regimes.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-035, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations: some classical solvers like Goemans–Williamson often fail to find the optimum, and commercial solvers may change their search behavior unpredictably, complicating fair scaling comparisons. For the quantum side, the authors note that the extrapolation scheme is less stable for feature selection and exhibits outlier behavior for some clustering sizes, indicating fragility of the learned schedules on certain problem classes. Crucially, they state that the cost of finding optimized circuit parameters is not included in their quantum runtime metric, even though the extrapolation-based analysis still grows with problem size, and they position their study as assessing LR-QAOA potential under the assumption that good parameters are already known or can be found efficiently. They further highlight that their observations regarding success probability and conjectured polynomial scaling are based on relatively small problem sizes (up to N = 28), so the exponential-versus-polynomial scaling question remains unresolved.
    [codes: C-021, C-022, C-023, C-038, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors call for extending the analysis to larger problem sizes beyond N = 28 to clarify whether LR-QAOA can achieve polynomial-time scaling for some combinatorial optimization problems, explicitly flagging the broader open question of whether quantum optimization can yield polynomial-time solutions in such settings. They also propose that methods based on extrapolation and scaling of circuit parameters with increasing problem size are a promising direction for future research on QAOA parameter setting and should be further developed and tested.
    [codes: C-043, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is the development of an extrapolation-based method to set the two parameters of a linear-ramp QAOA schedule using optimized solutions from small sub-instances, thereby largely avoiding expensive variational optimization while evaluating QAOA runtime scaling on multiple combinatorial problems. Building on observed smooth patterns in optimal QAOA parameters and a prior conjecture about constant optimal-solution probability under fixed linear ramps, the authors claim to systematically address the formerly unresolved problem of how to find suitable linear-ramp parameters and to demonstrate, in simulation, an indicative scaling improvement over a classical heuristic for portfolio optimization.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study defines quantum runtime as the median total circuit depth over all circuits needed to find the optimum, combining QAOA depth and required shots, and optimizes QAOA depth p by minimizing this estimated depth. The parameter extrapolation protocol is described in detail: random sub-instances of increasing size are sampled, grid search over Δγ and Δβ is iteratively refined via fitting a multivariate skew Gaussian to the success-probability landscape, and then the inferred optimal parameters are extrapolated under a linear log–log assumption. The classical benchmarking is also systematically designed, with multiple sampled instances per size, repeated runtime measurements, and robust log2-linear fits to estimate scaling exponents, while noting solver-dependent irregularities and failures. The authors frame their work as an exploration of LR-QAOA’s potential under an idealized assumption that suitable parameters can be efficiently obtained, and conclude that extrapolation and scaling-based parameter strategies appear promising but still require further validation.

=== PAPER 4a6b7f9ddc5a (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses online portfolio selection framed as a sequential decision problem, where a portfolio vector is updated over time in response to adversarially chosen price relatives while maintaining simplex constraints. The setting is an online optimization problem with provable guarantees that hold even when an adversary knows the algorithm’s strategy, and the authors build on a multiplicative-weights/exponentiated-gradient style formulation suited to later quantum implementation. The quantum version assumes online access to price-relative information via oracles to support these updates.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum method is obtained by stepwise transforming a multiplicative-weights-based online portfolio algorithm into a quantum version, first via a sampling-based classical variant, then an approximate inner-product version, and finally a fully quantum algorithm. The final algorithm relies on quantum arithmetic circuits to compute update quantities, quantum state preparation combined with ℓ1-norm estimation to represent portfolio vectors implicitly, and quantum inner-product estimation and quantum multi-sampling (amplitude-amplification–type primitives) to implement the exponentiated-gradient updates and trading decisions under the online gain-oracle model. The authors also explicitly use a union bound to coordinate success probabilities across these quantum subroutines.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The quantum algorithm claims a quadratic speedup in the number of assets n relative to a classical approximate counterpart, with total runtime scaling as Õ(T³√(n/r_min) log^{1.5}(1/δ)) and regret only worse than the original full-information baseline by a constant factor. Both the classical sampling-based and quantum algorithms achieve transaction costs that are independent of n due to sampling, while preserving regret bounds that are close to those of the full-investment algorithm, supported by a general convergence result for approximate ("erroneous") updates under specified inner-product and normalization error tolerances. The paper also reports explicit regret and runtime bounds for the intermediate sampling-based and approximate-classical algorithms, showing how regret constants increase (e.g., from Algorithm 1 to the sampling-based and then to classical and quantum approximate variants) while enabling improved transaction-cost scaling and eventual quantum runtime advantages in n.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-007, C-009, C-012, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The work starts from a classical online portfolio algorithm by Helmbold et al. that uses linear time and space in the number of assets to update the portfolio at each step, and then introduces a sampling-based classical variant whose transaction cost is independent of n while incurring higher runtime and a slightly larger regret constant. An approximate classical version further relaxes inner-product computations via sampling-based estimation, again increasing the regret constant, and serves as the immediate baseline for the quantum algorithm, which achieves a quadratic speedup in n while maintaining a regret bound larger than that of the original full-information Algorithm 1 only by a small factor. Across these variants, the authors systematically compare regret bounds, runtime complexity, and transaction-cost scaling to clarify what aspects are improved (e.g., transaction cost independence of n and quantum speedup in n) and what aspects degrade (e.g., regret constants and T-dependence in runtime).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-007, C-009, C-012, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that constructing the required price-relative oracles is a practical bottleneck for their quantum algorithm, suggesting that the oracle model may be difficult to realize in practice for real financial data. They further note that building a QRAM for each oracle entails O(T n log n) time and O(T n) space, highlighting substantial implementation overheads that could dominate the purported speedup and limit real-world applicability.
    [codes: C-014, C-034]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the paper suggests extending the online portfolio optimization framework to include additional constraints beyond the unconstrained setting considered, and exploring robust optimization variants. Specifically, the authors mention investigating different flavours of robustness—constraint, objective, and relative robustness—combined with various uncertainty sets as promising directions.
    [codes: C-035, C-036]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main contribution is a quantumized version of a classical online portfolio optimization algorithm by Helmbold et al., obtained through a structured, step-by-step transformation that introduces sampling and approximation before quantization. The novelty lies in showing that, under an online gain-oracle model, quantum inner-product estimation, quantum multi-sampling, and quantum state preparation can be combined to achieve a quadratic speedup in n while keeping regret close to that of the original algorithm and transaction cost independent of n, and in formalizing an erroneous update framework that guarantees convergence under controlled approximation errors. The work is also positioned against prior quantum finance research as addressing an online, unconstrained portfolio selection setting, complementing earlier quantum algorithms for unconstrained portfolio problems.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-024, C-026, C-030, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is entirely theoretical and proceeds in a carefully staged way: it first reformulates the classical multiplicative-weights portfolio update in an exponential-cumulative form amenable to quantum implementation, then introduces a sampling-based classical algorithm, then an approximate classical variant using sampling-based inner-product estimation with explicit multiplicative error tolerances, and finally a quantum algorithm that replaces classical subroutines with quantum versions. The analysis defines precise error models for approximate inner-product and normalization computations, proves regret and convergence bounds under those error parameters (including separate parameter regimes), and carefully aggregates success probabilities across subroutines using a union bound. However, no empirical datasets or numerical experiments are used; the setting is abstract and adversarial, with data accessed via oracles under bounded price relatives, and portfolio vectors in the quantum algorithm are not stored explicitly but represented implicitly via state-preparation and arithmetic circuits, which enhances theoretical space efficiency but leaves implementation-level reproducibility dependent on oracle and QRAM assumptions.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-013]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Beyond the main algorithmic and theoretical developments, the paper notes that the quantum algorithm does not need to store portfolio vectors explicitly at each time step, which it highlights as a space-efficiency property facilitated by the quantum representation and arithmetic circuits. This point complements but is somewhat orthogonal to the primary focus on regret, runtime, and transaction-cost bounds.
    [codes: C-013]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses a real‑world financial problem of predicting cross‑sectional stock returns for portfolio construction, focusing on Japanese equities in the TOPIX500 universe. It formulates the task as a cross‑sectional prediction problem where firm‑level features are used to forecast next‑period returns, enabling portfolio backtesting over a 10‑year horizon. Quantum and quantum‑inspired machine learning models are applied to this cross‑sectional stock return prediction setting alongside classical benchmarks.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-014, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs quantum circuit learning, described as a variational supervised quantum neural network, where inputs are normalized and encoded into quantum states and the output is obtained as the expectation value of a Pauli Z observable on the first qubit. It also uses a quantum‑inspired tensor network approach based on matrix product states, constructing a regression model whose MPS tensors serve as trainable variational parameters. Both quantum and tensor models are optimized with stochastic gradient descent, and gradients for the quantum circuit are computed via the parameter‑shift rule.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-008]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across the full backtest, the tensor network model achieves the best portfolio performance, delivering superior excess return and information ratio compared with all benchmarks, despite having the fewest parameters. The quantum neural network (QCL) is overall inferior to classical neural networks in risk‑adjusted excess return, though it attains excess returns competitive with them at the cost of higher tracking error. Performance is time‑varying: before 2016 QCL behaves similarly to linear regression, but after 2016 it outperforms the linear model, and in the latest market environment both the quantum and tensor models outperform classical neural networks, while neural networks perform particularly poorly in the last three years.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-047]

The quantum neural network underperforms neural networks over the entire period in risk‑adjusted terms but remains competitive in excess return and eventually surpasses linear regression after 2016. The authors interpret the superior performance of quantum and tensor models over linear regression as indicating an ability to learn nonlinear relationships, while neural networks appear prone to overfitting and fail to adapt in the latest market regime.

The quantum experiments are conducted in a noiseless simulation, so no hardware noise or error‑correction issues are addressed, and the work is situated in the NISQ era where full‑scale error correction is not yet available. The authors also acknowledge that their hypothesis about quantum techniques better controlling overfitting is unconfirmed and requires further examination, and they note that it is unknown whether the observed superiority of tensor networks would persist with more features and parameters.

=== PAPER 53cdbb737343 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses Markowitz-style mean–variance portfolio optimization and notes that traditional classical methods struggle with the computational complexity of large, diverse portfolios. It formulates the problem as a QUBO, where binary variables indicate asset inclusion/exclusion and the objective trades off expected return and variance, then maps this QUBO to an Ising model suitable for quantum algorithms. The authors emphasize that QUBO problems become particularly challenging for classical resources as problem size scales, motivating a quantum-oriented formulation.
    [codes: C-005, C-011, C-012, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses quantum optimization algorithms targeting QUBO/Ising formulations, specifically QAOA and VQE in a hybrid quantum–classical setting. The cost Hamiltonian encodes portfolio variance and expected returns, a mixer Hamiltonian based on Pauli-X operators promotes exploration, and the QAOA ansatz alternates cost and mixer unitaries while a classical optimizer iteratively tunes parameters. In their implementation, the QAOA circuit itself serves as the ansatz within a VQE framework, with the classical component updating variational parameters based on Hamiltonian expectation values.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that GPU-accelerated quantum simulation via CUDA Quantum significantly outperforms traditional CPU-based simulations in execution speed for the portfolio optimization task, with the performance advantage increasing as the number of assets grows and demonstrated empirically up to 30 assets. Timing results show that CPU simulation time remains relatively stable at small sizes but rises sharply beyond about 15 assets, while GPU time stays comparatively flat up to around 27 assets before exhibiting a spike, indicating substantial gains but also the onset of increased computational cost at larger scales. They interpret the inflection in GPU timing as evidence of rapidly growing combinatorial complexity as asset count increases.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper explicitly compares GPU-based quantum simulation to CPU-based simulation of the same quantum portfolio optimization algorithm, finding that CUDA Quantum on GPUs "significantly outperforms" traditional CPU runs in computational speed. The results figures show CPU runtimes relatively stable at low asset counts but increasing dramatically after about 15 assets, whereas GPU runtimes maintain a consistent advantage, with only minimal increases up to the mid-20s in asset count and a more moderate rise at the same thresholds, illustrating a clear empirical speed advantage of GPU-accelerated simulation over classical CPU simulation for this workload.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-012, C-018, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that access to real quantum hardware with many low-noise qubits and deep circuits remains challenging, so their work relies on simulators rather than physical devices. They also state that the current GPU-accelerated implementation, although showing substantial benefits, needs rigorous testing across more diverse scenarios to assess robustness and versatility, and they note observed anomalies in execution time for certain asset counts that require deeper investigation to understand their causes and implications.
    [codes: C-007, C-015, C-017, C-043, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work proposed by the authors includes evaluating performance on multi-GPU systems and extending experiments to multi-node architectures to study distributed scalability of the quantum simulations. They also plan further analysis using TensorNet, suggesting exploration of alternative or more advanced simulation backends to better understand and potentially extend the performance characteristics observed.
    [codes: C-044, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to illustrate the transformative potential of integrating quantum optimization algorithms with GPU computing to tackle portfolio optimization, positioning GPU-accelerated quantum simulation as a powerful approach when real quantum hardware is limited. They present empirical evidence, for portfolios up to 30 assets, that CUDA Quantum can deliver substantial performance gains in simulating hybrid QAOA/VQE-style portfolio optimization compared to CPU-based simulators, thereby highlighting the practical value of such accelerated simulators in the NISQ era.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study operates entirely on quantum simulators, justified by limited access to sufficiently powerful quantum hardware, and emphasizes the critical role of simulators—particularly GPU-accelerated ones—in the NISQ era. The authors use real-market data: 30 stock tickers chosen to span multiple industries, with adjusted closing prices over a two-year window from Yahoo Finance, processed into log returns, mean returns, and a covariance matrix, which is also visualized as a heatmap. They implement the portfolio QUBO, perform QUBO-to-Ising conversion, and then run hybrid QAOA/VQE circuits within NVIDIA’s CUDA Quantum and cuQuantum ecosystem, leveraging GPU parallelism to enhance simulation efficiency and scalability; however, while they provide qualitative runtime curves and describe asset-count ranges, they do not detail anomaly diagnostics or robustness tests and explicitly note the need for broader scenario testing.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The background sections emphasize that quantum computing is framed as offering "groundbreaking" processing capabilities for hard optimization problems, and that algorithms like QAOA, VQE, and quantum annealing have been developed specifically to attack QUBO-based combinatorial optimization. The authors also repeatedly stress that mean–variance portfolio optimization, and the associated covariance structure of asset returns, underpins concepts like the efficient frontier in modern portfolio theory.

The authors also cite Google’s 53‑qubit Sycamore random-circuit-sampling demonstration as an empirical indication of quantum advantage feasibility and explain that QKD can detect eavesdropping due to fundamental quantum principles.

  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts quantum and classical capabilities conceptually rather than via new benchmarks: it argues that quantum computers, leveraging qubits, superposition, and entanglement, can tackle computations intractable even for the most powerful classical supercomputers, especially as classical computation approaches its limits. It notes that Shor’s algorithm threatens classical public-key cryptosystems like RSA and ECC, motivating post-quantum cryptography, and defines quantum advantage as solving tasks infeasible for classical supercomputers, using Google’s Sycamore experiment as a debated but indicative example. In applications, it states that quantum simulation can directly capture molecular behavior whereas classical supercomputers can only approximate this at prohibitive cost.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge several major limitations and challenges. At the physics level, environmental interactions cause decoherence that destroys fragile superposition and entanglement, with qubits being highly sensitive to noise; quantum error correction is essential but resource‑intensive, and practical scaling is constrained by the need to integrate millions of qubits to reach fault-tolerant systems. They underscore that algorithmic progress lags behind hardware and that NISQ-era variational methods face issues such as barren plateaus. The paper also notes that experimental claims of quantum advantage, exemplified by Google’s Sycamore demonstration, remain debated, underscoring that real-world quantum advantage over classical supercomputers is not yet definitively established.

It also points to prospective application areas such as finance, where quantum optimization (e.g., via QAOA and quantum Monte Carlo) may in the future enhance portfolio optimization, derivatives pricing, and risk simulations, and suggests materials design and energy applications as promising domains for quantum simulation.

=== PAPER 596d3496c56c (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum architecture design as a critical bottleneck for variational quantum algorithms, where traditional human-driven search is constrained by limited expertise and cognitive bias, and positions portfolio optimization and other combinatorial finance/optimization tasks by mapping them into quadratic problems and then to Ising Hamiltonians suitable for VQE-style treatment. Problems are encoded into text prompts that describe the task and requirements, GPT‑4 proposes structures, GPT‑3.5 translates selected designs to QASM, and the circuits—constrained to fixed blocks and qubits per block—are trained and evaluated on TorchQuantum and Qiskit Runtime backends, including noisy IBM device models; LLMs also act as controllers for classical optimization and for generating parameter-initialization heuristics in chemistry VQE tasks.

On chemistry benchmarks, QGAS achieves slightly better results than the problem‑specific UCCSD "golden" ansatz and performance comparable to the QuantumNAS architecture search baseline, while in a noisy MNIST classification setting its performance is worse than QuantumNAS but still significantly better than randomly generated ansätze.

They report that performance gains via increasing gate counts and depth saturate and then reverse once a threshold is exceeded, and that conveying realistic quantum noise environments to GPT remains difficult, which reduces QGAS’s adaptability on noisy hardware. More broadly, they caution that public quantum‑computing information used to train GPT‑like models can be misleading, that current GPT cannot think dynamically about quantum physics to design genuinely new algorithms, and that it loses coherence and may contradict itself in long conversations; these issues collectively limit its reliability as an autonomous quantum‑architecture designer.

=== PAPER 5a5bcd7b5e90 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies failures of adiabatic quantum optimization (AQO) caused by anticrossings with exponentially small gaps between eigenstates associated with global and local minima, which make AQO inefficient on hard optimization problems such as maximum independent set (MIS) formulated as an Ising Hamiltonian where maximal independent sets are local minima and maximum independent sets are global minima. The authors’ objective is to design a heuristic algorithmic path (via parameter tuning) that avoids such detrimental local–global perturbative crossings in general problems. Although evaluated on MIS, the broader framing concerns the generic dependence of AQO success on minimum gap scaling and the structural role of clusters of nearby local minima in creating small gaps.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a heuristic adiabatic quantum algorithm that iteratively eliminates exponentially small gaps arising from local–global anticrossings by tuning single‑qubit tunnelling strengths. In each iteration, they deliberately run the AQO evolution non‑adiabatically so that the system is driven into excited states; sampled bitstrings from these fast runs reveal which local minima are being reached, and this information is then used to penalize pathways to those minima by adjusting the initial Hamiltonian, specifically by reducing Δi more strongly on qubits with higher estimated contributions to the problematic curvature. The update is implemented via a weighted geometric averaging rule for Δi that preserves some memory of past penalties, and the overall procedure consists of a repeated anneal–sample–classical‑update loop whose classical processing step (computing penalties from samples) can be done in O(r n²) time per iteration.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On analytically motivated grounds, the paper notes that perturbative anticrossings can cause the minimum gap to decrease exponentially with the Hamming distance between local and global minima, and that first‑order corrections vanish whereas second‑order corrections are always negative for minima, so large clusters of mutually nearby minima can create strong negative curvature leading to anticrossings. Using specially generated 64‑qubit MIS instances with a unique MIS and between 10^5 and 10^6 highly degenerate local minima, quantum Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed algorithm can trivially solve all hard instances in roughly 10 iterations, with all 50 difficult instances solved within 13 iterations and an overall average of about 3 iterations. The simulations further indicate that repeated penalization iterations progressively move the anticrossing earlier in the schedule or effectively remove it, which is visible in diagnostics of ground‑state magnetization, and the authors conclude that their adiabatic algorithm is effective at eliminating extremely small gaps caused by clusters of local minima.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-010, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present a direct performance comparison between the proposed AQO‑based heuristic and classical optimization algorithms; instead, classical computation is used as a subroutine for tasks such as computing update quantities and generating hard MIS instances. The authors do, however, briefly mention that certain assumptions common in previous AQO scaling studies may be questionable, implicitly positioning their algorithm as addressing issues not handled by those prior (partly classical‑inspired) analyses rather than as a head‑to‑head competitor to specific classical solvers.
    [codes: C-013, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and trade‑offs. First, they note that their procedure for generating extremely hard MIS test instances, which relies on iteratively modifying graphs to enforce a unique MIS and many local minima, requires time exponential in the number of nodes when the desired MIS size scales linearly, limiting instance generation to moderate graph sizes. Second, they state that naive generation of uniform random graphs would not reliably produce instances with extremely small gaps, highlighting a reliance on targeted, non‑generic benchmarks. Third, they discuss a tuning‑parameter trade‑off: choosing a small value of the memory parameter β causes the Δi updates to be conservative and may require more iterations to escape a cluster of local minima, whereas larger β risks oscillatory behaviour, indicating potential inefficiency or instability in the update dynamics. Finally, they emphasize that previous work on random tunnelling strengths only established a non‑zero probability of finding a good path, without a constructive method to find such paths, which motivates but also bounds the generality of their current heuristic approach.
    [codes: C-029, C-032, C-044, C-016]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper does not explicitly outline formal future work directions, but by highlighting that prior results only showed a non‑zero probability of eliminating anticrossings via random tunnelling strengths without giving a constructive path‑finding method, and by positioning their own method as a heuristic for general problems, the authors implicitly suggest extensions toward more systematic or provably efficient ways to choose tunnelling parameters and to generalize their approach beyond the specific MIS setting and instance sizes studied.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core claimed contribution is a simple, constructive adiabatic quantum algorithm that adaptively tunes single‑qubit tunnelling energies to penalize pathways to clusters of local minima, thereby eliminating exponentially small gaps arising from perturbative anticrossings between local and global minima. Unlike earlier observations that random choices of Δi can sometimes remove such anticrossings, the authors design a heuristic algorithm that uses information gathered from non‑adiabatic runs to steer the system toward a favourable adiabatic path for general optimization problems.
    [codes: C-002, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study focuses on MIS instances mapped to an n‑qubit Ising Hamiltonian via a standard binary‑to‑spin substitution, ensuring that maximal independent sets correspond to local minima and maximum independent sets to global minima. The authors use low‑order perturbation theory to analyze energy level crossings and estimate curvatures, which then guide their parameter‑update rule based on sampled local minima. Their experimental design employs specially constructed 64‑node graphs guaranteed to have a unique MIS of fixed size and between 10^5 and 10^6 highly degenerate local minima, because uniform random graphs would rarely yield sufficiently small gaps; this targeted generation is itself computationally expensive and tailored to produce hard instances. Simulations are carried out with quantum Monte Carlo using annealing schedules and energy scales extracted from superconducting flux qubits, and a clear operational success criterion is defined in terms of anneal time and success probability over 500 runs per iteration. The authors also describe the classical computational cost of the update step, noting it scales as O(r n²), which aids reproducibility and complexity assessment.
    [codes: C-011, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper includes a broader methodological critique by noting that several common assumptions in prior studies of AQO scaling are often made and may not always hold, which motivates their focus on perturbative anticrossings and parameter tuning. They also cite prior work showing that changing free parameters in MIS encodings can significantly increase the minimum gap and that choosing non‑uniform tunnelling strengths at random can sometimes eliminate problematic anticrossings, contextualizing their own contribution within this line of research.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is relevant to portfolio_optimization because it studies how to avoid exponentially small gaps by tuning problem encodings and single-qubit tunnelling strengths, which is directly analogous to improving quantum optimization paths for portfolio selection and rebalancing formulations. Its main value for this silo is the iterative anneal-sample-update idea, which suggests a way to adaptively steer hard portfolio instances away from clusters of poor local optima.
    [silo_relevance_score: medium]

    [codes: C-002, C-023, C-043  dim_source: dimension_2]

=== PAPER 5a9835a859bf (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses mean-variance portfolio optimization for diversified investment, using expected returns and the covariance matrix of asset returns to construct long-only, fully invested portfolios with various objectives such as minimum volatility, maximum return, maximum Sharpe ratio, and multi-objective risk–return trade-offs. For quantum computation, the problem is reformulated as a binary asset-selection task where asset weights become binary variables and the objective is encoded as a QUBO energy function suitable for a quantum annealer.
    [codes: C-009, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use quantum annealing as a meta-heuristic optimizer by casting the portfolio problem into a QUBO model, where each asset is represented by a binary variable indicating selection. The QUBO energy function encodes the mean-variance objective with Qii terms proportional to negative expected returns and Qij terms equal to covariances; long-only and full-investment constraints are enforced by normalizing the resulting binary-based weights, and the potential benefit is framed in terms of quantum tunneling helping to find global minima.
    [codes: C-011, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the backtests on nine ETFs show that the various mean-variance portfolio configurations behave as expected: minimum-return portfolios exhibit lowest volatility, maximum-return portfolios achieve highest returns, and maximum Sharpe ratio portfolios balance the two. The authors report that the binary multi-objective portfolio based on the QUBO formulation performs well despite its binary weights, suggesting potential for quantum computers in portfolio optimization, and also note observed patterns such as higher returns and higher volatility for equities and gold versus fixed income and that low-correlation assets like aggregate bonds and gold contribute to diversification.
    [codes: C-016, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-055]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: PortFawn implements several classical baselines, including market-cap-weighted, equal-weighted, minimum volatility, maximum return, maximum Sharpe ratio, and multi-objective portfolios for real-valued weights, and compares their backtested performance. The authors indicate that the binary multi-objective portfolio (intended for quantum annealing) performs "very well" relative to these classical formulations, and they highlight that many of the optimized portfolios, including classical ones, are highly correlated in their return series, while the equal-weight portfolio offers a practically attractive trade-off of acceptable return and volatility with simplicity.
    [codes: C-002, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly states that PortFawn is for educational and research purposes only and should not be used as an investment analysis tool. It acknowledges conceptual and practical limitations of mean-variance portfolios, including oversimplification by summarizing return data solely via expected returns and the covariance matrix and ignoring other information; unrealistic liquidity assumptions for some assets; omission of transaction and management costs; reliance on statistical assumptions such as i.i.d. returns whose validity must be checked for specific data; the often-poor predictive quality of expected returns; exclusion of dividends when computing returns; and a tendency to produce portfolios concentrated in a few assets. The authors also flag that a naive single-window backtest is an insufficient evaluation method, motivating their use of multiple overlapping rolling windows instead.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-038, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.

=== PAPER 5bd5a79bc18a (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the portfolio optimization problem, aiming to find an asset allocation that maximizes expected return while minimizing financial risk, with risk computed via portfolio diversification and subject to a full‑budget allocation constraint. This portfolio optimization problem (POP) is explicitly formulated to work on predicted future asset values rather than historical data, and is cast into a form suitable for a quantum annealer through a QUBO/Hamiltonian representation of return, risk, and budget terms.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The system uses a quantum annealing approach on D‑Wave hardware, encoding the POP as a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian H = αHA + βHB + γHC, where HA models expected return, HB encodes covariance-based risk, and HC penalizes budget violations. Binary variables are solved by the quantum annealer, and the solution is embedded in a three‑module architecture where the Quantum Computing Solver (QCS) works after the predicted‑data generator (PDG) and the Assets Universe Reduction (AUR) module, iteratively reducing the asset universe to fit NISQ‑era limitations before calling the quantum solver.
    [codes: C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report preliminary results at the module level: the Predicted Dataset Generation (PDG) module has been successfully tested using expert-provided predicted values, and the AUR + QCS modules have been jointly evaluated on a real dataset from Welzia Management over six constructed use cases, each run six independent times. The resulting portfolios and their metrics were reviewed and approved by domain experts after several technical meetings, and the authors emphasize that classical performance indicators like the Sharpe ratio alone are not sufficient to assess practical quality.
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Rather than a head‑to‑head algorithmic benchmark, the paper uses expert judgement as the primary comparison point: portfolios generated by the quantum‑based system are compared qualitatively to industry expectations and expert‑constructed portfolios, with experts approving the results after review. The authors also caution that relying solely on academic metrics like the Sharpe ratio can give overly triumphal conclusions that clash with real‑world industry behavior, underscoring that standard quantitative comparisons may not fully capture practical performance.
    [codes: C-035, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several limitations. At the hardware/method level, the AUR module is motivated by current NISQ‑era constraints such as finite qubit counts and noisy processes that affect quantum solver performance. Within the PDG module, there is a stated failure condition: if the required root for the bias fitting does not exist, PDG cannot find a good solution. At the system level, Q4FuturePOP is described as being in a prototypical development stage and has not yet been fully validated as an integrated end‑to‑end system. Finally, the authors note that academic performance measures like high Sharpe ratios can lead to triumphalist conclusions that may conflict with industry reality, due to market volatility that is difficult for a computer to perceive.
    [codes: C-023, C-032, C-033, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work includes completing the validation of the full Q4FuturePOP system as a unified workflow, fine‑tuning the parameters involved in generating the QUBO formulation of the POP, and evaluating additional quantum‑based solvers beyond the D‑Wave annealers currently used.
    [codes: C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contributions are a quantum computing‑based system for portfolio optimization (Q4FuturePOP) that operates on predicted future asset values instead of historical data, and an automatic Assets Universe Reduction (AUR) module designed to intelligently reduce the investment universe to mitigate quantum hardware limitations. The three‑module architecture (PDG, AUR, QCS) and the workflow that starts from the full asset universe, generates a future‑consistent dataset with matched covariance and expected returns, iteratively identifies a reduced subset A′, and then solves the POP on this subset using a quantum annealer are presented as key innovations.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper provides relatively detailed descriptions of the data and modeling pipeline: it distinguishes notation for historical versus predicted data, imposes specific constraints on generated future datasets (covariance matching and expected return matching), and uses a Cholesky‑based transformation and Taylor approximation within PDG to enforce these constraints. The evaluation protocol for AUR+QCS uses six use cases with six independent runs each, leveraging a proprietary real‑world dataset from Welzia Management and expert‑provided predictions, though the overall system is still labelled prototypical and lacks full validation. The authors explicitly stress the importance of expert involvement for interpreting results, noting that standard academic metrics like Sharpe ratio alone may not reflect industry realities.
