=== PAPER 75d6acf76068 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses quantum portfolio optimization, where accurate estimation of expectation values is crucial for reliable portfolio construction and Sharpe-ratio-based performance evaluation in financial applications. The portfolio optimization problem is formulated by mapping the Markowitz mean–variance model into an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes asset allocations, and whose expectation value is used as the optimization target but is distorted by NISQ noise. The authors frame the central problem as the impact of time-varying, spatially and temporally correlated hardware noise on these expectation values, which undermines financially meaningful optimization.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-014, C-020, C-026, C-027]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses a gate-based quantum portfolio optimization approach built on QAOA, where the portfolio objective is encoded as an Ising-type cost Hamiltonian and its expectation value is used as the variational objective under NISQ noise. Zero-noise extrapolation is employed as the core error-mitigation method: circuits are executed at multiple amplified noise levels via unitary folding and related control-scaling strategies, and the results are extrapolated to the zero-noise limit, with Richardson/polynomial extrapolation forming the static ZNE baseline against which the proposed method is evaluated.
    [codes: C-013, C-015, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-040, C-041, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors report that noise induces a measurable bias in benchmark expectation values, and that static ZNE can be unstable, even amplifying error in low-noise regimes and failing to generalize across circuit depths and noise profiles. The proposed ML-ZNE with a calibration-driven CNN–LSTM architecture is said to converge to near-zero training loss, consistently reducing absolute extrapolation errors compared to static ZNE, maintaining lower errors as circuit depth increases, and yielding higher Sharpe ratios in portfolio optimization experiments; these improvements are interpreted as enhanced stability and coverage of the quantum optimization process and better reliability for financial institutions.
    [codes: C-006, C-012, C-019, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily compares the ML-ZNE approach against static, polynomial/linear zero-noise extrapolation and unmitigated noisy optimization, treating these as the de facto classical or baseline mitigation strategies for NISQ devices. The authors claim that ML-ZNE achieves lower extrapolation error and improved Sharpe ratios relative to both static ZNE (including second-order polynomial fitting) and unmitigated execution, and they highlight that polynomial extrapolation, while sometimes stable for specific circuits, does not generalize well across varying depths and noise profiles, unlike the adaptive ML-based approach.
    [codes: C-004, C-015, C-018, C-037, C-040, C-050, C-051, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations of their ML-ZNE framework. They explicitly note that the CNN–LSTM model requires substantial training datasets across diverse noise scenarios, a demand that may be unfeasible on actual quantum hardware and limits practicality. They further state that model performance degrades when applied to different qubit topologies or noise regimes not represented in the training set, indicating limited generalization across devices and operating conditions. Additionally, they report that the noise-scaling and prediction process introduces latency (around 23 ms per prediction on their testbed), which they flag as problematic for high-frequency trading, constraining the method’s suitability to slower-rebalancing financial applications.
    [codes: C-057, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the paper proposes extending the ML-ZNE framework to larger-scale portfolios and exploring alternative neural architectures, such as reinforcement-learning-based or otherwise more scalable models, to improve adaptability and performance. The authors also suggest that quantum-inspired classical models could serve as interim or complementary techniques while hardware matures, and they outline potential new application domains—including more complex portfolio strategies, derivative pricing where expectation precision directly affects option values, and risk-parity allocations where improved Hamiltonian-term estimation may better preserve risk budgets under noise—which they see as promising avenues to test and refine their approach.
    [codes: C-060, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is a machine-learning-driven zero-noise extrapolation framework that replaces traditional static extrapolation with a data-driven, adaptive approach tailored to NISQ quantum finance. Specifically, the authors introduce an ML-ZNE method that dynamically estimates noise-free expectation values from sequences of noise-scaled measurements using a hybrid CNN–LSTM architecture that explicitly models both spatial and temporal correlations in hardware noise, incorporates real-time calibration data to refine noise-scaling factors, and is positioned as enhancing expectation-value accuracy, optimization stability, and portfolio reliability beyond what conventional ZNE can offer.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study builds a synthetic quantum calibration dataset by extracting per-qubit features (T1, T2, readout error, SX, CX) from a 27-qubit IBM FakeMontreal noise model, forming 27×5 feature matrices and adding Gaussian perturbations over ten time steps to simulate temporal drift; 100 such samples are used to train the CNN–LSTM, which is optimized with Adam for 100 epochs to map noisy to ideal expectation values in a supervised manner. Quantum noise is modeled via a Qiskit Aer density-matrix simulator using a measured FakeMontreal noise profile including decoherence and gate and readout errors, and QAOA-based portfolio Hamiltonians derived from a long-horizon financial dataset are used to assess portfolio performance via Sharpe ratios; evaluation metrics include mean absolute error between mitigated and ideal expectations, comparative accuracy of adaptive versus static extrapolation, and generalization across circuit depths, with explicit baselines defined for static ZNE using fixed scaling factors and polynomial fitting. The authors also highlight that hardware noise characteristics, including their dependence on device parameters, act as important contextual factors influencing mitigation effectiveness, underscoring the need for calibration-informed modeling.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-021]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Beyond core methods and results, the authors emphasize that NISQ noise has both spatial and temporal correlations and that its profile can evolve over time due to environmental factors and calibration drift, reinforcing their motivation for adaptive mitigation; they also argue more broadly that error mitigation is essential on current devices to enable meaningful quantum finance applications and claim that improved estimation accuracy can enhance the stability and coverage of quantum optimization algorithms, which they frame as reducing the reliability gap for financial institutions considering quantum portfolio methods.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-010, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-012]

=== PAPER 76ee9fd77e4e (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles portfolio optimization by formulating both a risk parity (RP) model—minimizing pairwise deviations in risk contributions—and a mean–variance (MV) model as combinatorial optimization problems suitable for QAOAz-based quantum circuits. The RP objective is explicitly written as a double summation over squared deviations between assets’ risk contributions, which is then mapped to a Hamiltonian for quantum optimization.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-007, C-010, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ the Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOAz), a variant of QAOA tailored to general operators and constraints, with an alternating structure of problem and mixer unitaries to solve RP and MV portfolio models. They use an XY-mixer that preserves constant Hamming weight to enforce fixed-cardinality portfolio constraints and choose a ring-structured mixer to obtain shallower circuits. Higher-order (including quartic) Hamiltonian terms are implemented directly using a parity-check inspired construction, and a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm is integrated as a derivative-free classical optimizer whose fitness evaluation loop calls a quantum device.
    [codes: C-002, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-021]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For the RP setting, the PSO-enhanced quantum approach (PSO-QAOAz-RP) is reported to achieve significantly better portfolio optimization performance than several swarm-intelligence baselines and a non-PSO QAOAz-RP variant across eight portfolios, with consistently lower standard deviations indicating more stable optimization. The authors also note that the QAOAz-RP model alone attains better average optimization values than the classical baseline model on many portfolios. In the MV experiments, PSO-QAOAz-MV achieves the best average optimization values on six portfolios and exhibits markedly lower variability than competitor algorithms, with quantitative claims that it improves the approximation ratio over QAOA by about 54.79% and over plain QAOAz by about 15.38% on average.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-025, C-026, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The proposed PSO-QAOAz-RP is compared against classical swarm-intelligence algorithms ABC-LP, GWO, and GA, and is claimed to be significantly better for portfolio optimization on eight portfolios by all reported metrics, including approximation ratio and objective values. For the MV model, PSO-QAOAz-MV is contrasted with quantum baselines QAOA and QAOAz, and is reported to deliver higher approximation ratios—on average 54.79% better than QAOA and 15.38% better than QAOAz—highlighting an incremental improvement over existing quantum approaches. At the same time, the authors acknowledge that for certain portfolios (7–8) the quantum RP methods underperform some classical counterparts, which they associate with possible trapping in local optima.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-023, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The study explicitly notes that current quantum hardware limitations force experiments to very small problem sizes—only six specific stocks per portfolio are used to ensure feasibility—which constrains the scalability and realism of the tests. The authors also observe that for some portfolios (notably 7 and 8) their quantum RP methods perform worse than classical algorithms and suggest that the hybrid QAOAz-RP and PSO-QAOAz-RP may be prone to local optima. In addition, they state that quantum noise and hardware errors are not modeled in this work, so results are obtained under idealized simulation assumptions, and they acknowledge a short-term focus with no analysis of long-term market dynamics or external factors affecting portfolio performance.
    [codes: C-020, C-027, C-028, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future research, the authors propose extending quantum portfolio methods to handle both short- and long-term investment objectives, thereby incorporating longer horizon dynamics and broader market conditions. They also suggest exploring how QAOA and related quantum algorithms could be applied to a wider range of financial domains beyond the specific RP and MV portfolio problems studied here.
    [codes: C-036, C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its main contribution a novel QAOAz-based solution for the risk parity portfolio problem (QAOAz-RP) and an enhanced hybrid variant where PSO is used to optimize quantum circuit parameters, aiming to improve solution quality and stability. The authors further argue that using meta-heuristic optimizers like PSO is particularly effective when many variational parameters are involved, positioning their PSO-QAOAz designs for RP and MV as improved quantum heuristics over existing QAOA/QAOAz formulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-017, C-025, C-030]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study bases its empirical evaluation on real-market data across multiple regions: portfolios drawn from Chinese A-shares, U.S., European, and emerging markets, though each portfolio is restricted to six stocks due to hardware constraints. The quantum circuit depth is fixed at five, with this choice later justified as a reasonable trade-off between expressivity and resource limits, and PSO hyperparameters (number of iterations, particles, and inertia coefficient) are explicitly specified, with the authors arguing that ten iterations suffice to improve performance without excessive computation. An additional approximate ratio metric is introduced to better quantify optimization effectiveness, and the authors contend that meta-heuristic methods like PSO can search parameter space more efficiently than other gradient-free optimizers, implicitly supporting their hybrid design choice.
    [codes: C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also emphasizes that the RP model’s reliance on historical volatility rather than return forecasts can make allocations more robust relative to the traditional MV model, which serves as an additional motivation for considering RP in the quantum setting.

=== PAPER 78cc9d5068f3 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses constrained Markowitz-style portfolio optimization, aiming to minimize quadratic risk subject to target return, linear budget-type constraints, and non-negativity of asset weights, explicitly formalized as min xᵀMᵀMx s.t. μᵀx = R, Ax = b, x ≥ 0. The authors emphasize that, unlike the unconstrained case, this general constrained problem lacks a closed-form solution and thus requires algorithmic treatment. They frame this as a key application in mathematical finance where quantum computers could potentially offer significant speedups.
    [codes: C-005, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach reduces the constrained portfolio problem to a second-order cone program (SOCP) and then applies a quantum short-step interior-point method (IPM) for SOCPs as the main algorithmic engine. The quantum IPM builds on a recently developed quantum interior-point method, using quantum linear algebra with block encodings and QRAM-based data structures to solve the Newton linear systems sublinearly by encoding vectors as quantum states and then performing tomography to recover classical updates. Algorithmically, each iteration constructs a block encoding for the Newton system, solves it via a quantum linear system routine, and uses tomography-based estimation to obtain approximate Newton directions while maintaining strict feasibility of iterates.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-046]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main theoretical result guarantees that the algorithm outputs a portfolio whose objective value is within εr of the optimum and that satisfies inequality constraints exactly and equality constraints to precision δ, with a running time given as T = Õ(√r log(n/ε) · n κ ζ / δ² log(κζ/δ)). Both the classical and quantum interior-point methods converge in O(√r log(n/ε)) iterations, but the quantum per-iteration cost yields an overall scaling summarized as Õ(n¹․⁵ ζ κ / δ² log(1/ε)) and, under favourable conditioning, can constitute a significant polynomial speedup over the classical O(n³․⁵ log(n/ε)) algorithm. The authors also prove that approximate Newton updates preserve strict feasibility and decrease the duality gap by a constant factor, and that infeasibility of the final iterate is bounded by the tomography precision; empirically, they observe that worst-case condition number growth is not attained, that tomography precision requirements scale roughly linearly with n, and that for most tested instances the quantum algorithm exhibits an almost O(n) speedup with an empirically fitted complexity exponent supporting this behaviour.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The classical baseline is the short-step interior-point method for SOCPs, whose convergence to ε-duality gap is established with time complexity O(√r n^ω log(ν₀/ε)), often approximated as O(n³․⁵ log(n/ε)) in practice, and whose cost is dominated by solving dense linear systems. The quantum algorithm retains the same iteration count but replaces each classical solve with a quantum linear-system routine, leading to a runtime Õ(n¹․⁵ ζ κ / δ² log(1/ε)), which the authors argue yields a significant polynomial speedup when the Newton matrices are well-conditioned. Experiments further compare these scalings and suggest that, for most instances, the quantum method could achieve an almost O(n) speedup over its classical counterpart in terms of asymptotic complexity, although this is inferred from simulation-based complexity estimates rather than hardware timing.
    [codes: C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-041, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress that translating theoretical quantum speedups in mathematical finance into real-world use will require much more advanced hardware than currently available, highlighting a practical deployment limitation. They identify constraint handling as a key shortcoming of prior unconstrained quantum portfolio algorithms, motivating their more complex SOCP-based approach, and note that there is no closed-form solution for the general constrained problem, necessitating iterative algorithms. On the quantum side, they acknowledge that tomography introduces approximation error so that solutions may not be exactly feasible, with tomography cost scaling linearly in the state dimension and the final infeasibility directly tied to tomography precision. Their experimental setup also fixes ε at a relatively loose value, explicitly justifying this by arguing that financial market stochasticity dominates numerical error, which signals that their empirical study does not probe high-precision regimes.
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-013, C-026, C-031, C-039, C-048]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to develop the first quantum algorithm for the constrained portfolio optimization problem, extending prior quantum work that addressed only unconstrained formulations. The authors position their main technical contribution as a quantum SOCP interior-point method (Algorithm 2) tailored to the portfolio problem via reduction to SOCP, and they argue that under reasonable problem-dependent parameters this algorithm can attain a polynomial, potentially near-linear-in-n speedup over the best classical constrained-portfolio solvers.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-007, C-008, C-020, C-025, C-028, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is primarily theoretical but is supplemented by simulations on real-market portfolio instances where the authors solve a slightly simplified constrained Markowitz problem using historical S&P-500 data from the cvxportfolio repository. The experimental design emphasizes complexity-relevant quantities—such as condition number behaviour, tomography precision scaling, and fitted power-law exponents for average-case runtime—rather than wall-clock performance on actual quantum hardware. They explicitly fix the target precision ε in experiments, arguing that higher numerical accuracy is not justified given market noise, and they include an experimental caveat that this choice shapes the interpretation of their observed almost O(n) speedup.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-024, C-028, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes elaborate technical framing that does not fit neatly elsewhere: the authors explain that optimization problems with constraints generally require multi-step computations depending on the number of constraints; they define complexity parameters n and r for SOCP, describe how positivity and equality constraints are encoded via Lorentz cones in the SOCP standard form, and remark that quantum linear-algebra routines require efficient block encodings and QRAM data structures whose construction and update cost is assumed efficient. They also note that quantum algorithms represent vectors as quantum states, which underpins the need for tomography in their overall pipeline.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies large-scale dynamic portfolio optimization with realistic market frictions, including transaction costs and short selling, where dynamic trading strategies must adapt asset allocations over time under cash, budget, and asset-count constraints. The problem is framed as a discrete, NP‑hard optimization over binary selection trajectories across multiple periods, reformulated into a QUBO so it is compatible with both classical and quantum computing and allows precise measurement of solution optimality. The benchmark instances are sizable, reaching up to 499 stocks over 15 time steps with explicit modeling of risk–return trade-offs, transaction and short-selling costs, and path-dependent cash constraints.

They state that QAOA is specifically designed to solve QUBOs and implement a VQE-style algorithm using IBM Qiskit; in addition, they test quantum annealing on a D-Wave device and a quantum-inspired solver from InfinityQ as part of the benchmarking. The paper emphasizes that current quantum hardware cannot support many QAOA steps, and it uses the QUBO–Ising mapping mainly to create a comparable problem representation across digital, gate-based, and annealing-style quantum approaches.
    [codes: C-004, C-014, C-015, C-027, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]

ABS2 often converges faster than Gurobi to good solutions on harder settings, but their economic outcomes (e.g., holdings) can differ despite similar performance. On the larger 499‑stock, 15‑step benchmark, only digital methods are currently solvable; early in the run (e.g., 120 seconds), QUBO-based heuristics often achieve better objective values than the BQP formulation, but by 1,800 seconds their results converge. Economic metrics show that, for low q, Sharpe ratios from BQP and QUBO digital solutions are very close, while quantum and quantum-inspired solvers (D-Wave and InfinityQ) deliver significantly lower Sharpe ratios than digital algorithms. Overall, the authors conclude that with the current state of technology, substantially better quantum results are unlikely.
    [codes: C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054]

In the medium-scale experiment, Gurobi and ABS2 exhibit similar performance in easy regimes, while ABS2 converges faster on harder q values. In the large-scale benchmark, QUBO heuristics initially outperform BQP in early time-to-solution but converge to similar objectives over longer runs, and economic metrics such as Sharpe ratios show digital methods dominating quantum and quantum-inspired solvers. === PAPER 7b4b01100661 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: Within finance, the paper instantiates its general discrete-optimization framework on a portfolio rebalancing problem, modeling each asset’s position as a ternary discrete variable with states {long, no-hold, short} mapped to |0>, |1>, |2> and formulating the objective in terms of DQIR primitives. The authors emphasize that this is one of several benchmark application classes (alongside graph coloring, TSP, scheduling, and ILP) used to study encoding-dependent resource trade‑offs, rather than a production-scale financial model.
    [codes: C-004, C-045, C-055]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper develops a discrete quantum intermediate representation (DQIR) that is encoding‑independent, mapping classical discrete and qudit-valued variables to quantum levels and expressing objectives and constraints using indicator, value, and transfer primitives composed into multivariate operators and Boolean-logic-based Hamiltonians. On top of this representation, the authors design cost Hamiltonians and constraint penalties, along with families of mixers for QAOA-style algorithms—including single‑variable shift partial mixers, graph‑derived partial mixers (GDPMs), and permutation-preserving mixers—while supporting mixed encodings, hardware‑agnostic analysis, and automated lowering to specific qubit encodings.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-043, C-045, C-047, C-048, C-058]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that the compact, encoding‑independent DQIR representation simplifies compilation and enables richer programmability across diverse discrete optimization problems, including scheduling where the cost function can be written very compactly. Numerically, unary encodings typically yield the shortest-depth circuits for diagonal operators, but there are important classes (e.g., certain An and F_sum terms, scheduling at power‑of‑two cardinalities, and the portfolio-rebalancing Hamiltonian) where compact codes (standard binary and Gray) achieve over an order-of-magnitude lower depth and are preferred. Block unary frequently lies on the space–depth Pareto front, often between compact and unary encodings, and can be optimal for some hardware parameter regimes. For mixers, designed GDPMs in compact encodings up to d≈15 generally outperform naive product‑formula approximations, and compact GDPM mixers are often even shallower than unary mixers; gate-decomposition refinements further reduce depth for key controlled rotations. Overall, DQIR plus automated encoding screening show that encoding choice, including mixed encodings and penalty-exchange strategies, can significantly trade off circuit depth versus qubit count.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-022, C-031, C-039, C-041, C-044, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present explicit performance comparisons against classical optimization algorithms; its comparisons are intra‑quantum, across different encodings and mixer designs in terms of circuit depth and resource trade‑offs.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-049, C-051, C-053, C-055, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize several limitations and caveats. Penalty-based constraint enforcement with finite weights does not strictly preserve the feasible subspace, so feasibility can be violated unless post‑processing or large penalties are used, and linear-constraint penalties can lead to operators with many terms depending on matrix sparsity, making them resource‑intensive. Validity penalties for compact encodings can be prohibitively costly for non‑compact (e.g., unary) encodings due to the large number of required terms. For mixers, simple binary shift mixers are strict (leakage‑free) only when the domain size is a power of two, and strict permutation mixers in compact encodings are substantially harder to design and remain high-depth compared to unary, so permutation penalties and mixers can offset depth advantages seen in cost terms. The paper notes that one often must trade increased circuit depth for tighter leakage guarantees in approximate mixers, that pseudo‑Toffoli-style gate simplifications must be used with caution, and that their ILP formulations concentrate algorithmic complexity in the constraints rather than the objective.
    [codes: C-023, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-032, C-033, C-042, C-046, C-054]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors state that several important open directions remain, including understanding how encoding choices and mixer designs affect actual algorithmic performance metrics (such as solution quality and time-to-solution) rather than just circuit depth, and how hardware topology and connectivity constraints interact with these encoding trade‑offs.
    [codes: C-060]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing the DQIR framework—an encoding‑independent discrete intermediate representation with indicator, value, and transfer primitives and associated Boolean-logic constructions—that supports hardware‑agnostic preparation and manipulation of discrete optimization problems, automated conversion to multiple encodings (including qudits and mixed encodings), and systematic construction of penalties, mixers, and initial states. It further contributes a library of low‑depth, graph‑derived partial mixers (including permutation GDPMs) up to moderate variable cardinalities, gate-level decomposition improvements, and a toolkit that enables automated screening of encodings and reveals new cases where compact encodings are more QAOA‑friendly than previously thought.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-047, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is presented as a design and compilation toolkit rather than an end‑to‑end performance study: the authors implement a Python prototype of DQIR, use it to automatically generate and compile Hamiltonians and mixers, and measure logical circuit depth (often via exact exponentials of diagonal operators) across encodings. They rely on an all-to-all connectivity assumption and simulator-based compilation, focusing on depth and locality rather than noise or hardware-specific error models. The use of abstract benchmark problems (graph coloring, TSP, scheduling, ILP, and a stylized portfolio-rebalancing model) and compact DQIR expressions is intended to isolate encoding and mixer trade-offs; the authors explicitly highlight that DQIR enables automated comparison of many encoding options, while also acknowledging complexity growth in certain penalty constructions.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-008, C-014, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-051, C-052, C-056, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes elaborate technical features that complement but do not change the main storyline: the paper discusses that the original discrete domain is often smaller than the embedded Hilbert space introduced by encodings, motivating validity penalties and leakage analysis; emphasizes generality beyond qubits by allowing qudit-level variables; and notes that block unary and domain-wall-inspired encodings display characteristic bitmask structures affecting operator locality. It also formalizes strict versus approximate mixers, defines leakage as a quantitative metric of feasibility violation, and introduces the penalty-exchanging strategy (trading exact feasibility for depth reduction) as a general design pattern.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-014, C-018, C-020, C-022, C-028, C-029, C-034, C-037]

=== PAPER 7bdb6593ec48 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles bi-objective portfolio optimization where risk and return must be jointly balanced, arguing that conventional single-solution optimization struggles with large search spaces and diverse investor preferences, especially in high-dimensional, constraint-rich, cross-market settings (DJIA + Nikkei) that enlarge the solution space and complexity. The problem is formulated via a trend ratio (TR) model capturing temporal dynamics of risk and return, with integer allocation variables (0–100% per asset) and a budget constraint, and is scalarized into a single objective whose solutions approximate a Pareto front of non-dominated portfolios reflecting different investment strategies.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use quantum annealing within D-Wave’s hybrid constrained quadratic model (CQM) solver, emphasizing QA’s potential to escape local optima via quantum tunneling and CQM’s ability to encode constraints as equalities/inequalities without heavy penalty terms while scaling to thousands of variables and constraints. The bi-objective TR-based portfolio problem is reformulated into a CQM-compatible minimization by treating deviation risk as a positive term and deviation expected return as a negative term, then scalarized with a weight λ (stepped over a grid defined by Δλ) to generate multiple single-objective problems whose non-dominated solutions approximate the Pareto front; implementation details also include a share-calculation workaround to handle integer percentage allocations.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The proposed QA–CQM bi-objective framework is reported to produce high-quality, well-distributed Pareto-like sets, with experimental evidence that it consistently shows strong potential compared with conventional multi-objective algorithms, achieving the highest hypervolume and HV rate, the lowest IGD, and the largest number of non-dominated solutions in the 60-stock cross-market case. Cross-market portfolios are found to deliver the best overall results across markets, offering better quality and diversity than single-market portfolios, and the method is particularly effective at discovering numerous low-risk solutions that are otherwise hard to find; sensitivity analysis shows that smaller Δλ improves HV, HV rate, IGD, and solution count, though with diminishing returns, leading the authors to recommend moderate Δλ values (around 0.1) as a practical balance between quality and runtime.
    [codes: C-006, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-045, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Compared with classical multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, the hybrid QA–CQM approach is claimed to achieve superior overall performance in the cross-market scenario, with higher hypervolume and HV rate, lower IGD, and more non-dominated solutions, while also being characterized as effective and practical in terms of runtime. At the same time, the authors acknowledge that the non-dominated solutions produced by conventional algorithms remain highly competitive, particularly in the challenging 60-stock cross-market case, indicating that the advantage of the quantum-enhanced approach is quantitative rather than absolute.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-038, C-039, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper notes several limitations and challenges: traditional and classical multi-objective methods struggle with vast, high-dimensional portfolio search spaces and complex investment constraints, especially when moving to realistic settings, motivating but not eliminating such difficulties in their own approach. They highlight that multi-objective QA requires scalarization into a single objective, which implies dependence on weight selection and repeated runs, and report that finding solutions in the low-risk domain is challenging due to increased complexity, even though their method performs relatively better there. Parameter analysis shows that decreasing Δλ greatly increases runtime, with growth described as almost exponential, and that solution-quality improvement is not proportional to this runtime increase, revealing diminishing returns and a practical trade-off between granularity of the trade-off exploration and computational cost.
    [codes: C-008, C-010, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-040, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors position their work as among the first QA-based frameworks for bi-objective portfolio optimization, and specifically as the first application of quantum annealing to bi-objective weighted portfolio optimization. They claim novelty in combining a TR-based bi-objective weighted formulation with QA/CQM and a scalarization-based non-dominated analysis to generate Pareto fronts reflecting different investment strategies, and in extending this to cross-market (DJIA–Nikkei) settings for international diversification.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-020, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study grounds its formulation in the TR model, argued to better capture temporal dynamics of return and risk, and explains the detailed scalarization scheme using λ (including extreme and balanced settings and a grid over [0,1]) to systematically explore trade-offs. The evaluation constructs an approximate reference Pareto front via a combined non-dominated set (combined NDS) and assesses solution sets using standard MOO metrics—IGD for convergence and distribution quality and hypervolume/HV rate for dominated volume—while also conducting a self-analysis of Δλ to study the balance between solution quality and runtime, leading to a recommended moderate Δλ (≈0.1). The use of D-Wave’s CQM is justified both for flexibility over QUBO penalty encodings and for stated capacity to handle up to about 5,000 variables and 100,000 constraints, supporting claims of scalability to larger, more constrained problems.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-042, C-045, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates itself within the broader context of quantum finance as a promising interdisciplinary area, citing prior work showing QA’s effectiveness on TR-based portfolio optimization as a foundation for their extension to the bi-objective, cross-market setting. It also reiterates that the cross-market configuration provides meaningful international diversification benefits and that the hybrid solver yields high-quality, well-distributed solutions with favorable runtime characteristics.
    [codes: C-007, C-019, C-037, C-047, C-048]

Under realistic noise, however, QAOA optimization becomes highly unstable, with minimum energy deviations worsening as two‑qubit gate error rates increase and portfolio return errors degrading to the point of approaching a random, unoptimized baseline; noisy output distributions also lose any clear peak corresponding to the optimal bitstring. By contrast, the QITE‑based approach is found to be more robust on IBM hardware, yielding portfolio return errors that are typically modest (with F Error reported below 1 for some instances and ranging roughly from 1 to 6 over an additional 50 cases), while still preserving a clearly identifiable optimal bitstring in the measured distribution. Even in nominally noiseless simulations, they note that a finite number of circuit executions imposes intrinsic sampling error that prevents exact convergence to the ground state. Under more realistic noise, QAOA specifically is described as highly unstable, with its performance strongly degraded as gate error rates increase, and the algorithm also demands extensive quantum resources, typically requiring hundreds to thousands of circuit evaluations. For scalability, they explicitly omit noisy simulations for larger‑scale QAOA instances, acknowledging this as a scope limitation. In contrast, QITE’s main limitation is a shift of burden from quantum to classical computation, as it trades lower quantum cost for substantial classical optimization overhead.

=== PAPER 7c6e8af63f61 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles a constrained portfolio selection problem for direct indexing, formulated as a K-of-N cardinality-constrained choice of assets where exactly K names must be selected from N candidates. This is cast into a quantum-friendly form as a K-of-N selection (Hamming-weight–K) problem, with the objective encoded via a cost Hamiltonian over binary inclusion variables that represent the discrete portfolio choices.
    [codes: C-001, C-012, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hard-constraint QAOA variant that operates entirely within the feasible subspace by combining Dicke-state initialization with an XY-mixer that preserves Hamming weight, so only valid K-of-N portfolios are explored. The cost Hamiltonian encodes expected returns and covariances, and the algorithm uses a Trotterized, adiabatic-inspired warm-start schedule for QAOA parameters, with depth p varied from 1 to 6 and a readout filter that retains only sufficiently probable, feasible bitstrings for a second-stage continuous Sharpe-max allocation and HRP fallback when that optimization fails.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On a 10-asset 2025 backtest, the QAOA-XY approach achieved the highest total return (30.09%) and Sharpe ratio (1.81), with volatility of about 18.6% and a maximum drawdown of −8.27%, comparable in drawdown to the baselines. As circuit depth increased from p=1 to p=6, the optimized cost generally decreased (from −0.1488 to −0.5355) and gradient norms increased rather than vanishing, which the authors interpret as evidence that their Trotterized initialization mitigates barren plateaus. They also observe non-monotonic behavior at intermediate depths and that computational cost per iteration scales approximately linearly with depth, and qualitatively describe QAOA allocations as high-conviction and more rapidly reconfiguring over time compared to smoother HRP allocations.
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QAOA-XY strategy is compared against simulated annealing (SA) and hierarchical risk parity (HRP). In the 2025 backtest, QAOA-XY delivers the highest total return (30.09%) and a Sharpe ratio of 1.81, outperforming SA’s 24.17% total return and 1.31 Sharpe (a 38% Sharpe improvement) and HRP’s 10.88% total return and 0.98 Sharpe, while all three exhibit similar maximum drawdowns. HRP is highlighted as achieving the lowest volatility but at the cost of substantially lower returns, whereas the authors argue that classical heuristics like SA and genetic algorithms can get trapped in local minima, motivating their quantum approach and the use of HRP both as a robust allocation baseline and a fallback when the quantum or SA selector fails.
    [codes: C-004, C-007, C-008, C-016, C-018, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that the QAOA-XY strategy exhibits substantially higher average monthly turnover (76.8%) than SA (21.0%) and HRP (21.6%), creating a trade-off between theoretical optimality and practical implementation costs, and limiting applicability to liquid, low-fee markets rather than illiquid or high-cost segments. They also emphasize that their experiments are limited to N=10 assets and note that scaling to larger universes remains an open question, and that their results are obtained on a noiseless simulator, so testing on noisy hardware or realistic noise models is needed to assess robustness and real-world viability.
    [codes: C-005, C-033, C-034, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include incorporating turnover directly into the selection objective so that trading intensity becomes an explicit optimization target rather than a post hoc diagnostic, and more broadly treating turnover as a first-class objective in real-world deployments. The authors also call for systematic investigation of scalability beyond 10 assets and for implementing and testing their QAOA-XY ansatz on noisy quantum hardware or under realistic noise models to better understand sensitivity and practical performance.
    [codes: C-035, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The key contribution claimed is a hard-constraint QAOA tailored to the K-of-N direct-indexing problem, using Dicke-state initialization and an XY-mixer that strictly preserves Hamming weight so that feasibility is guaranteed by construction. In addition, the authors present a Trotterized, adiabatic-inspired parameter initialization scheme intended to avoid barren plateaus, and position their approach as a hybrid pipeline combining constraint-preserving QAOA selection, classical Sharpe-max allocation, and HRP fallback that behaves like a high-conviction, rapidly adapting discrete selection strategy.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-038, C-039]

The pipeline includes a continuity bonus to discourage excessive churn, explicit candidate filtering based on feasibility and minimum probability, and a two-stage procedure where discrete selections from QAOA or SA feed into a continuous Sharpe-max allocation with HRP fallback, indicating attention to practical portfolio construction and backtesting protocol design.
    [codes: C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors interpret their depth experiments in operational terms, suggesting p=3 as an appropriate operating point when rebalance time budgets are tight and p=6 when optimization can run offline or with relaxed latency constraints, connecting algorithmic settings to deployment modes. They also qualitatively describe QAOA-XY allocations as pronounced and high-conviction while HRP allocations remain smoother and more diversification-driven, which provides a practitioner-oriented interpretation of how the quantum strategy behaves relative to classical methods.

Across experiments, CMA-ES generally outperforms COBYLA in both success rate and convergence speed, with COBYLA failing to match CMA-ES even with substantially more iterations; the authors also observe optimizer–cost-function compatibility effects and consistency between success‑rate and sampling‑probability trends. In the appendix, they find that energy-based exponential weighting performs worst, rank-based exponential weighting works particularly well at large α, and a piecewise exponential version slightly but not significantly outperforms rank‑based weighting.

=== PAPER 7e636e790901 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets portfolio optimization, aiming to maximize revenue while minimizing risk over future time steps under a budget constraint, and maps this to an Ising-type cost Hamiltonian where the budget constraint is encoded as a penalty term in the objective function. The authors position this as a representative NISQ-era finance use case in the broader search for quantum advantage in financial applications.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ digitized counterdiabatic quantum optimization (DCQO) operated in the impulse regime, where counterdiabatic terms dominate the dynamics, and implement it as a gate-based protocol that can realize arbitrary CD terms not available on analog devices. They approximate the CD gauge potential using nested-commutator-based constructions, truncate the Trotterized evolution by neglecting late steps and gates with small rotation angles, and introduce a hybrid h-DCQO ansatz that keeps only the CD term with one variational parameter per CD operator. The approach starts from adiabatic evolution between mixer and problem Hamiltonians, extends prior CD-augmented QAOA schemes, and is digitally realized on fully connected trapped-ion hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that its DCQO-based protocols achieve substantial circuit-depth reductions—by factors between roughly 2.5× and 40×—while maintaining or improving solution quality, and that this makes the approach suitable for current quantum processors. In simulations, CD-only DCQO yields about a twofold enhancement in a mean-based approximation ratio compared with non-CD baselines at fixed depth, and seven DCQO Trotter steps (reduced to one step after gate cut-off) perform comparably to 80 steps of finite-time digitized adiabatic evolution. For the hybrid variant, a one-layer h-DCQO circuit achieves similar performance to a five-layer QAOA while requiring fewer layers to reach a given target accuracy, and real-hardware runs on up to 20 qubits on an IonQ trapped-ion device show that error-mitigation techniques can further boost the approximation ratio.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-028, C-039, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors benchmark their methods primarily against QAOA and finite-time digitized adiabatic evolution rather than purely classical optimizers, emphasizing that the CD-only and hybrid DCQO variants reach comparable or better approximation ratios at significantly reduced circuit depths. They highlight that h-DCQO, despite having similar parameter counts and more two-qubit gates per layer than standard QAOA, can match the performance of a five-layer QAOA using only one layer and overall fewer layers for a target performance threshold.
    [codes: C-005, C-018, C-019, C-027, C-028, C-035, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that standard QAOA exhibits discrepancies between theoretical proposals and hardware realizations due to depth and noise, motivating the search for more hardware-efficient approaches. It also notes hardware constraints such as a minimum reliably resolvable gate angle (e.g., 0.00628 on IonQ devices), which informs their gate-cutoff strategy, and concedes that further noise-suppression techniques beyond the employed error mitigation are needed to close the remaining performance gap between hardware and idealized simulations.

=== PAPER 7f8c8060e256 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the discrete global minimum-variance portfolio (DGMVP) problem, where asset positions are constrained to discrete trading lots, and seeks the portfolio of risky assets with the lowest possible risk under these discreteness and budget constraints. This financial optimisation task is mapped to a qubit-based Hamiltonian via a discrete formulation that enforces the number of traded assets and portfolio weights to be discrete binary-encoded variables.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-014]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors design an end-to-end QAOA tailored to the DGMVP, using a dense cost circuit with depth scaling linearly in the number of qubits and a custom hard mixing operator that preserves the portfolio budget constraint. They employ binary block encoding to represent discrete weights with exponentially fewer qubits than one-hot encoding, benchmark several initial states (max-biased and ranked warm-start) and choose a nearest-neighbour hard mixer based on a "quantum bridge" connectivity phenomenon. The study systematically tests layerwise training strategies (frozen and unfrozen), optimisation routines (COBYLA vs dual annealing), and uses statevector reconstruction for some analyses to eliminate shot noise, while also introducing post-selection as a noise mitigation step.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-024, C-028, C-034, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Numerical simulations show that dual annealing combined with layerwise optimisation—especially the unfrozen-layerwise variant—yields the most robust performance, with global-minimum success probabilities exceeding 80% for depth p ≥ 3 in the tested instances. Among initial states, the max-biased and ranked warm-started states outperform other baselines, and optimisation tends to skew the outcome distribution towards the global minimum even when the mean cost increases. The quantum algorithm achieves significantly better approximation-ratio statistics than the max-bias classical portfolio baseline, and fitted scaling exponents for the inverse global-minimum probability suggest favourable (sub-exponential) sample-scaling for both warm-start and max-bias initial states, with the warm-started state approaching the classical global minimum solution. The authors also find that a mixer with smaller interaction range (M1) is easier to optimise under stochastic shot noise and that dual annealing uses fewer cost-function evaluations than COBYLA to reach better approximation ratios.
    [codes: C-005, C-007, C-008, C-011, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-031, C-033, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum DGMVP solver is benchmarked against classical strategies such as the max-bias portfolio and constrained random sampling, with the authors reporting that their QAOA-based method achieves significantly lower approximation ratios than the max-bias method across tested quantiles and minimum values. In scaling analyses, fits of the inverse global-minimum probability versus feasible-region size show exponents (b ≈ 0.76 for warm-start and b ≈ 0.51 for max-bias) that the authors interpret as indicating more favourable sample-scaling than classical constrained sampling, though they present this as an indication rather than a rigorous proof of quantum advantage. They also note that the warm-started state constructed from a rounded classical continuous solution can itself approach the global minimum, providing a strong classical-quantum hybrid baseline.
    [codes: C-011, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-031, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that realistic thermal relaxation noise severely degrades their algorithm’s performance, precluding any practical quantum advantage on near-term noisy devices. While post-selection on feasible states can partially mitigate this, they stress that it substantially increases the number of measurements required to keep stochastic noise fixed, introducing a significant sampling overhead. They also observe that as hardware improves and decoherence is reduced, stochastic measurement noise will become the dominant error source, implying that practical gains depend sensitively on both hardware noise profiles and sampling budgets.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-027, C-029]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper concludes that drastic reductions in physical error rates or the advent of fully fault-tolerant quantum computation will be required before this type of quantum portfolio optimisation becomes practically viable in finance. It also frames the observed favourable shot-scaling as a conditional indication that, asymptotically in the number of assets and discretisation bits, their QAOA approach may outperform classical methods in the number of samples required to find the DGMVP solution, suggesting further large-scale studies are needed to validate any genuine quantum advantage.
    [codes: C-030, C-032]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors present an end-to-end implementation of a QAOA tailored to the discrete global minimum-variance portfolio model, including a full algorithmic pipeline and explicit analysis of viability on noisy intermediate-scale hardware. Novel elements include a binary block encoding that reduces qubit counts relative to one-hot schemes, a hard budget-preserving mixer motivated by a "quantum bridge" excitation phenomenon, and a systematic benchmarking of warm-started and max-biased initial states, layerwise training strategies, and classical optimisers under realistic noise and shot constraints. They particularly highlight their empirical quantification of how noise sources and sampling requirements impact the possibility of quantum advantage in portfolio optimisation.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-024, C-028, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work emphasises a complete pipeline from financial model to quantum circuit, including resource-aware choices such as binary block encoding and linear-depth dense cost circuits. The authors perform systematic optimiser and ansatz studies—comparing COBYLA vs dual annealing, frozen vs unfrozen layerwise optimisation, and several initial states—with hyperparameter settings chosen as explicit trade-offs between optimisation quality and cost. They use statevector simulations to remove shot noise in scaling studies, and where noise is included, they detail the use of post-selection to enforce constraints, while noting the resulting measurement overhead, indicating a careful though simulator-based assessment of NISQ viability.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-024, C-028, C-034, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper introduces and names a "quantum bridge" phenomenon involving two- and three-qubit excitations, which underpins the design and analysis of their hard mixing operators, but whose broader implications go beyond the immediate portfolio-optimisation task.
    [codes: C-015, C-035, C-036]

=== PAPER 81f92de64876 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles simulation-based optimization problems where the objective is expensive to evaluate and must be approximated via simulation, targeting objective functions expressed as expectation, variance, CDF, or (C)VaR of random variables and functions thereof. It frames these as optimization tasks over continuous or discrete decision variables, including illustrative cases such as a quadratic loss, the newsvendor inventory problem, and portfolio optimization with a VaR-based risk penalty.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-005, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum-enhanced simulation-based optimization (QSBO) approach that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) to accelerate evaluation of expectation-based objectives, encoding probability distributions into amplitudes and mapping function values via Taylor-based approximations and controlled rotations. They support both continuous decision variables treated as parameters in f(X, y) and discrete decision variables represented on qubits with a parameterized trial state and linear entangling ansatz, evaluated with continuous-estimate QAE variants that reduce width/depth compared to canonical QAE; specific financial mappings rely on comparators and value-register constructions for piecewise costs and VaR.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-028, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QAE provides an estimation error scaling of O(M^-1) with circuit depth O(M), in contrast to classical Monte Carlo’s O(M^-1/2) error, leading to a quadratic speedup for objective evaluation in QSBO. In experiments, they show that canonical QAE induces a stepwise objective landscape, whereas a maximum-likelihood QAE variant yields continuous estimates that better mirror smooth objectives, and that in toy applications the method identifies the optimal or best portfolio or decision with high sampling probability—for example, stock level s = 2 in the newsvendor problem with probability close to one, and selecting only the first asset in the portfolio example with probability about 0.9.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare QAE-based evaluation to classical Monte Carlo, stating that QAE achieves a quadratic speedup because its estimation error scales as O(M^-1) versus the Monte Carlo standard deviation scaling as O(M^-1/2) for M function calls, while maintaining circuit depth O(M). This comparison is presented at the level of asymptotic error scaling and not as an empirical runtime benchmark.
    [codes: C-003, C-007, C-008, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper notes that QAE is probabilistic and therefore must be repeated with aggregation (e.g., via medians) to obtain a reliable estimator with high confidence, which adds practical overhead. The authors also acknowledge that the performance of QSBO depends on the chosen parameterized trial state for the decision variables and state that it requires further in-depth investigation to understand this influence and to design problem-specific trial states, similar in spirit to QAOA.
    [codes: C-009, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors point to the need for systematic study of how different trial states affect optimization performance and whether one can construct problem-specific ansätze for QSBO, analogous to problem-tailored designs used in QAOA.
    [codes: C-038, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The central claimed contribution is the introduction of a quantum-enhanced algorithm for simulation-based optimization that leverages QAE to achieve a theoretical quadratic speedup in objective evaluation over classical Monte Carlo while handling both continuous and discrete decision variables. They position QSBO as particularly suitable for objectives involving expectations, variance, CDF, and (C)VaR, and demonstrate it on financial and operations examples including portfolio optimization with a VaR constraint and a newsvendor inventory problem.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper uses Qiskit’s uncertainty models to load probability density functions exactly into quantum states and applies a classical COBYLA optimizer in the hybrid loop, with a linear entangling ansatz for the parameterized trial state. The applications are all small, illustrative, and simulator-based, with distributions (e.g., normal demand and joint asset returns) and truncations explicitly specified; however, the codes do not mention public code release, noise modeling, or empirical comparisons to classical solvers beyond asymptotic scaling arguments.
    [codes: C-006, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-030, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: No additional verified codes fall outside the above dimensions.

=== PAPER 822dbee7acfe (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets portfolio diversification in equity markets, formulating it as a Max-Cut graph optimization problem where assets are nodes and conflicting (high-covariance/correlation) pairs are edges to be cut. The authors build a 71-node graph from S&P 500 assets, apply a correlation threshold to avoid a fully connected graph, and map each node to a qubit, using repeated bisection to generalize beyond two portfolios.
    [codes: C-004, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is based on QAOA for graph optimization, combined with a circuit-cutting framework (QuantCut) that automatically decomposes two-qubit entangling gates into smaller sub-circuits using quasiprobability decomposition and then reconstructs expectation values via parallel post-processing. Cut placement is formulated as a constrained optimization over qubit connectivity, solved with evolutionary computation, and integrated into an iterative expectation-value optimization loop where cuts are found once and reused across iterations.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-028, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On a noisy 10-node Max-Cut toy model, the authors report that increasing QAOA depth improves expected performance and that, for multi-layer ansätze, circuit cutting yields a consistent improvement in accuracy compared to uncut noisy executions, although it underperforms for a single layer. For the 71-qubit S&P 500 diversification instance, they observe a decreasing cost function indicative of successful optimization and claim that QuantCut enables effective large-scale quantum computations and provides a competitive workflow that may improve resilience to quantum noise.
    [codes: C-006, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-041, C-008]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: In the 71-qubit diversification experiment, the QAOA-based approach with circuit cutting is reported to outperform random sampling but to be outperformed by a classical evolutionary algorithm baseline, with the authors suggesting that deeper QAOA circuits might close this performance gap.
    [codes: C-039, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: current quantum hardware restricts the execution of large-scale circuits, motivating the use of circuit cutting. They note that both flavors of circuit cutting incur overhead that scales exponentially with the number of cuts, and that reconstructing full state vectors is limited to small qubit counts due to exponential memory requirements, a caveat reiterated in the conclusions. They also mention SWAP-gate overhead when adapting circuits with non-neighboring gates to nearest-neighbor or MPS-friendly structures.
    [codes: C-001, C-012, C-021, C-031, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include increasing the number of QAOA layers to potentially reach solutions comparable to the evolutionary algorithm, exploring alternative problem mappings that assign more than one asset per qubit, and conducting a broader analysis of performance and the resilience of circuit cutting under different types of quantum noise.
    [codes: C-040, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper introduces QuantCut as an automatic circuit-cutting framework and claims, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, to provide the first disclosed implementation of an automatic algorithm that identifies suitable gate cuts under device constraints. They further position their overall workflow for portfolio diversification as competitive and potentially more noise-resilient when combined with circuit cutting.
    [codes: C-002, C-018, C-041, C-008]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Gate-cut placement is explicitly encoded as a constrained optimization over binary connectivity variables, solved via evolutionary computation within QuantCut, which is designed to minimize the number of cuts subject to device restrictions. Post-processing reconstructs expectation values (and, where feasible, states) from sub-experiments and is parallelized over CPUs or QPUs to improve runtime, while tensor-network simulation is used for solution extraction in the large-scale finance case, with calculations reported on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. The noise-resilience study uses a toy Max-Cut instance with an explicit readout-noise model, and the finance graph is constructed with an empirically tuned correlation threshold and a simplified one-asset-per-qubit encoding.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors choose a specific entangling gate (CRZ) to reduce the complexity of circuit experiments, use repeated bisection to extend Max-Cut-based diversification beyond two portfolios, and highlight that more QAOA layers generally improve performance in their experiments. They also note that QuantCut performs three gate cuts per layer in the main 71-qubit QAOA ansatz.
    [codes: C-025, C-027, C-034, C-038]
