=== PAPER 845689734409 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses finding extrema or roots of discrete objective functions arising in combinatorial optimisation, with portfolio optimisation used as the main use case. Portfolio construction is formulated as a binary combinatorial problem via an equal‑investment simplification, encoding each asset’s inclusion as a binary variable and targeting a benchmark‑tracking portfolio under a soft budget constraint. The authors highlight that the portfolio search space grows exponentially with the number of candidate assets.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed Quantum Search for Extrema and Roots Algorithm (QSERA) maps a discrete objective function f(x), potentially with arbitrary higher‑order terms, to an oracle function u(z) and then applies Grover’s unstructured search algorithm, starting from a uniform superposition and alternating a phase‑flip oracle with a diffusion operator for an optimal number of Grover iterations. The oracle is built by rescaling f(x) to the unit interval, raising it to an integer power to sharpen selectivity, and encoding the resulting powered polynomial as a phase operator via Z‑based projectors, ancilla‑assisted phase shifts for constant terms, and controlled phase gates for linear, quadratic, and higher‑order terms; coefficients for the powered function are computed classically beforehand. The method also allows for discretisation of continuous functions into a finite grid so they can be treated within the same framework.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-033, C-043]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim that, when the global minimum and maximum of the objective are known and the oracle‑sharpening power is sufficiently large, QSERA can identify the optimal solution in O(√N) Grover iterations and, ideally, in a single quantum execution. In the portfolio example, they report that the algorithm is expected to identify the optimal portfolio bit‑string that minimises the objective and closely tracks the benchmark, while also noting the presence of a near‑optimal alternative portfolio with a comparable objective value. They also reiterate that QSERA can handle objective functions with higher‑order terms beyond standard QUBO formulations.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-016, C-029, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper frames combinatorial optimisation, including portfolio selection, as NP‑hard and notes that many such problems are usually treated within QUBO or Ising formulations, which only include up to second‑order terms. QSERA is positioned as offering a Grover‑based quadratic speed‑up in query complexity over classical unstructured search and a more general treatment of objective functions than QUBO, but no explicit empirical runtime or solution‑quality comparison with specific classical algorithms is reported.
    [codes: C-003, C-007, C-018]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that constructing the oracle requires a priori knowledge or approximations of the global minimum and maximum of the objective function to perform the rescaling step, and that QSERA nominally requires some prior knowledge of extrema but can still only provide approximate solutions if these conditions are not exactly satisfied. They describe a key trade‑off in which the number of operations needed to map f(x) to the oracle u(z) determines both the achievable accuracy and the circuit depth, implying potential resource overheads. They also note that using a finite sharpening power n yields only an approximate oracle, and that poor estimates of the objective’s bounds can destroy oracle selectivity: in the limiting case, large n can drive all oracle values toward zero, collapsing the probability of measuring the optimum. Relatedly, they report that in their portfolio example the single‑shot success probability is less than one because they used approximate bounds, and they argue there should be an intermediate, problem‑dependent optimal power n that balances selectivity against this suppression effect, but its choice is nontrivial.
    [codes: C-004, C-006, C-019, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that QSERA may be particularly useful for optimising continuous functions that are noisy or have steep gradients, where gradient‑based classical methods risk getting trapped in local extrema, provided such functions are discretised appropriately. This points to future exploration of QSERA in challenging continuous optimisation landscapes beyond the discrete finance example presented.
    [codes: C-033, C-034]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its main contribution the Quantum Search for Extrema and Roots Algorithm, which maps general discrete objective functions into an oracle suitable for Grover’s unstructured search, enabling search for extrema or roots in O(√N) iterations. A key novelty asserted is that QSERA can handle objective functions with higher‑order terms, described by an arbitrary‑order polynomial‑like expansion, thus going beyond the commonly used QUBO/Ising frameworks that are limited to first and second order. The authors further emphasise that, when bounds are known and the oracle power is chosen appropriately, the method can, in principle, achieve single‑shot identification of the optimal solution.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-017, C-018, C-029, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: All quantum computations are reported as being carried out on a zero‑noise classical simulator using Qiskit, rather than on physical hardware, which avoids noise but does not capture hardware constraints. The authors provide a fairly explicit gate‑level construction of the oracle, including ancilla usage and decomposition of constant, linear, quadratic, and higher‑order terms into phase gates, and they describe classical recursion for computing coefficients of the powered objective, which supports reproducibility of the circuit synthesis workflow; however, no real‑market data or large‑scale financial datasets are discussed in the extracted text.
    [codes: C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-044]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors emphasise that the portfolio example is based on a discrete, equal‑investment encoding where the number of assets in candidate portfolios is small enough to enumerate and visually inspect, and they note that no portfolio exactly matches the benchmark’s return and volatility, which motivates the use of a soft budget constraint and near‑matching optimisation objective. They also remark that the combinatorial search space for more realistic asset universes grows exponentially, underscoring the motivation for search‑based quantum algorithms but without providing empirical scaling studies.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039]

=== PAPER 852010d3745d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core technical problem as applying sequences of affine transformations within quantum circuits, which is challenging because quantum operations must be unitary while affine maps are not, and because directly adding or subtracting bias terms from amplitudes breaks normalization (C-006, C-014, C-020). Within finance, this is instantiated as a portfolio-return / financial risk–assessment setting, where combinatorial amplitude patterns are used to compute portfolio returns via sums of amplitudes in a knapsack-like construction (C-003, C-004, C-020, C-033).
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-014, C-020, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The method is a gate-based routine that embeds each linear part A of an affine map into a unitary via block encoding while handling the translation term B through Hadamard-supported conditional initialization on ancilla branches (C-002, C-009, C-012, C-015, C-017, C-021, C-026). Hadamard-supported element-wise addition generates scaled sums and differences of amplitudes while preserving normalization, using measurement on an ancilla to select the desired branch, and realizing a sequential, recursively defined series of affine transformations with known global scaling (C-014, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-027, C-028). For the finance application, the authors iteratively grow the register and apply Hadamard-supported add/sub steps with asset blocks Bk to construct combinatorial signed sums of asset amplitudes, and for signal processing they apply QFT, a single affine transformation in the Fourier domain, then inverse QFT (C-018, C-021, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-034, C-040).
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-034, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their routine can encode both element-wise sums and differences of amplitude vectors, scaled to maintain normalization, and that after k affine steps the final state represents the desired sequential affine transformation up to a known factor 1/2^k that can be corrected classically (C-016, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-043, C-044). In a gate-count comparison on a small instance, they claim their approach uses a smaller block-encoded matrix (4N^2 vs 16N^2) and achieves about 32% fewer total gates than an augmented-matrix block-encoding baseline, although with more multi-qubit gates (C-011, C-030, C-031). For the finance use case, they derive a closed-form combinatorial expression for amplitudes over portfolio configurations and note that measurement frequencies estimate squared amplitude magnitudes, with a bias such that larger assets are more likely to appear; in the signal-processing example, they state that the affine-in-frequency workflow enables selective enhancement or suppression of signal components (C-003, C-004, C-016, C-023, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-041, C-043, C-044).
    [codes: C-011, C-016, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-003, C-004]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The only explicit comparison is against another quantum block-encoding construction rather than a fully classical algorithm: the authors compare their block encoding of A with a block-encoded augmented-matrix approach that embeds an enlarged matrix Ã, reporting a reduction from 16N^2 to 4N^2 in matrix size and 32% fewer total gates on a toy instance (C-009, C-010, C-011, C-029, C-030). They acknowledge that this advantage in total gate count is tempered by a higher number of multi-qubit gates, which may change the effective hardware cost (C-031).
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly note that standard block-encoding procedures become increasingly computationally demanding as matrix size grows, motivating their alternative construction but also indicating scaling challenges (C-010). Their divide-and-conquer state-preparation scheme achieves exponential depth reduction at the expense of using O(N) ancilla qubits instead of O(log N), highlighting a substantial qubit-overhead trade-off (C-018, C-019). They also acknowledge that many of the generated quantum basis states store "useless" values that are never measured, implying wasted Hilbert space and potential inefficiency (C-025). In their gate-count comparison, they concede that the proposed method introduces more multi-qubit gates than the baseline, which may raise implementation cost on actual hardware (C-031).
    [codes: C-010, C-018, C-019, C-025, C-031]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that their affine-sequence framework could underlie further applications in quantum combinatorial optimization, signal processing, and quantum machine learning beyond the exemplars presented (C-013). They also propose extending the portfolio-return construction with techniques like amplitude amplification to increase the probability of sampling desirable configurations (C-038). In the signal-processing context, they envision stacking multiple affine layers in the frequency domain to implement different filters, and more generally, they point to extending their routine to multidimensional transformations (C-042, C-045). They further speculate that their gate-count advantages may grow with the number of qubits, hinting at better performance at larger scales (C-032).
    [codes: C-013, C-032, C-038, C-042, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce a novel technique and routine for applying sequences of affine transformations to the probability amplitudes of a quantum state, addressing the challenge of implementing non-unitary affine maps within unitary quantum circuits (C-001, C-006, C-043). The key novelty is the use of Hadamard-supported conditional initialization and block encoding of A (rather than the augmented matrix) to efficiently generate combinatorial amplitude patterns while keeping the state normalized, and to support specific applications such as portfolio-return computation and discrete signal processing (C-002, C-011, C-014, C-044).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-011, C-014, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is primarily constructive and illustrative: the finance and signal-processing examples are toy constructions without real financial datasets, focusing instead on synthetic amplitude encodings and closed-form expressions for the resulting amplitudes (C-003, C-004, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-040). The authors provide a detailed algebraic description of the recursive affine steps and explicitly describe how measurement on ancilla qubits selects desired branches and allows classical rescaling, but they do not discuss noise, hardware execution, or empirical robustness (C-017, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-034). The gate-count comparison is limited to a small instance and framed in terms of decomposed circuit gate totals rather than end-to-end runtime or error, emphasizing conceptual resource trends over full-stack performance evaluation (C-011, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032).

=== PAPER 858a41cdb5b2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as designing quantum algorithms that can efficiently handle and manipulate arrays (including matrix-like data structures) by directly embedding their entries into quantum amplitudes, and providing an end-to-end pipeline from data loading through arithmetic manipulation to information extraction that can support such array-based tasks. The authors argue that direct amplitude embedding simplifies subsequent algebraic operations on the stored information compared with register-based encodings.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed method is a direct amplitude-embedding framework where array entries f(i,j) are stored as amplitudes c_ij of a two-register 'quantum matrix' state, with indices i and j representing rows and columns respectively, and arithmetic is performed directly on these amplitudes without square-root encodings or register-based value representations. The pipeline is modularized into separate stages for data loading (including pointwise loading under an efficient-oracle assumption and specialized constant-array loading), an arithmetic toolkit on arrays (reversal, permutations, pairwise sums, reductions, scalar and array multiplication, scalar products), and information extraction via a Quantum Coin amplitude-estimation scheme enhanced by an iterative Grover-style zoom-in procedure and amplitude shifts over confidence intervals. Specific gate-level mechanisms include masking and controlled-X for row reversal, pivot-based recursive multi-controlled-X permutations and cyclic permutations with added controls, Hadamard-based pairwise addition and Walsh–Hadamard reductions, controlled rotations for multiplication by constants within [0,1], array multiplication with products encoded in specific ancilla branches, and composition of array products with reductions to obtain scalar products.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-013, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that state-of-the-art generic n‑qubit state preparation requires a number of CNOT gates scaling as 2^{n+1}, motivating their search for more efficient loading in structured cases such as constant arrays. For constant arrays, they state that their loading procedure uses, in the worst case, n_I X-gates, two Y-rotations, and a single multi-controlled NOT, and from this they infer that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed on a quantum computer to load a constant array than in the generic case. Within the arithmetic layer, they quantify that whole-matrix reversal can be more efficient than row- or column-only reversal, that reductions place row sums into the first column, and that array multiplication encodes the product of two arrays in the joint |0⟩ ancilla branch, which can then be combined with reductions to yield scalar products. For readout, they show that their Quantum Coin method with amplitude shift and iterative Grover amplification increases the measurement probability of the target basis state according to the standard amplification relation, effectively boosting the success probability within a specified confidence interval.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily contrasts quantum vs. quantum approaches to state preparation, noting that existing generic loading techniques require exponentially many CNOTs in the number of qubits, whereas their constant-array loading uses only a number of gates scaling with the number of row qubits and a single multi-controlled NOT. On this basis, they claim that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed to load constant arrays on a quantum computer, though the detailed comparison to classical loading costs is not elaborated beyond this asymptotic statement.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and conditional assumptions. They state that pointwise loading of generic arrays is 'generically not efficient', underscoring that their loading advantages are restricted to structured cases such as constant arrays and that the overall efficiency of their array multiplication procedure is tied to the efficiency of the underlying loading process. They explicitly assume the existence of a suitable efficient oracle for data loading, without which the end-to-end scheme would not be efficient. They also note that multiplication by a constant via controlled rotations is initially restricted to numbers between 0 and 1. At the operation level, they point out that swaps of two entries in an array are demanding operations, reflecting a cost overhead for fine-grained permutations. For their approximation of linear shifts via step functions, they caution that the method becomes inefficient if the required precision scales as 1/N in the number of discretisation points, indicating unfavorable scaling for high-accuracy piecewise approximations.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-040]

    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its novelty in offering a general-purpose framework for quantum algorithms that operate on arrays via direct embedding into amplitudes, thereby avoiding square roots and register encodings and, according to the authors, enabling simpler handling and combination of stored information. They highlight the modularization of the quantum algorithm pipeline into data loading, arithmetic manipulations, and read-out, and the construction of an efficient toolkit of quantum arithmetic operations on arrays, including explicit examples on manipulating generic oracles such as constant shifts and step-function approximations to linear shifts. They further claim that for constant arrays this framework can, in principle, achieve an exponential reduction in the number of operations required for loading compared with generic state-preparation methods.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors emphasize a modular pipeline that treats data loading, arithmetic operations, and read-out as separable components, allowing each to be analyzed in terms of gate counts and efficiency. For resource estimates, they adopt the customary use of CNOT counts as a primary complexity indicator for state preparation and articulate explicit gate-level procedures (e.g., masking with controlled-X for row reversal, recursive pivot-based permutations, Hadamard-based reductions, controlled rotations for scalar multiplication, and Quantum Coin Grover iterations for readout). However, the codes do not indicate the use of real financial datasets, benchmark instances, or reproducible code artefacts; rather, the work is presented at the level of abstract array manipulation and oracle examples, with performance characterized via analytical gate counts and scaling arguments.

=== PAPER 881dd9b94148 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets qubit scarcity on NISQ hardware by focusing on reducing the number of variables required in QUBO reformulations of constrained combinatorial problems, and instantiates this on the Max-Profit Balance Settlement (MPBS) problem from finance, which is NP-hard and subject to node-wise CAP/FLOOR and IN/OUT constraints. The authors emphasize that standard QUBO constructions for these nonlinear constraints can be extremely inefficient and incur a high slack-variable cost per node, especially for CAP/FLOOR, motivating more compact encodings. They further characterize MPBS as a locally constrained problem on transaction graphs, where constraints are defined node-by-node based only on incident arcs.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-008, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors develop two QUBO construction techniques—the iterative quadratic polynomial (IQP) and master-satellite (MS) methods, collectively referred to as IQPMS—that implement nonlinear equality and inequality constraints without approximations and with fewer slack variables than the standard penalty approach. The baseline method enforces constraints via quadratic penalties with disjoint slack variables per constraint and an explicit formula for total slack count, whereas IQP iteratively increases slack variables to gain free parameters for a quadratic polynomial representation and MS exploits synergies among constraints that share binary decision variables, with extensions to concatenated MS for three or more shared constraints. They highlight that these methods operate directly on the original optimization problem, avoiding the need to first solve preliminary QUBOs or approximate constraints, and then evaluate them on D-Wave quantum annealers using these QUBO encodings.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-026, C-028, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main result is that IQPMS formulations drastically reduce slack variables—around 90% fewer than the standard method—leading to much smaller QUBOs, with experiments on MPBS showing a reduction from roughly 4.88 to 1.30 variables per arc and about 2 physical qubits per arc after embedding. For MPBS CAP/FLOOR and IN/OUT constraints, the new methods yield implementations where slack-variable usage depends only on graph topology, and the authors derive closed-form QUBOs for nodes with at most five incident arcs, which matches the low average degree observed in realistic datasets. On D-Wave systems, these more compact encodings translate into fewer required qubits, shorter chains, and considerably higher correct solution rates, with gains in both optimal and 95%-of-optimum success frequencies that increase monotonically with the number of arcs in the MPBS instances.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not report a direct performance comparison against classical optimization algorithms; instead, classical exhaustive search is used only to certify optimal solutions and 95%-of-optimum benchmarks for the quantum runs. The primary comparative baseline is a standard QUBO reformulation procedure for constrained problems, against which the IQPMS encodings are evaluated in terms of variable count, required slack variables, embedding qubits, and annealer success rates on D-Wave hardware.
    [codes: C-010, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note that in the master-satellite approach the quadratic forms associated with satellite constraints can accidentally create incentives that compete with the master constraint, requiring careful tuning of relative multipliers to correct this behavior. They further caution that large imbalances between penalty and objective terms in a QUBO can be problematic on quantum annealers, which constrains how aggressively penalties can be scaled when enforcing constraints and thus affects the practical deployment of their methods.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-031]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions include applying the IQPMS framework to other combinatorial optimization problems beyond MPBS and exploring its use on different NISQ architectures, such as within the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. The authors also propose performing more extensive comparative studies, specifically suggesting a head-to-head evaluation with techniques presented in a referenced prior work.
    [codes: C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is presented as introducing the IQP and master-satellite methods as novel QUBO formulation strategies that drastically reduce the number of slack variables needed to encode nonlinear equality and inequality constraints without approximation, particularly for locally constrained graph problems like MPBS. The authors emphasize that their approach leverages constraint sharing across variables, yields closed-form encodings for small-degree nodes in realistic sparse financial transaction graphs, and improves annealer performance, all without requiring preliminary QUBO solving or modification of the original optimization problem.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-006, C-007, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-023, C-025, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper carefully defines a standard QUBO baseline with disjoint slack variables and an explicit slack-count scaling formula, then constructs IQP and MS encodings in a way that exploits shared-variable constraints and, when necessary, concatenated MS structures for multiple constraints. The evaluation focuses on locally constrained, low-degree graph instances of MPBS motivated by realistic financial datasets, and compares the resulting QUBO formulations on D-Wave annealers using a consistent setup against the baseline, highlighting variable and qubit counts as well as solution-quality metrics; the discussion also explicitly acknowledges the need for penalty and multiplier tuning when deploying these encodings on hardware.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also includes a hardware-level comparison between two generations of D-Wave quantum annealers, noting that the newer system is described as a prototype with enhanced performance relative to the earlier device.
    [codes: C-009, C-030]

=== PAPER 88e005f67ca2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses cross-sectional equity return prediction in noisy, non-stationary financial markets, motivated by the view that many classical forecasting models struggle with noisy inputs, regime shifts, and limited generalization capacity. The task is instantiated using the JPX Tokyo Stock Exchange Kaggle competition, predicting a two-day holding return target for a universe restricted to more liquid stocks and evaluated via long-short portfolio performance. The authors frame quantum machine learning as a potentially promising pathway to enhance stock market prediction under these challenging data conditions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-010, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core method is a hybrid Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Network (QTCNN) that combines a classical temporal encoder with parameter-efficient quantum convolution circuits, where the encoder extracts multi-scale patterns from sequences of technical indicators and passes compressed representations to the quantum part. Classical feature vectors are standardized cross-sectionally by day, then encoded into quantum states using angle embedding on multiple qubits; the quantum circuit applies hierarchical convolution–pooling with parameter sharing and leverages superposition and entanglement, and predictions are obtained by measuring Pauli observables. The study also implements several quantum or hybrid baselines, including a pure quantum neural network (QNN) classifier, a PQC-enhanced gradient boosting model (PQC+LGBM), a quantum LSTM (QLSTM), and a quantum adaptive self-attention (QASA) architecture to contextualize QTCNN’s design.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-014, C-015, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-027, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In out-of-sample tests on the JPX dataset, the proposed QTCNN achieves an annualized Sharpe ratio of about 0.538±0.042, which the authors note as the highest among all models evaluated. They report that quantum-based architectures occupy the top three performance ranks, while a classical LSTM baseline attains the lowest Sharpe ratio (≈0.044±0.029). Ablation and scaling analyses indicate that adding the quantum circuit to the temporal encoder yields a statistically significant Sharpe improvement, that entanglement via CNOT gates materially contributes to performance, and that QTCNN’s Sharpe rises with the number of qubits up to around 10 before slightly declining at 12 qubits. Additional analyses show that QTCNN maintains superior gradient variance scaling relative to other quantum models, and that it remains above the best classical Sharpe ratio up to a simulated depolarizing error rate of roughly 0.01, with amplitude damping noise degrading performance less than depolarizing noise.
    [codes: C-006, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors benchmark QTCNN and other quantum architectures against a suite of classical baselines including Transformer and LSTM-based time-series models, as well as a temporal-convolution-plus-MLP architecture (TConv-MLP). QTCNN is reported to outperform all classical baselines in terms of out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, with the headline claim that its Sharpe of 0.538 represents roughly a 72% improvement over the best-performing classical baseline. Ablation results using TConv-MLP as a classical-only counterpart suggest that the quantum circuit on top of a temporal encoder delivers an additional statistically significant performance gain over the purely classical temporal model.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-025, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly cautions that its experiments are conducted entirely in a classical simulation regime and therefore do not constitute evidence of a computational quantum speedup, noting that they do not claim any such speedup under their current setup. The qubit scalability and noise-resilience findings are obtained under idealized or simplified noise models on simulators rather than on real NISQ hardware, implying that hardware-specific issues such as decoherence, gate infidelity, and readout noise are not fully captured. More broadly, although not made explicit in the codes, the reliance on a relatively short 22-day out-of-sample evaluation window and stride-subsampled data suggests limited statistical power for assessing long-horizon portfolio performance, and this should be treated as an implicit caveat about the robustness and generalizability of the reported Sharpe ratios.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is the design of a Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Network that fuses a classical temporal encoder—capturing multi-scale sequential patterns—with a parameter-efficient quantum convolutional circuit employing hierarchical convolution–pooling and parameter sharing, specifically tailored for cross-sectional equity return prediction. The authors further claim novelty in empirically analyzing quantum enhancement mechanisms such as Hilbert space expressibility, entanglement-enabled feature interactions, and quantum interference acting as an implicit feature selection process, and in providing a comparative benchmark where quantum-based architectures dominate performance rankings on the JPX financial forecasting task.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-033, C-035, C-038, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses the JPX Kaggle dataset with a clearly defined two-day holding-period return target based on raw closes while deriving features from adjusted close prices, and restricts the universe to officially flagged liquid stocks (Universe0) to avoid illiquid securities. Features are winsorized and then standardized cross-sectionally each day using L-score normalization, with fixed-length sequences (default length 20) formed for time-series models, and a weakly supervised labeling scheme where only the top and bottom p-ranked stocks by cross-sectional target are used as positive and negative classes. To manage computational cost and preserve market-regime diversity, the authors use stride-based subsampling of trading days combined with year-wise stratified sampling, and evaluate models via a long–short portfolio protocol using out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratio as the primary metric, supported by paired bootstrap tests of performance differences. These design choices suggest attention to financial realism in data preprocessing and to statistical rigor in evaluating model differences, even though experiments are conducted on a reduced subset of days and in simulation.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-031, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors provide a conceptual discussion of possible quantum enhancement mechanisms: they emphasize Hilbert space expressibility as a means of representing complex financial patterns, entanglement via CNOT gates as a way to model interactions between different financial features, and quantum interference as an implicit feature selection effect that may help control overfitting in noisy market data.
    [codes: C-043, C-044, C-045]

=== PAPER 8a2ce0575ff1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies sector rotation in the Taiwan stock market, framing it as a sequential decision problem where an RL agent allocates capital across multiple industry sectors to maximize long-term investment returns. Sector rotation is described as reallocating capital between sectors across economic phases to generate alpha and manage risk, and is cast into an MDP where at each time step the agent observes an engineered financial state vector and selects sector allocations. The work specifically focuses on training an RL agent for this task within a hybrid quantum-classical framework.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ a hybrid quantum-classical reinforcement learning framework based on PPO, where the policy and value networks can be instantiated with quantum-enhanced backbones including a QNN, a QRWKV model, and a QASA Transformer variant. The QNN uses angle embedding to map classical features into low-dimensional quantum states processed by a variational quantum circuit; QRWKV replaces part of RWKV’s channel-mixing layer with a variational quantum circuit; and QASA replaces classical dot-product attention with a quantum attention mechanism implemented via a variational quantum circuit. All quantum models are relatively small NISQ-style circuits, e.g., the QNN is configured with 4 qubits and 2 quantum circuit layers, and are integrated into the PPO agent as function approximators.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-013, C-022, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the quantum-enhanced models (QNN, QRWKV, QASA) consistently achieve the highest cumulative training rewards within the PPO framework, with QASA attaining the highest final reward among all models. However, across backtests on the Taiwan market, these quantum models underperform classical LSTM and Transformer backbones on real-world investment metrics including cumulative return, annualized return, Sharpe ratio, and drawdown, with QASA showing the most pronounced mismatch by pairing the highest reward with the lowest cumulative and risk-adjusted returns. The authors also observe that classical models learn more stable allocation policies that are better aligned with long-term investment outcomes, and interpret the overall pattern as a significant gap between training rewards and realized investment performance.
    [codes: C-004, C-014, C-041, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-056, C-060]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Within a shared PPO framework with unified feature engineering and shared hyperparameters, the study systematically compares classical LSTM and Transformer backbones against quantum-enhanced QNN, QRWKV, and QASA networks. While quantum models often obtain higher training rewards, the LSTM and Transformer baselines deliver higher cumulative and annualized returns, better Sharpe ratios, and comparable or slightly better drawdown statistics, indicating that classical architectures are more aligned with long-term financial objectives in this setting. The authors highlight that classical models appear to learn more stable and generalizable policies, whereas quantum models tend to fit the proxy reward signal more aggressively but translate that less effectively into portfolio performance.
    [codes: C-002, C-013, C-017, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-056]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper identifies several limitations. First, at the finance/RL level, the authors stress that reward design is a persistent challenge in RL for financial decision-making and that their proxy reward—based on correctly predicting next-step top-N sector leadership—does not directly optimize long-term objectives such as cumulative return or Sharpe ratio, potentially incentivizing overfitting to short-term volatility rather than risk-adjusted returns. They explicitly interpret the observed reward–performance gap as an instance of this known issue. Second, on the quantum side, they note that practical QRL is constrained by NISQ hardware limitations, including significant noise, shallow circuit depth, and barren plateau phenomena, and further emphasize the expressiveness and optimization instability of quantum circuits under such constraints. They also mention broader training challenges for quantum models, such as susceptibility to noise and decoherence and the lack of standardized quantum-compatible financial environments. Empirically, they argue that the quantum models’ high expressiveness may make them more prone to overfitting the proxy reward and learning strategies that exploit reward-specific patterns that do not generalize to real-world portfolio behavior, especially when risk and volatility are considered. For QASA in particular, they suggest that its quantum attention mechanism may overemphasize spurious correlations or suffer from optimization instability, contributing to its poor out-of-sample performance.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-012, C-020, C-024, C-039, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-060, C-007]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose several directions for future research. They plan to refine reward shaping and regularization within the PPO framework to better align the learning signal with long-term investment goals, aiming to bridge the observed discrepancy between training rewards and actual performance. They argue that realizing practical benefits from quantum-enhanced models will require more robust encoding schemes, regularization methods, and reward designs tailored to financial objectives. They also explicitly call for future studies to investigate whether, under reward signals that more faithfully reflect long-term risk-adjusted returns, quantum models can not only match but potentially exceed classical baselines.
    [codes: C-018, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s contributions are framed as threefold: (1) introducing a reproducible QRL benchmark for sector rotation using real Taiwan stock market data; (2) providing a systematic comparison of classical and quantum-enhanced policy networks within a unified PPO-based hybrid framework; and (3) analyzing the discrepancy between training reward and investment performance, offering actionable recommendations for reward shaping and regularization. The authors also position their work as filling a gap in the literature by delivering empirical QRL evidence on a real-world financial task and by surfacing practical challenges of deploying quantum reinforcement learning in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-023, C-024, C-008]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study employs a flexible PPO agent with interchangeable classical (LSTM, Transformer) and quantum-enhanced backbones, trained under shared hyperparameters to ensure a fair comparison. The authors construct a unified automated feature engineering pipeline that extracts technical indicators from sector-level price and volume data into a common feature matrix, and define a clear MDP setup with state, action (top-10 sector selection), and proxy reward specification. They train and evaluate on a large real-market dataset covering 2,646 listed companies grouped into 47 sectors over 2007–2025, using a fixed training–backtesting temporal split and a rolling-window simulation to approximate real-time decision-making and out-of-sample generalization. Performance is assessed with standard financial metrics (cumulative/annualized return, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown), and the authors emphasize that their PPO-based framework and dataset choices are intended to yield a reproducible benchmark for future QRL studies in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-008]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors situate their work in broader literatures, noting that RL has been applied to tasks such as portfolio rebalancing, asset allocation, algorithmic trading, and hedging strategies, and that quantum machine learning has been proposed for applications including portfolio optimization, option pricing, credit risk modeling, and market simulation. They further emphasize that the reward–performance gap observed in their experiments is not unique to quantum models but reflects a known challenge in deep RL for finance more generally, reinforcing the cross-cutting importance of careful reward design.
    [codes: C-019, C-021, C-057, C-060, C-010]

=== PAPER 8d08019fb608 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper is framed as an extensive survey of how quantum machine learning (QML) can be applied to core quantitative finance problems, including portfolio optimization, market prediction and trading, option pricing, risk measurement (VaR/CVaR), credit risk, and fraud detection as anomaly detection. It motivates these applications by arguing that quantum properties such as superposition and entanglement could improve on traditional financial modelling and ML methods. The authors also carefully define central financial tasks and metrics (e.g., portfolio optimization, Sharpe ratio, VaR/CVaR, credit rating categories, and the treatment of fraud detection as a special case of anomaly detection) to ground the surveyed QML work in standard finance problem formulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a survey, the paper covers several families of quantum and quantum‑hybrid methods rather than implementing one specific algorithm. It explains basic gate‑model concepts (qubits, superposition, unitary gates) and positions QML within the NISQ era, emphasizing hybrid quantum–classical algorithms where parametrized quantum circuits (QNNs) are trained via classical optimizers. The authors describe key building blocks such as QAOA for combinatorial optimization, QAE for amplitude estimation, HHL for linear systems, and quantum PCA for eigenvalue problems, and then map these to finance use cases (e.g., QAOA and VQE for portfolio optimization, QAE and qGAN-based loading for derivative pricing, quantum kernels and QSVMs for classification and anomaly detection, and quantum GANs and kernel methods for fraud and credit risk). They also highlight architectures such as feature‑map plus variational layers in QNNs and multiple quantum kernel learning schemes used in risk and fraud contexts.
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-053, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064, C-070, C-074, C-075, C-083]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors compile reported results across several financial subdomains. For portfolio optimization, cited work using quantum annealers and variational algorithms reports that optimized reverse annealing can be more than 100× faster than forward annealing, that gate‑model rebalancing on small portfolios is feasible on NISQ devices and can find portfolios within 5% of optimal adjusted returns, and that VQE can yield solutions close to exact ones under suitable hyperparameters. In market prediction and trading, they report studies where quantum deep hedging policies based on QNNs significantly outperform Black–Scholes hedges, quantum‑assisted feature selection improves predictive accuracy with lower dimensionality, quantum Elman networks achieve similar prediction quality with much smaller hidden/context layers, and hybrid deep QNNs demonstrate high forecasting accuracy across regression and extrapolation tasks, including for churn prediction and stock prediction. For pricing, the survey cites evidence that qPCA reduces noisy factors in interest‑rate models, qGAN‑based loading is gate‑efficient, QAE-based methods achieve quadratic or near-quadratic speedups for option pricing, shallow circuits can accurately price European and Asian options, unary encodings may be advantageous on near‑term devices, and several quantum approaches (including on IBM Q hardware) demonstrate quadratic or exponential speedups in steps or dimensionality for Monte Carlo and PDE‑based pricing. In risk management and fraud/credit analytics, the authors report that QAE-based methods offer near‑quadratic speedups for VaR and CVaR estimation, quantum feature selection on real credit risk data can match or surpass state‑of‑the‑art classical methods, quantum kernels can improve average precision as system size grows, QSVMs can deliver lower false positives and higher precision in fraud detection, QBoost offers interpretability benefits over classical boosting, quantum GNNs achieve AUC around 0.85 in graph‑based fraud detection, and quantum GAN and kernel setups show competitive or superior performance on anomaly detection benchmarks.
    [codes: C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064, C-065, C-066, C-067, C-068, C-069, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-076, C-079, C-081, C-084, C-085]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Across the surveyed studies, quantum methods are usually benchmarked against classical baselines. For optimization, the authors describe QA and VQE approaches that come close to or match the performance of existing classical solvers on problems of comparable size, and note that VQE can approximate exact solutions under good hyperparameter choices. In trading and hedging, QNN-based deep hedging strategies reportedly significantly outperform the Black–Scholes hedge, and quantum‑assisted feature selection and QENN architectures match or exceed classical models with fewer parameters. In risk and fraud analysis, QAE‑based VaR/CVaR estimation is claimed to surpass classical Monte Carlo in efficiency, quantum feature selection for credit risk can compete with or surpass state‑of‑the‑art classical methods, quantum kernels can outperform standard approaches in average precision as problem size grows, and QSVMs are reported to have lower false positives and higher precision than both classical and other quantum baselines. Some comparisons are negative or neutral: QSVMs in certain stock prediction experiments do not show clear advantages over classical SVMs, and in a blockchain phishing study no performance improvement is observed when increasing the number of qubits, which tempers expectations of uniform quantum superiority.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges that current quantum hardware and algorithms face substantial limitations that constrain practical impact. At a general level, the authors stress that existing NISQ devices and simulators are still far from demonstrating robust quantum advantage, being restricted by limited qubit counts, noise, and decoherence. They note that scalability, hardware limits, and algorithmic complexity remain overarching challenges. In specific applications, they report that current hardware issues hindered QAOA-based FX reserves management to the point that only a few demonstrations succeeded even for a five-variable problem, and that available QPUs were not sufficiently stable or error‑tolerant for fraud detection at realistic scales. They also highlight more nuanced limitations in QML experiments: QSVMs show no clear performance advantage over classical SVMs in some stock prediction tasks, increased qubit counts did not yield better performance in a blockchain phishing detection setting, and certain speedup claims are theoretical or emulator-based rather than demonstrated on large‑scale, noisy hardware. === PAPER 8dad17700137 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses portfolio optimization as a trade-off problem between maximizing expected return and minimizing risk, moving from a continuous Markowitz-style formulation to a constrained integer/binary problem that becomes combinatorial and NP-hard as the number of assets grows. To make it amenable to quantum computation, the authors convert the constrained integer quadratic formulation into a QUBO and then to an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal portfolio.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses a hybrid VQE algorithm to solve the QUBO/Ising portfolio optimization problem, mapping the QUBO to an Ising Hamiltonian and using the variational principle to approximate its ground state. The Hamiltonian is built from binary-encoded asset positions via a conversion matrix that reduces qubit count, with a penalty coefficient λ enforcing budget constraints, and is implemented with parameterized circuits (various ansatz families and entanglement structures) optimized by classical optimizers within Qiskit on both simulators and multiple IBM NISQ devices.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-017, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-044]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main reported outcome is a set of best practices for hyperparameter choices in VQE-based portfolio optimization, including the finding that COBYLA is the most stable and adequate optimizer and that PauliTwo ansatz achieves fast early convergence while TwoLocal and RealAmplitudes with linear or pairwise entanglement perform best under noise. The authors identify a 'Goldilocks' interval for the penalty coefficient λ (neither too small nor too large) and show that solution quality depends strongly on hardware size/quantum volume and hyperparameter selection, with some real IBM devices (Toronto, Kolkata, Auckland) matching the classical optimal solution and, more generally, achieving solutions very close to the exact one with strong convergence toward the classical solution even without error mitigation.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-043, C-045, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: As a classical benchmark, the authors use a branch-and-bound method to obtain the exact discrete solution, and they compare the quantum VQE outcomes to this classical solution. They report that, with suitable hyperparameters and on better IBM devices, the quantum algorithm can reach solutions that perfectly match or are very close to the classical optimum, and discuss convergence toward this classical solution in terms of energy and portfolio quality rather than speed.
    [codes: C-015, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-006, C-007, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several limitations: classical exact methods for the discrete formulation face exponential growth of the search space as assets increase, which is also a challenge for quantum approaches in terms of required qubits. The authors restrict themselves to small-sized portfolio instances (up to four assets) due to current hardware constraints and note that NISQ noise from decoherence, gate infidelities, and measurement errors significantly hinders VQE convergence by slowing it or shifting the minimum energy upward. They further highlight the risk of barren plateaus in training expressive ansatzes, the sensitivity of performance to the penalty coefficient λ (too small fails to enforce constraints, too large overwhelms the objective), and show that long-range qubit connectivity on actual hardware introduces gate overhead that increases circuit depth and error rates. Moreover, they deliberately do not use any error-mitigation techniques, framing this as both a methodological choice and a limitation of the reported performance.
    [codes: C-009, C-014, C-020, C-021, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-041, C-042, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors envisage applying their approach to real-life portfolio optimization with larger market sizes once quantum hardware with sufficient size and characteristics becomes available. They also plan to refine the mathematical formalization of the portfolio problem using more advanced formulations and to conduct a dedicated follow-up investigation into how hardware topology affects the performance of quantum variational algorithms.
    [codes: C-008, C-050, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as an empirical study of 'best practices' for performing VQE-based portfolio optimization on NISQ devices, focusing on identifying effective hyperparameter settings—such as ansatz choice, entanglement structure, optimizer, and penalty coefficient λ—that allow small real quantum computers to approximate the classical optimal solution without error mitigation. The authors also emphasize the observed dependence of solution quality on hardware characteristics like quantum volume and topology as part of their novel practical insights.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-018, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses real historical price data, computing daily returns, expected returns via historical averages, and variances/covariances from the time series to instantiate a realistic but small-scale portfolio problem. The constrained Markowitz-style objective is systematically converted into a QUBO and then an Ising Hamiltonian using a binary encoding that reduces the number of qubits via price-dependent binarizing elements, and the penalty coefficient λ is treated as a critical hyperparameter whose suitable range is empirically determined. The experimental design systematically varies ansatz families, entanglement patterns, and classical optimizers, runs both ideal and noise-model simulations plus real-device experiments on several IBM QPUs without error mitigation, and uses a classical branch-and-bound solver as a benchmark; however, experiments are limited to at most four assets and the code availability is not discussed in the codes provided.

VaR is similarly computed by applying QAE to a discretized loss distribution with a threshold function to extract the desired quantile. Portfolio optimization is handled through a hybrid QAOA workflow: the mean‑variance problem is converted into an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal asset subset, solved approximately by a NISQ‑suitable variational QAOA routine, followed by classical routines to infer final asset weights. The BQ-Bank platform is designed to run these quantum routines either on real superconducting hardware or via classical emulation and to reuse the option‑pricing backend for the revenues module.

For VaR, they report that the quantum VaR estimate more closely matches the parametric VaR than the Monte Carlo VaR at the same sampling points and analytically claim a quadratic speedup over MC‑VaR in terms of precision. The authors state that in their examples, quantum option prices are closer to the Black–Scholes value than the Monte Carlo output, and that quantum VaR is closer to parametric VaR than MC‑VaR at equal sampling effort, with BQ‑Bank also providing classical Monte Carlo solutions natively to facilitate such comparisons.

In their portfolio optimization example, they impose strong simplifying assumptions: all assets are assumed to have identical price (set to 1), the investment budget must be an integer multiple of this price, and the entire budget must be fully invested. For the QAOA-based portfolio solver, they explicitly recognize that finite circuit depth leads only to approximate solutions, so the variational procedure may not reach the true optimum. === PAPER 8e52ff85234f (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles multi-objective portfolio optimization, emphasizing the inherent conflict between maximizing return and minimizing risk for investors with different preferences, and frames the task as finding a non-dominated set (Pareto front) of portfolios. The model is a multi-objective weighted portfolio formulation that accommodates heterogeneous risk preferences while targeting simultaneous return maximization and risk minimization over real-world financial data. Within this framing, all solutions in the non-dominated set are interpreted as optimal trade-offs between risk and return for different investor profiles.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-015, C-017]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum component is a multi-objective quantum annealing (MoQA) scheme that uses scalarization to convert the bi-objective risk–return problem into a single energy function E(ω) = λ·DR − (1−λ)·DER, where λ tunes the trade-off between objectives. Different λ values, spaced by a step size Δλ, generate multiple scalarized subproblems, and smaller Δλ values allow a finer exploration of risk–return trade-offs and investor preferences. The non-dominated set obtained from MoQA then serves as the starting point for a classical post-processing phase.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-011, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the hybrid framework generates diverse non-dominated portfolios that better cover a broad range of investment preferences and extends the Pareto front toward higher-return and lower-risk regions. The entanglement move (EM) substantially enhances optimization performance and hit rate, particularly by improving high-return regions and expanding Pareto-front diversity beyond what MoQA alone achieves, while MoQA remains strong in low-risk areas. Against classical multi-objective algorithms, the hybrid approach achieves higher hypervolume, hypervolume rate, and hit rate, along with lower GD and IGD, indicating superior convergence and diversity on real-world financial data.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors report that their hybrid quantum–classical approach outperforms both quantum annealing alone and several classical multi-objective optimization algorithms in terms of solution quality, convergence, and diversity. Specifically, compared to classical MOO algorithms, the hybrid method attains higher hypervolume, hypervolume rate, and hit rate, and lower GD and IGD, and produces a non-dominated set that extends further toward higher returns and lower risk, thereby offering a greater variety of portfolio options. They also state that, on real-world financial data, the hybrid framework shows promising performance relative to classical baselines.
    [codes: C-007, C-014, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper sections provided do not explicitly describe any limitations, caveats, or constraints of the proposed hybrid framework, its scalability, or its dependence on current quantum hardware or problem size.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors indicate that future work will extend the proposed hybrid portfolio optimization approach to international cross-market settings, implying plans to test the framework on broader and more diverse asset universes.
    [codes: C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to present the first integrated hybrid framework that combines quantum annealing-based scalarization with a quantum-inspired entanglement move and a trend ratio model for multi-objective weighted portfolio optimization. This hybrid MOO algorithm is positioned as a novel way to merge quantum and classical computing strengths to tackle complex financial optimization problems and to generate a more diverse non-dominated portfolio set aligned with varying investor preferences.
    [codes: C-004, C-011, C-012]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study employs a clearly specified multi-objective weighted portfolio model with integer-valued asset weights evaluated via a trend ratio model, and defines the scalarized energy function and λ-grid construction that govern the MoQA subproblems. Experiments use real-world data on Dow Jones Industrial Average constituents over a 40‑month period with monthly re-evaluations, and performance is assessed using standard multi-objective metrics (HV, HV rate, hit rate, GD, IGD, NDS size), providing a relatively transparent experimental setup on realistic financial time series.

=== PAPER 8e9d2c7faf8e (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets a broad class of combinatorial optimization problems—including unconstrained and many constrained cases—by representing them as cost functions over a feasible subset F of {0,1}^n, and then searching within this feasible domain without modifying the objective via penalties. The authors explicitly emphasize that their method can address a wide range of such problems while preserving feasibility of all sampled solutions.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-013, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core method is a classically-boosted hybrid quantum optimization algorithm (CBQOA) that first uses an efficient classical routine to generate a high-quality seed and then applies a continuous-time quantum walk (CTQW) on a specially constructed graph to create a superposition over nearby feasible solutions, followed by a QAOA-like variational ansatz whose evolution is confined to the feasible subspace. Graph construction relies on efficiently computable permutations and edge weights defined via a sigmoid function of local cost differences, and the CTQW is implemented via simple Trotterization; for some problems (Max 3SAT) the walk is exact on the hypercube, while for others (Max Bisection) it is an approximate walk using XY mixers and swap-based constructions. Parameters (walk time and variational angles) are tuned by minimizing the CVaR of the cost, with feasibility preserved throughout by design.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On synthetic hard instances of weighted Max 3SAT and Max Bisection, the authors report that CBQOA increases the probability of producing 'good' solutions—defined via a performance metric measuring improvement over random guessing—relative to seeds and prior quantum approaches, with deeper circuits generally yielding better performance but with diminishing returns as depth grows. They also present a classical simulation technique for CBQOA that is more efficient than a naive approach in terms of space and time complexity.
    [codes: C-005, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors claim empirical evidence that CBQOA outperforms previous approaches, including classical approximation algorithms used to generate seeds and GM-QAOA, on hard instances of Max 3SAT and Max Bisection. They highlight that even when the classical preprocessing produces only mediocre solutions, CBQOA can noticeably boost the probability of finding high-quality solutions, and that GM-QAOA with comparable depth underperforms CBQOA in their benchmarks.
    [codes: C-005, C-025, C-027, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper notes that penalty-term approaches for constrained optimization are less efficient because they must search an enlarged space that includes many infeasible states, motivating CBQOA’s feasible-subspace design. It acknowledges that prior quantum-walk-based methods require efficient indexing of feasible solutions, a requirement CBQOA avoids, but also that its own structural Assumption 3.1 does not hold for some constrained problems such as Knapsack, limiting applicability. The authors further observe that deeper CBQOA circuits yield diminishing returns in performance, and that fully exploring all connected components of the feasible domain may require running the CTQW from multiple seeds to obtain adequate coverage.
    [codes: C-008, C-010, C-011, C-024, C-038, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include developing stronger classical algorithms for generating seeds that CBQOA could then boost, and exploiting the structure of the CBQOA circuit to reduce the number of iterations needed for parameter tuning. The authors also explicitly pose the open question of designing structured parameter schedules tailored to CBQOA that might yield excellent performance with less optimization overhead.
    [codes: C-043, C-044, C-045]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies the portfolio optimization problem, emphasizing that its computational complexity grows exponentially with the number of assets and motivating it as a challenging finance task for quantum methods. The authors focus on combinatorial/QUBO-style formulations of portfolio optimization, arguing that these are difficult to scale classically but promising targets for quantum computing. They frame quantum computing as potentially offering more efficient and effective portfolio optimization via quantum parallelism, while noting that current quantum computers do not fundamentally reformulate the problem.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-014, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work centers on hybrid NISQ algorithms, particularly VQE and CVaR‑VQE, which use a quantum processor to find the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian encoding the portfolio objective, interpreted as the optimal portfolio. The formulation proceeds by transforming a quadratic programming problem into a QUBO via binary variables and penalty terms on the budget constraint, then mapping this QUBO to an Ising Hamiltonian suitable for quantum optimization. The authors position VQE as attractive because it uses relatively short circuits for current noisy devices, contrast it with longer‑circuit approaches like QAOA and Grover‑adaptive search, and recommend COBYLA as the classical optimizer; they also describe hardware‑aware qubit mapping and transpilation strategies to minimize depth and avoid SWAPs on specific IBM devices.

In small‑scale hardware runs a 3‑asset VQE execution on a real device does not reach the exact optimum in 20 iterations, whereas the simulator can reach the desired optimum given more iterations. For larger hardware runs (19–28 qubits), they show that CVaR‑VQE converges quickly and that the quantum and classical portfolios differ by only one stock in a 19‑asset instance; they also provide concrete execution times and circuit depths for 27‑ and 127‑qubit experiments. In extensive backtesting with 10,000 simulations on IBEX35 subsets, the simple SMA baseline performs poorly, high variance across runs reflects market unpredictability, and after filtering on intrarecord variance quantum algorithms—especially QAOA and CVaR‑VQE—stand out more frequently, though the authors still refrain from declaring a clear overall winner.
    [codes: C-003, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-050]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper explicitly positions its contribution as a systematic backtesting comparison between quantum and classical portfolio optimization algorithms, applied under equivalent conditions. The authors compare four quantum and three classical algorithms and find that quantum methods can match or slightly outperform classical ones in some cases, but also emphasize that there is no definitive overall winner across all backtests. Classical quadratic programming is noted as susceptible to getting stuck in local optima, and convex methods, while promising, are deemed less suitable for fair backtesting versus current quantum approaches; SMA is used as a naive baseline and shown to perform poorly. In terms of computational performance, classical step times are observed to grow exponentially with the number of assets, while per‑step quantum times exhibit a better (sub‑exponential) scaling trend in their experiments.

They highlight several hardware-related constraints: using real quantum computers with more than 100 qubits is challenging; circuit depth must be minimized to stay within coherence times; noise and limited qubit connectivity require careful mapping; and real hardware runs are dominated by queue time, so they restrict real-device executions mainly to validation and illustration rather than full backtesting. Algorithmically, approaches like QAOA and Grover‑adaptive search have circuits that are too long for reliable use on error‑prone NISQ devices, and convex classical methods are noted as less suitable for a fair comparison in their framework. In the results, they point out that a small 3‑asset real‑hardware VQE run fails to reach the optimal solution, that there is high variance in backtesting outcomes due to market unpredictability, and that it remains difficult to determine conclusively which algorithm is best. === PAPER 93ff9980959f (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles collateral optimization, defined as minimizing the cost of collateral needed to secure transactions or portfolios while maintaining sufficient protection, and shows this can be cast as a bipartite matching MILP with exposure, no–short-selling, and additional eligibility/group constraints. The authors then reformulate this collateral optimization problem, and a related knapsack benchmark, into QUBO form via binary discretization of allocations and slack/penalty constructions to make it suitable for NISQ and quantum-inspired solvers.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-011, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs QUBO-based quantum and quantum-inspired optimization routes, emphasizing hardware-agnostic formulations that can in principle be used with annealing, variational gate-based, and digital annealer backends, all sharing a common LP-to-QUBO conversion step. It explores a “standard” balanced slack-variable penalization for constraints as well as an unbalanced penalization scheme that reduces the number of binary variables, and tests these using simulated annealing and digital annealer SDKs as proxies for NISQ-era devices believed to be promising for financial applications.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-014, C-028]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In small-scale tests, QUBO-based approaches for collateral optimization and knapsack generally fail to reach the global optimum but produce solutions reasonably close to it, especially when using the unbalanced penalization formulation. Quantitatively, the unbalanced formulation reduces the required binary variables (e.g., from 298 to 228 for a sample collateral instance) and yields objective values closer to the global optimum than the balanced slack-variable approach, though all heuristic runs converge to different local minima.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors contrast their QUBO-based heuristic results with high-quality MILP/LP solvers, noting that MILP has exponential worst-case complexity but attains global optima on the tested small instances, whereas heuristic quantum-inspired methods often miss the optimum. They emphasize that because the QUBO heuristics can be close but not optimal on sizes where MILP performs well, their heuristic nature can obscure where they are actually advantageous, and that formulation choice strongly affects how quantum-ready and competitive the approach is against classical optimization.
    [codes: C-004, C-006, C-010, C-031, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations: MILP solvers can become impractically slow on large-scale instances due to exponential worst-case complexity, motivating but not guaranteeing a role for quantum methods. Heuristic QUBO-based approaches, including those run on simulated annealing, may hide their true applicability because they often fail to reach global optima on instance sizes where MILP still performs well, and simulated annealing itself is highly sensitive to problem structure. The standard slack-variable one-hot encodings scale poorly in binary variable count, and while unbalanced penalization reduces resources, it makes it less likely that the ground state corresponds to the true optimum. For the collateral optimization demonstration, the authors simplify the setting to continuous cash-only allocations, introduce binary discretization that trades precision against resource cost, and relax exposure from an inequality to an equality constraint, all of which restrict realism. Constraint handling is further limited by treating consistency as a hard constraint and exposure as soft, and by omitting some business constraints (e.g., many-to-one and some eligibility/group constraints) in the numerical instance. Practically, penalty (Lagrange multiplier) tuning is described as difficult and the limited number of annealing runs likely prevents sufficient exploration of the search space, contributing to the observed convergence to suboptimal local minima.
    [codes: C-006, C-010, C-013, C-015, C-022, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that better solutions could be obtained by increasing the number of annealing runs, adjusting step sizes, and generally using more compute and improved penalty tuning. They also state that several additional improvements to the QUBO formulations remain to be explored, including alternative encodings such as implicit penalization via restricted Hamiltonian dynamics in parallelized QAOA, and exploring stochastic quantum Monte Carlo algorithms that mimic quantum annealing as promising candidates for large-scale collateral optimization.
    [codes: C-034, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution centers on formulating a realistic collateral optimization problem as a hardware-agnostic QUBO, comparing balanced slack-variable and unbalanced penalization encodings, and empirically illustrating how these choices impact resource requirements and solution quality for NISQ and quantum-inspired solvers. By highlighting that formulation choice (e.g., binary discretization, constraint relaxation, and penalization schemes) materially affects quantum readiness and performance, the paper positions itself as clarifying modeling trade-offs for applying near-term quantum optimization to collateral management, an area where open literature is sparse due to competitive concerns.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-014, C-017, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper confines itself to small-scale, local computational tests using various SDKs and simulated annealing/digital annealer backends, and supplements these with a knapsack interlude to benchmark and inform the collateral formulation. Some approaches discussed are only surveyed without experimental analysis, and the authors note that several improvements and more extensive tuning and compute are still needed to obtain higher-quality solutions, implying current experiments are exploratory rather than fully optimized. The work also emphasizes that penalty-weight selection is delicate and that constraint priorities (e.g., hard consistency vs. soft exposure) and discretization precision directly influence both feasibility and interpretability of results.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-016, C-024, C-027, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-038]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors note that literature on collateral management optimization is sparse because such strategies confer competitive advantage to institutions. They also describe domain-specific aspects of the objective, such as favoring allocations of higher-quality assets to short-duration trades, and highlight the conceptual distinction between hard business-critical constraints (like consistency/no short selling) and optional but desirable constraints (eligibility and grouping) within their framework.
    [codes: C-005, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021]
