    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-035]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a conceptual review, the paper surveys multiple quantum approaches for AI rather than implementing a specific method. It describes quantum support vector machines based on quantum-enhanced kernel estimation and quantum kernel methods for computing inner products in Hilbert space, quantum neural networks that integrate quantum circuits with classical training, and variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) as a key near-term framework using a hybrid quantum–classical optimization loop. It also covers quantum PCA for dimensionality reduction and emphasizes hybrid quantum–classical architectures as the preferred design in the NISQ era.

On hardware, current NISQ devices suffer from limited qubit counts, noise, decoherence, short coherence times, and high gate error rates, making deep circuits impractical. On the algorithmic side, QAI faces issues of algorithmic stability, notably barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms that hinder training, as well as challenges around data encoding/quantum feature mapping and readout. The authors stress that classical ML scalability constraints motivate QAI but also highlight that QAI itself is nascent, lacks standardized benchmarks for quantum advantage, generalizability, and robustness to noise, and must contend with broader ethical concerns around bias, fairness, security, and accountability. They emphasize the need for scalable, fault-tolerant hardware, efficient hybrid quantum–classical algorithms and interfaces, and standardized benchmarks for evaluating quantum learning models. === PAPER 954608913b5d (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets constrained optimization problems, which the authors note are ubiquitous in science and industry, and instantiate this via discrete Markowitz portfolio optimization with both equality and inequality constraints on portfolios (e.g., budget, minimum return, and cardinality constraints). Constraints are treated very generally, with the only structural assumption being that there exists an efficient oracle to test whether a candidate solution is feasible. The portfolio benchmark is formally posed as minimizing a quadratic risk–return objective over a feasible set F defined by these constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-011, C-014, C-028, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core method is a general quantum Zeno dynamics framework that enforces arbitrary (including inequality) constraints by repeatedly projecting the evolving quantum state onto the in-constraint subspace via projective measurements implemented through constraint oracles. This framework is integrated into quantum optimization algorithms such as QAOA—where measurements are inserted around mixer layers because the cost-phase operator is constraint-preserving—and L-VQE, with a layerwise Zeno-QAOA construction and heuristic rules for setting the measurement frequency parameter η. The authors give detailed constructions of constraint oracles based on quantum arithmetic for both equality and inequality constraints, including implementations that exploit quantum conditional logic (QCL) to reduce auxiliary-qubit usage and a general argument for building measurement oracles from polynomially-expressed Boolean constraints while reusing ancilla qubits across multiple constraints.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-033, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-048, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the authors prove that repeated constraint-preserving measurements can maintain the state in the feasible subspace with probability at least 1−δ, derive how the required number of measurements scales for general parameterized evolutions, and show that for digital adiabatic evolution their Zeno approach recovers the optimal in-constraint solution, with measurement count scaling at most quadratically in qubits (and only linearly in QAOA depth). Numerically on portfolio benchmarks, they report significant improvements over penalty-based baselines in both approximation ratio and in-constraint probability, including high-accuracy performance for L-VQE with Zeno dynamics and effective parameter transfer across different measurement schedules. On Quantinuum H1-2 hardware, they demonstrate that increasing the number of mid-circuit Zeno measurements improves in-constraint probability for small portfolio problems, validating the feasibility of the required mid-circuit measurement and QCL primitives.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-012, C-013, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-025, C-029, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The primary comparison is against quantum penalty methods rather than fully classical solvers: the authors state that their Zeno-based approach yields better solution quality and higher feasibility than state-of-the-art penalty techniques, and in numerical portfolio tests they report ‘significant improvements’ in approximation ratio and in-constraint probability relative to tuned penalty baselines. They further observe that penalty methods exhibit a tradeoff where increasing the penalty factor improves feasibility but degrades objective quality, and they cannot simultaneously optimize both, whereas Zeno dynamics avoids this tuning conflict and supports more robust parameter transfer across instances.
    [codes: C-006, C-009, C-029, C-032, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. First, they note that penalty-based methods suffer from sensitivity to penalty strength and become prohibitively expensive to tune in multi-constraint settings, motivating but not eliminating the challenge of constraint handling. Second, constructing constraint-preserving mixers directly is NP-complete even for linear constraints, framing why they avoid that route. Third, in their own Zeno framework, some choices of mixer can yield trivial or ineffective dynamics in the constrained subspace (PFB²P = 0), so mixers must be analyzed carefully before use and high-connectivity mixers may entail tradeoffs. Fourth, for practical implementation, they caution that realizing constraint oracles often requires quantum arithmetic and can incur high gate counts for complex constraints, and that QCL-based resource savings do not apply in all cases, such as inequality constraints requiring coherent QFT. Finally, they explicitly warn that an important step when applying their technique is to check whether the chosen mixer exhibits problematic behavior under Zeno projection.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-026, C-027, C-032, C-038, C-042, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The discussion positions the method as asymptotically efficient and therefore viable for future fault-tolerant quantum devices, implying further exploration in that regime, and suggests that additional performance gains on noisy hardware could be pursued by combining their Zeno framework with advanced, algorithm-specific error mitigation techniques.
    [codes: C-045, C-046]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim a generally applicable technique for constrained quantum optimization that uses quantum Zeno dynamics and repeated projective measurements to enforce multiple arbitrary constraints, including inequalities, with low auxiliary-qubit overhead and no post-selection, assuming only access to an efficient feasibility oracle. They emphasize the broad applicability of this framework by demonstrating it within both QAOA and variational circuits, providing analytical guarantees (e.g., in the digital adiabatic limit) and measurement-scaling characterizations, and highlighting an asymptotic efficiency that they argue makes the approach suitable for future fault-tolerant devices.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-025, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors restrict their numerical experiments to portfolio optimization with equality and inequality constraints using QAOA and L-VQE, clearly describing benchmark sets with single and multiple constraints and specifying the portfolio objective. They design numerical studies to probe Zeno versus penalty performance, including parameter-transfer experiments and practical rules for fixing η to ensure a constant minimum in-constraint probability per layer. For hardware validation, they choose small proof-of-concept portfolio instances specifically to test mid-circuit measurements, QCL, and oracle constructions, and describe ancilla usage and resource-saving strategies (e.g., QCL-based oracles and ancilla reuse) that are relevant for reproducibility and full-stack assessment.
    [codes: C-014, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-039, C-041, C-048, C-050]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that constraint-preserving projective measurements corresponding to different constraints commute, which supports modular composition of multiple constraints within their Zeno framework, and that a simplified heuristic allows efficient estimation of in-constraint probabilities by measuring a single auxiliary qubit for a fixed η, both of which are cross-cutting technical observations not tied to a specific result or limitation.
    [codes: C-018, C-024]

=== PAPER 9636cfb13bd3 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets constrained Markowitz portfolio optimization, where the classical objective is to minimize risk and maximize return subject to a budget equality constraint and asset-specific threshold inequalities that lead to a mixed-binary optimization formulation. It reframes this finance problem as a mixed-binary optimization (MBO) and then a QUBO suitable for quantum processing, explicitly modeling the portfolio vector as a quantum state and introducing slack variables to convert inequality constraints into equalities for Hamiltonian encoding.
    [codes: C-008, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-021]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a QAOA-based approach in which the constrained Markowitz problem is transformed into a QUBO and then into an Ising Hamiltonian whose expectation value is minimized. Inequality constraints are handled by embedding slack variables directly into the problem Hamiltonian, mapping each slack variable to a dedicated ancilla qubit, so that constraint satisfaction is internalized in the energy landscape; the resulting Hamiltonian decomposes into interaction, field, and constant terms after a standard binary-to-Ising substitution.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In noiseless statevector simulations on a three-asset synthetic testbed, the slack-ancilla QAOA consistently finds the optimal feasible portfolio, matching the classical ground-truth objective value and achieving 100% feasible portfolios in under one second at depth p=2 with three system qubits plus ancillas. The authors also report that this architecture allows the required constraint penalty strength β to be reduced by an order of magnitude (10^4 to 10^3) without loss of solution quality, and they speculate that the quantum framework may shorten optimization runtimes from hours to minutes in larger settings.
    [codes: C-005, C-009, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-044]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The proposed slack-ancilla QAOA is compared against a standard penalty-based QAOA and classical methods on the same three-asset instance. While the penalty-based QAOA with large uniform penalties frequently converges to an infeasible '111' portfolio despite full feasibility being attainable, the slack-ancilla QAOA finds the true optimal portfolio that matches the classical ground truth, thereby illustrating both the sensitivity of conventional penalty methods to hyperparameter tuning and the improved feasibility and objective performance of the proposed formulation within the tested regime.
    [codes: C-005, C-026, C-027, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge multiple limitations: the study is conducted on a very small, synthetic three-asset instance with an idealized setup, strong assumptions, and limited data, which constrains the generality of the findings. They stress that results depend heavily on the attainability of constraints, and note that current quantum hardware suffers from noise, errors, and limited qubit counts and coherence times, all of which restrict scalability and practical deployment of the proposed model.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include refining the portfolio formalism to reduce quantum resource demands so that such models align better with contemporary hardware capabilities, and developing normalization schemes over the total weighted probability to enhance the interpretability of quantum portfolio representations. The authors also suggest extending their risk–return variance bound discussion to settings with genuinely non-commuting mixers or penalty terms, where full Robertson-style uncertainty relations might impose stricter trade-offs.
    [codes: C-025, C-038, C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in architecturally redesigning the problem Hamiltonian via a slack-ancilla scheme that embeds constraints directly into the quantum state, thereby modifying the energy landscape to more robustly handle mixed-binary constrained optimization. The authors position this as a general pathway for constrained problems in quantum finance, and further introduce a conjectured risk–return variance bound, framed as a commuting-limit Robertson–Schwarz relation linked to quantum-mechanical arguments about the ground state of the measurement system.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-006, C-014, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a controlled synthetic three-asset dataset constructed to satisfy all constraints, with fully specified instance parameters and an adaptive penalty schedule during classical optimization, and reports comparative baselines including classical COBYLA and standard penalty-based QAOA. The authors emphasize that penalty terms were added to encourage convergence and that simulations are performed in a noiseless setting, while also explicitly noting the need for further refinement and normalization of the portfolio representation to improve practical relevance and resource efficiency.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-037, C-038, C-041]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper opens by situating the work within broader claims that quantum computing can offer exponential speed-ups and exploit quantum parallelism for complex constrained optimization in finance, and suggests that, particularly for large-scale problems, such quantum approaches could outperform classical methods, although these broader performance advantages remain speculative and are not empirically demonstrated in this study.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles portfolio optimization in financial services, formulating it as a mean–variance-style optimization over 20 NSE stocks, where the objective is to maximize expected return minus a risk penalty based on the covariance matrix of asset returns, with a risk factor q=0.5 and a budget constraint set to half the number of assets. The optimization problem is expressed as maximizing f(x) = μᵀx − q·xᵀΣx, derived from historical adjusted closing prices with returns, normalization, and standardization applied, and then encoded for quantum and classical solvers.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study evaluates three quantum approaches for portfolio optimization: an Exact Minimum Eigen Solver using NumPyMinimumEigensolver on the problem Hamiltonian, a hybrid Sampling Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) that minimizes a quantum system’s energy, and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) targeting the combinatorial optimization formulation. VQE and QAOA iteratively update quantum circuit parameters to minimize the portfolio objective function, leveraging quantum properties such as superposition and parallelism that the authors frame as enabling exploration of large solution spaces in ways impossible for classical algorithms.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-028]

The authors characterize these results as demonstrating "quantum supremacy" or superior predictive accuracy of MES and QAOA relative to other algorithms in the study.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-027, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical baselines include Mean-Variance Optimization, Genetic Algorithms, and Simulated Annealing, against which the quantum algorithms are explicitly compared. The best-performing classical method, the Genetic Algorithm, has an MSE of 0.0105—higher than all three quantum methods—while MVO and SA show significantly higher error metrics overall, leading the authors to describe traditional approaches as relatively inefficient in this setting. They also note that classical algorithms like MVO and GA are well established and deterministic on small and medium-sized datasets, in contrast to quantum methods that gain precision by scanning a large solution space via quantum parallelism.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-029, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that their findings are not yet validated in live trading: they state that further advancement in quantum computing technology is essential to test these algorithms in real trading scenarios in order to establish scalability and live performance.     [codes: C-038, C-039]

It further presents the observed lower error metrics of MES and QAOA as evidence of "quantum supremacy" within the scope of their benchmark setup and suggests hybrid quantum-classical designs as a promising direction for scalable and reliable portfolio optimization.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-027, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses real historical adjusted closing prices for 20 NSE stocks over a three-year window and performs standard preprocessing steps: checking data completeness, excluding missing values, computing daily returns as percentage changes, and applying normalization and standardization. The portfolio optimization problem is defined via the covariance matrix of returns and expected returns, with a specified risk factor and budget constraint. Performance evaluation employs risk–return measures (Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, maximum drawdown) and forecast error metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE) computed on expected future returns for each portfolio. The description of quantum and classical algorithms (exact eigensolver, VQE, QAOA, GA, SA) is conceptual rather than implementation-heavy; specific hardware or noise assumptions are not detailed in the coded excerpts.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors provide a broader motivation, asserting that quantum algorithms can process information in ways impossible for classical algorithms by leveraging superposition and quantum parallelism, which they claim considerably reduces time to obtain an optimal portfolio. They situate their work within a broader trend of applying quantum computing to high-processing-demand industries such as encryption, drug discovery, and especially finance, and note growing interest in using machine learning for portfolio management as an adjacent methodological area.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010]

=== PAPER 99b07636e459 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets portfolio optimization under modern portfolio theory, motivated by the high computational complexity of balancing return and risk across many assets and positioning this as a challenging combinatorial optimization problem for classical methods. It formulates the task as choosing discrete asset positions (short, long or no position) subject to a net-position constraint and a Markowitz mean-variance style cost function. The authors emphasise that quantum algorithms are explored because financial portfolio optimization can become intractable for classical algorithms at scale.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-010, C-019, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses the Quantum Walk-based Optimization Algorithm (QWOA), which extends QAOA by exploiting an efficient classical indexing of valid solutions to prepare an equal-superposition initial state over only the feasible subspace and then applying alternating phase-shift and continuous-time quantum walk operators. The phase-shift unitary encodes the Markowitz cost values as quality-dependent phases, while the mixing unitary is an indexed continuous-time quantum walk implemented on a complete graph over the valid-solution space; variational parameters (γ, t) are optimized classically. For the portfolio instance, two qubits per asset encode three discrete positions, but experimentally the authors implement a restricted version where valid solutions are classically computed, indexed, and encoded in a 7-dimensional photonic qudit, with arbitrary unitaries decomposed into two-level matrices and projective measurements used to estimate output probabilities.
    [codes: C-003, C-007, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Experimentally, the authors demonstrate that, for a three-asset portfolio instance with seven valid solutions, the probability of measuring the basis state corresponding to the optimal portfolio increases substantially as the number of QWOA iterations p grows from 1 to 6, reaching around 0.8 before slightly decreasing, while the objective function value shows a gradual downward trend that the authors interpret as an increasing probability of high-quality portfolios. They report that the experimental probabilities across iterations align closely with their theoretical noise-free predictions, and emphasize that they successfully realize a variational search up to p = 6 with strong agreement to the ideal model. They also highlight that QWOA reduces the search to a symmetric subspace of seven valid solutions, which, compared with QAOA over the full encoding, significantly reduces the search space and removes mixing asymmetry bias.
    [codes: C-004, C-021, C-022, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present direct empirical comparisons against classical portfolio optimization algorithms on runtime or solution quality; instead it relies on cited numerical work by Slate et al. showing that QWOA exhibited a significant advantage over previously explored methods. Within the paper’s own contribution, the comparison is mainly between QWOA and QAOA in terms of algorithmic search-space size and mixing symmetry, with QWOA claimed to reduce the search space and eliminate mixing bias in the studied instance, rather than a direct benchmark against classical solvers.
    [codes: C-008, C-022]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that their experimental results are affected by hardware imperfections, specifically imperfections in interferometers and inaccuracies in wave plates, which introduce dephasing and degrade performance. They explicitly identify dephasing as a limiting effect, estimating its impact on the objective function by modelling a dephasing rate of about 0.97. Additionally, the experimental implementation is restricted to a reduced Hilbert space where only valid solutions are encoded, with valid solutions and their indexing computed classically, implicitly limiting the scalability and faithfulness to a full, fault-tolerant implementation of QWOA.
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: In the conclusion, the authors state that their photonic implementation is direct and flexible and "holds the potential for scalability," suggesting an intent to extend the approach to larger problem instances and more complex implementations of QWOA in future work.
    [codes: C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to provide an experimental realization of alternating phase-shift and continuous-time quantum walk unitaries for QWOA applied to portfolio optimization, presenting this as strong evidence for the potential of quantum-walk-based algorithms to tackle complex, practically relevant optimization problems such as financial portfolio selection. The authors further argue that, by restricting the search to a symmetrically indexed valid-solution subspace and demonstrating variational search up to depth p = 6 with good agreement to theoretical predictions, their work offers strong evidence for practical applications of quantum-walk-based portfolio optimization and illustrates advantages over QAOA in terms of search-space reduction and mixing symmetry.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-009, C-021, C-022, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study clearly specifies the formal combinatorial optimization framework and the Markowitz-style portfolio cost function, including constraints on net position and the discrete asset encoding, providing transparency on the financial modelling choices. The experimental setup is described in detail: valid solutions are computed and indexed classically, an equal-superposition initial state over seven valid portfolios is prepared in a 7-dimensional photonic qudit, unitary operators are implemented via known decompositions into two-level matrices, and projective measurements yield squared overlaps with basis states. The authors also tune variational parameters using classical simulation (QuOp_MPI) before hardware execution, and explicitly quantify experimental probabilities with uncertainties and compare them to theoretical predictions, demonstrating reasonable experimental rigor and partial reproducibility, though they work with a small three-asset instance and a restricted subspace rather than a full qubit-based implementation.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes are accounted for in dimensions 1–8.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 99e391ee5e85 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets clustering of financial assets based on their correlation structure, arguing that relationships among assets are central to portfolio optimization and algorithmic trading and are naturally represented as signed, weighted graphs where both positive and negative correlations must be preserved. The clustering problem is formulated as an NP-hard signed-graph coalition structure generation task that maximizes intra-cluster edge weights, encouraging co-movement within clusters and discouraging negatively correlated pairs, and is cast into a QUBO form suitable for quantum processing.
    [codes: C-005, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose GCS-Q, a Graph-based Coalition Structure Generation algorithm that directly operates on signed, weighted correlation graphs and performs iterative partitioning via minimum cuts, using a stopping rule that dynamically infers the number of clusters. Each minimum-cut subproblem is formulated as a QUBO and solved on near-term quantum devices—primarily a D-Wave quantum annealer—with the option to use variational gate-model approaches like QAOA in hybrid workflows, enabling exploration of exponentially large solution spaces for NP-hard signed-graph clustering.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-011, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors report that GCS-Q consistently achieves higher clustering quality than classical baselines on both synthetic and real financial correlation graphs, measured by Adjusted Rand Index and a structural-balance penalty metric, while also determining the number of clusters automatically. On synthetic structurally balanced graphs and on real hourly Yahoo Finance data, GCS-Q attains the lowest penalty values, which the authors interpret as uncovering market structures that support diversification and mean-reversion strategies, and they further claim this constitutes the first demonstration of a quantum advantage in solution quality for practical asset clustering using real hardware. They also report that clustering 170 assets with k=10 on current hardware takes over 10 minutes, despite individual QUBO solve times being capped at one second.
    [codes: C-003, C-029, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts GCS-Q with classical clustering methods such as k-Means/k-Medoids, hierarchical clustering, PAM, and signed-graph spectral methods like SPONGE/SPONGEsym, arguing that these approaches suffer from limitations including lossy transformations of correlations into non-negative distances, manual hyperparameter tuning (especially the need to pre-specify k), and performance degradation when graphs are dense, have continuous weights, or exhibit heterogeneous cluster sizes. In experiments, PAM performs worst on synthetic data due to the correlation-to-distance transformation, and SPONGE-based methods degrade under continuous weights and stochastic cluster sizes, while GCS-Q outperforms all baselines in ARI and penalty measures even though the classical baselines are given k using the eigengap heuristic; the authors also note that prior quantum clustering work formulated a maximum clique QUBO that exceeded current annealer capacities, which GCS-Q avoids.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-012, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: synthetic experiments are noise-free, focusing on ideal structurally balanced graphs and thus not fully capturing real-market noise; current quantum hardware and its connectivity restrict GCS-Q to roughly 175 nodes, constraining scalability; access via shared cloud infrastructure introduces latency and queue delays, leading to practical runtimes of over 10 minutes for clustering 170 assets despite per-QUBO solve times being capped at one second. They also implicitly note that their classical complexity remains O(n2^n) when executed without quantum hardware, underscoring the underlying computational difficulty.
    [codes: C-023, C-026, C-030, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work includes applying the learned clusters to downstream financial tasks such as asset allocation and empirically evaluating performance with portfolio metrics like Sharpe Ratio and returns. The authors also propose technical extensions: deploying GCS-Q on improved D-Wave hardware with Zephyr topology and better connectivity, exploring custom embeddings, leveraging gate-model quantum solvers with more qubit-efficient strategies, and benchmarking GCS-Q’s QUBO formulations against strong classical optimizers such as Gurobi.
    [codes: C-044, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty on several fronts: it introduces a data-driven GCS-Q algorithm that directly clusters signed, weighted correlation graphs without heuristic correlation-to-distance transformations, automatically infers the number of clusters, and is robust to realistic conditions like continuous edge weights and heterogeneous cluster sizes that prior work treated under more idealized assumptions. Most prominently, the authors assert that this is the first demonstration, to their knowledge, of a quantum advantage in solution quality for a practical financial task—asset clustering—validated with real quantum hardware on both synthetic and real financial datasets.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-010, C-012, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-038, C-042]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study builds signed, weighted undirected graphs from asset Pearson correlations, explicitly preserving both positive and negative relationships, and optimizes an intra-cluster weight objective that aligns with financial interpretations of co-movement and anti-correlation. Synthetic data are carefully constructed to mimic financial correlation structure with continuous signed weights and heterogeneous cluster sizes via Dirichlet allocation, while withholding noise to isolate algorithmic behavior, and real data are sourced from Yahoo Finance hourly prices with rolling log returns over a specified period. Evaluation uses ARI on synthetic data and a structural-balance penalty metric on real data, with classical baselines SPONGE, SPONGEsym, and PAM configured using the eigengap heuristic for k, and the implementation is made available as open-source code, supporting reproducibility.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Additional contextual notes include the reiteration that optimally clustering signed graphs with edge weights in [−1, +1] is NP-hard and that, when executed purely classically, GCS-Q has complexity O(n2^n), with the exponential factor arising from solving minimum cuts and the linear factor from dynamically determining the number of clusters. The authors also argue that GCS-Q’s better alignment with signed-graph structure and avoidance of idealized assumptions (such as uniform clusters and ternary edge weights) position it as particularly suitable for real-world financial correlation networks and support broader claims about the practical utility of near-term quantum computing for graph-based unsupervised learning in finance.
    [codes: C-004, C-012, C-023, C-039, C-042]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to portfolio_optimization because it clusters assets using signed correlation structure, which is directly tied to diversification, co-movement control, and identifying groups that may support allocation decisions.     [codes: C-001, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-019, C-031, C-043, C-055]

The index‑tracking problem is formulated as a quadratic/binary quadratic optimization (QP/QUBO‑style) K‑medoids clustering problem solved with a commercial classical solver (Gurobi) on standard hardware, and quantum annealing is mentioned only as a possible future implementation route for the QUBO formulation. Quantum computing is framed as a potential refinement path for these optimization models, but all experiments remain classical.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-012, C-020, C-023, C-034, C-035, C-046]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For index tracking, the market‑graph‑based correlation‑clustering approach achieves low tracking errors relative to benchmark indices, with annualized tracking error within 10% for six of eight indices and R² values used to quantify close alignment between portfolio and index returns. The selected correlation‑based portfolios successfully track broad indices using relatively small subsets of assets, with portfolios that are well diversified and closely mirror benchmark sector distributions; annual rebalancing generally performs best over six years, though semi‑annual rebalancing can be preferable in specific volatile periods. The graph‑based method also outperforms a random‑selection baseline in tracking error and appears largely agnostic to the weighting scheme even though stock weights themselves significantly affect tracking error. For the IRL component, the parametric T‑REX model converges after about 3,200 epochs, inferring reward parameters that capture strong benchmark correlation, a high growth‑style preference, and low estimated trade‑volatility costs, and it preserves the ranking of funds in both train and test, indicating that the learned reward reproduces the preferred trading style.
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-010, C-016, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-056]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The index‑tracking approach is explicitly benchmarked against a random‑selector baseline, with the market‑graph portfolios outperforming random selection by yielding tracking errors consistently below the median or first quantile of the random portfolios. Within the classical design space, the study also compares two weighting schemes and multiple rebalancing frequencies, finding that while stock weights materially influence tracking error, the specific quadratic‑programming clustering method is largely insensitive to the choice of weighting, and that annual rebalancing tends to outperform more frequent schedules over the full sample, with exceptions in certain volatile years.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that adapting the proposed methods to real‑world data and fund operations remains challenging, particularly in the RL setting. The index‑tracking study is constrained by limited computing resources, forcing the use of standard hardware and a commercial binary quadratic optimizer rather than exploring larger instances or quantum hardware. In the IRL–RL study, limited open‑source fund‑position and trading data, due to confidentiality, hinder thorough benchmarking and implementation, and the uncertainty of cash inflows and redemptions makes it difficult to model these flows within the RL action space. Additionally, the implementation of the G‑learner and expected‑return model is still ongoing, so final RL performance results are not yet available.
    [codes: C-005, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future directions include refining the proposed portfolio‑optimization and RL models using quantum computing, specifically by testing the QUBO index‑tracking formulation on a quantum annealer once appropriate resources are available. The authors also suggest extending the RL framework by incorporating additional financial data and developing a reliable prediction model for cash inflows and redemptions to better integrate these flows into the action space. For index tracking, they recommend examining more frequent rebalancing during periods of high market volatility as a potential improvement.
    [codes: C-006, C-033, C-034, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The thesis claims novelty in two main ways: first, by extending a purpose‑built market‑graph clustering architecture (inspired by Hong et al. 2021) to a more recent and volatile period, validating its robustness for cardinality‑constrained index tracking using up‑to‑date data that include the 2020 market crash. Second, it proposes a two‑step IRL–RL framework that explicitly combines human and artificial intelligence, using T‑REX to infer a manager’s trading style from historical fund trajectories and G‑learning to translate this inferred style into adaptive allocation recommendations, with the expectation—based on prior work—that such a G‑learner could outperform traditional portfolio managers’ funds out of sample.
    [codes: C-001, C-018, C-019, C-031, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the index‑tracking study is structured as a detailed experimental framework: it constructs market graphs from daily log‑return correlations using a three‑year rolling window with one‑month smoothing, formulates k‑medoids clustering as a quadratic program, and employs a warm‑start strategy that initializes each new period’s optimization with exemplars from the prior rebalance to mitigate NP‑hardness and avoid random initialization. The experiments use a fixed three‑hour Gurobi time limit and evaluate multiple rebalancing frequencies, two weighting schemes, and both tracking‑error and dollar‑value performance metrics over a 2015–2023 dataset that includes extreme volatility. For the IRL–RL component, the authors reduce dimensionality by aggregating positions to sector exposures, adopt a parametric T‑REX due to limited data, and carefully design a quadratic reward with three tunable parameters that penalize underperformance versus a moving target and transaction‑like costs, enabling G‑learning to solve for optimal policies via linear‑algebra methods and backward induction without neural networks. They also clearly report T‑REX convergence behavior and interpret the learned reward parameters, and they are transparent about incomplete RL results and data constraints that affect reproducibility.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles a finance-native CSA collateral optimization problem under ISDA Credit Support Annexes, where integer lots, haircuts, rounding, MTA, and concentration caps create a rugged, legally bounded search space with significant operational and liquidity costs if handled suboptimally. The problem is formulated as choosing non‑negative integer lots subject to feasibility constraints on effective requirement and an optional coverage window buffer, while optimizing a scalar objective that trades off funding cost, movement, tail risk, and overshoot under these CSA rules.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-016, C-017, C-035]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach uses a quantum‑inspired hybrid search that interleaves simulated annealing with micro higher‑order QAOA (HO‑QAOA) jumps on small binding sub‑QUBOs (subset size n≈8–16, interaction order k≤4), encoding multi‑way couplings such as caps and rounding via a higher‑order Ising Hamiltonian. Higher‑order penalties allow HO‑QAOA to explicitly target the CSA‑specific couplings that defeat local swaps, with plateau‑triggered quantum jumps selected via a spectral interaction graph, followed by repair and feasibility checks, and CP‑SAT is used as a downstream arbiter to certify feasibility and objective gaps.

Ablation studies indicate that performance saturates around subset sizes n≈12, with smaller n underfitting multi‑way caps and larger n yielding diminishing returns, and that enabling higher interaction orders k=3 and k=4 improves performance near tight coverage windows, albeit with higher compilation cost. The authors also cite prior work showing 15–25% gains of higher‑order QAOA over vanilla QAOA in related financial portfolio settings, as contextual support for their design.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several practical limitations: ancilla‑based compilation for higher‑order terms can inflate the effective subset size beyond the n_max budget, in which case the quantum jump for that iteration must be skipped, reducing the frequency of HO‑QAOA use. To control circuit depth and noise, the interaction order is capped at k≤4; for higher‑order couplings, the method falls back to purely classical exploration, limiting the quantum component’s expressivity. The authors also note that when the user‑specified coverage buffer B is too tight, the problem becomes infeasible under the U‑cap, so they compute and report a minimal feasible buffer B* as a diagnostic rather than forcing a solution. Finally, they describe a fallback behavior in which, if ancilla inflation or compilation failure occurs, the algorithm reverts to simulated‑annealing/BL‑3 neighborhoods; while solution quality reportedly degrades gracefully, this implies that in such cases the search is effectively classical.

=== PAPER 9bd4d4752519 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets generic constrained binary optimization problems, motivated by multiple application scenarios such as facility location, k-partition, job scheduling, set cover, and graph coloring, where feasible solutions must satisfy linear constraints and be represented as basis states on a quantum computer. The authors emphasize that conventional VQAs (HEA and QAOA) start from a superposition over all basis states and then attempt to shrink the search space towards the feasible region, which they view as inefficient for constrained problems.
    [codes: C-009, C-011, C-024]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed method, Rasengan, is a transition-Hamiltonian-based variational algorithm that inverts the usual VQA strategy by expanding the search space outward from one known feasible solution instead of shrinking from a full superposition. Mathematically, the authors use the insight that one feasible solution can span the full feasible solution space via homogeneous basis vectors, and they define transition Hamiltonians that mutually convert between feasible basis states while Hamiltonian simulation creates superpositions of such states. The circuit implementation of these transition Hamiltonians has linear complexity in the number of nonzero elements of the basis vectors, and the authors introduce several implementation optimizations: Hamiltonian simplification and greedy basis reconstruction to reduce nonzero elements, pruning of transition Hamiltonians that do not introduce new feasible states, segmented execution that passes probability mass between segments, and a purification layer between segments that discards infeasible noisy outputs.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across five benchmark families, Rasengan is reported to significantly improve solution quality and circuit depth compared to VQA baselines, with large reductions in approximation ratio gap (ARG) and shallower execution circuits. The authors quantify that Rasengan reduces ARG by factors of 1954× versus HEA and 1897× versus penalty-term QAOA, and by 4.12× relative to the best prior QAOA variant (Choco-Q), while achieving roughly 1.96×–49× reductions in circuit depth across benchmarks. They further report that deeper QAOA layers (e.g., a 14-layer Choco-Q circuit with depth 1419) are required to approach Rasengan’s performance, whereas Rasengan maintains relatively small depth and scales to larger facility location instances with an observed depth bound around 3×10³. On noisy real devices, Rasengan is claimed to achieve a 100% in-constraints rate, and ablation studies indicate that purification yields a dramatic 303× improvement in hardware performance, while Hamiltonian pruning accelerates feasible-space exploration so that pruned chains cover the feasible space with substantially fewer transitions.
    [codes: C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The coded material does not report any direct comparison between Rasengan and purely classical optimization algorithms; all referenced baselines are quantum VQA variants such as HEA, penalty-term QAOA, commute-Hamiltonian QAOA, and Choco-Q. Thus, the paper’s comparative claims are framed entirely within the family of quantum approaches for constrained binary optimization.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations related to scalability, noise, and reproducibility. They note that as problem size increases beyond about 28 qubits under realistic noise, some execution segments fail to produce any feasible solutions due to high error rates, which can prematurely terminate the segmented execution and hinder scaling on current devices. Additionally, the public artifact scales down the experimental setup: the provided scripts use fewer benchmarks and reduce the number of cases per benchmark from 100 to roughly 10, indicating that full-scale experimental results are not directly reproduced by the shared code. These points indicate constraints on both practical deployment under NISQ noise and on exact reproducibility of the reported large-scale evaluations.
    [codes: C-031, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main novelty claimed is a conceptual inversion of standard VQA search: Rasengan starts from a single feasible solution and expands the search space using linear-algebraic structure, rather than beginning from a global superposition and shrinking towards feasibility. This is operationalized through the introduction of a transition Hamiltonian formalism, where feasible solutions are connected via homogeneous basis vectors and finite transition simulations are shown to cover all feasible solutions, with formal bounds for cases such as totally unimodular constraint matrices. The authors further position their circuit-level techniques—Hamiltonian simplification and pruning, segmented execution, and purification—as a distinctive optimization stack tailored to this transition-Hamiltonian approach.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work situates Rasengan against established VQA categories—HEA and QAOA—and carefully distinguishes penalty-term versus commute-Hamiltonian strategies for encoding constraints, which serve as main baselines. The authors provide explicit circuit-cost characterizations, noting that their decomposition of transition Hamiltonians has linear complexity in the number of nonzero basis elements, and they support their optimization techniques with quantitative ablations, including the impact of purification and pruning on hardware performance and search-space coverage. For reproducibility, they release an artifact, but explicitly state that the provided scripts operate on a scaled-down benchmark set with fewer cases than in the full evaluation, which is an important caveat for replicating the reported aggregate results.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses computational bottlenecks in financial risk measurement for large portfolios, where VaR, CVaR, higher-moment and systemic risk metrics are expensive to compute under complex correlation structures and dynamic market conditions. It reformulates portfolio risk and covariance structures as quantum observables and entangled states, posing risk computation and portfolio optimization as problems over quantum-encoded portfolios and risk Hamiltonians. The work is motivated by the limitations of classical Monte Carlo–based risk assessment and the lack of comprehensive theoretical foundations for quantum risk modeling.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-027, C-044]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a family of quantum methods: (i) encoding portfolios and their covariance matrices into quantum states with entanglement capturing asset correlations, and defining variance, VaR, CVaR and higher risk measures as quantum observables; (ii) using quantum amplitude estimation to compute VaR and CVaR with quadratic speedup; and (iii) formulating portfolio optimization as finding the ground state of a risk Hamiltonian and applying counterdiabatic quantum annealing (including approximate counterdiabatic evolution) to accelerate convergence. They also introduce methods for dynamic risk assessment with time-dependent covariance matrices, structural decompositions (e.g., block-diagonal sectors), and hybrid quantum–classical decomposition strategies for practical implementations.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-021, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-038, C-039, C-044, C-048]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports theoretical results including exponentially compact representations of high-dimensional portfolios and covariance structures, qualitative links between correlation strength and entanglement, and accuracy bounds plus convergence theorems for quantum algorithms computing VaR, CVaR and higher-moment risk measures. It establishes complexity expressions for quantum risk computation, showing quadratic speedups for VaR and CVaR via amplitude estimation and characterizing conditions (e.g., portfolio size, sparsity, and covariance conditioning) under which polynomial to exponential speedups over classical Monte Carlo can emerge. For portfolio optimization, the authors prove that counterdiabatic annealing can reduce annealing time, guarantee convergence to the ground-state (optimal) portfolio under uniqueness assumptions, and achieve (1+ε)-approximate solutions with specified overhead. They further show that in dynamic settings quantum risk algorithms adapt to time-varying covariance matrices with polynomial overhead and bounded incremental update costs, while also deriving theoretical bounds on noise tolerance and on fundamental limits to quantum speedup. Overall, they summarize these as comprehensive theoretical foundations with provable performance guarantees and practical design principles.

They derive classical versus quantum complexity expressions and argue that quantum algorithms, particularly those based on amplitude estimation, can reduce this dependence to achieve quadratic speedups in precision and, for well-structured or sparse covariance matrices and sufficiently large portfolios, polynomial to exponential speedups in overall complexity relative to classical baselines.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several theoretical and practical limitations. It also derives a maximum tolerable gate error rate for the proposed quantum risk algorithms, indicating that noise levels above this threshold would compromise performance guarantees. More broadly, the authors frame their results as contingent on structural properties such as favorable conditioning or sparsity of the covariance matrix, implying that in ill-structured or highly noisy regimes the advantages may be limited.

It emphasizes providing provable performance guarantees, identifying structural conditions for quantum advantage, extending the theory to dynamic risk assessment, and offering practical guidelines and pathways for realizing quantum advantage in real-world risk management.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames insurance and actuarial work as fundamentally about modeling and evaluating random risky events, and notes that growing data size and model complexity in insurance create computational challenges that motivate new approaches. Within this context, it systematically organizes insurance problems into stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine-learning-based tasks, covering non-life (e.g., policy excess, IBNR), life (e.g., contract valuation, Lee–Carter mortality forecasting, multi-period optimization), and risk management tasks (e.g., VaR, cVaR, reinsurance allocation).

Concretely, they discuss quantum stochastic modeling with amplitude encoding and quantum Monte Carlo, QUBO-to-Ising mappings for optimization solvable via quantum annealing and QAOA-like methods, and implement specific algorithms: a discrete quantum excess evaluation circuit using n+2 qubits, a reinsurance variance-minimization Hamiltonian optimized with a constraint-preserving ansatz and measurement-based error mitigation, and a Lee–Carter mortality solver based on quantum singular value decomposition on 4 qubits with real mortality data.

In numerical simulations of the quantum excess evaluation algorithm, the estimated excess payment converges toward the truncated reference value as the number of qubits increases. On real hardware, the reinsurance allocation experiment shows the loss function decreasing during variational optimization, and the Lee–Carter QSVD experiment similarly reports decreasing loss and improved fit over optimization steps. The authors further assert that solving the Lee–Carter mortality forecasting model on a quantum processor with real mortality data constitutes the first implementation of an insurance-specific quantum algorithm on a quantum processor using real datasets and, more broadly, the first time an insurance-specific real-world data problem is experimentally solved on real quantum computers.

=== PAPER a0e970f7273f (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies variational quantum optimisation for combinatorial problems mapped to QUBO, including Max-Cut, number partitioning, and NP-complete portfolio optimisation, the latter being the core finance application considered. The authors emphasize using hybrid quantum-classical algorithms in the NISQ era and focus on how measurement outcomes are used to define the objective function rather than on changing the ansatz or measurement scheme.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work proposes Ascending-CVaR, an evolving objective function for VQE/QAOA that starts from a CVaR-style tail objective and gradually approaches the full energy expectation, inspired by prior tail-based objectives and adiabatic quantum computing. The method varies the CVaR tail parameter α during optimisation using predefined linear or sigmoid schedules, optionally truncating the evolution before α reaches 1 and scaling the number of shots as K/α, with evaluations carried out on the Qiskit Aer simulator using COBYLA for all problem instances and using overlap with the optimal solution as the primary metric with a 10% success threshold.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-010, C-011, C-019, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across Max-Cut, number partitioning, and portfolio optimisation, Ascending-CVaR generally achieves higher overlap with the ideal ground state and better success rates than standard expectation-value objectives and constant-α CVaR, and is presented as a heuristic that can help avoid sub-optimal minima. Linear and sigmoid schedules were found to have the most steady behaviour, with sigmoid slightly slower but crucial for rescuing hard number partitioning instances where baselines struggled, and the method often required fewer iterations to reach 10% overlap, especially for VQE on portfolio optimisation and number partitioning. The authors also report that VQE with Ascending-CVaR consistently outperforms QAOA in these tests, that Ascending-CVaR can erase spurious local minima as α increases, and that on easy regular Max-Cut instances all objectives perform similarly while improvements are more pronounced on harder, irregular instances.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-025, C-026, C-030, C-031, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-049, C-051]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not compare to purely classical optimisation solvers; instead, it compares different quantum objective functions—Ascending-CVaR, constant-α CVaR, and expectation-value objectives—within the same variational frameworks. The authors position their results relative to prior CVaR-based objectives (e.g., Barkoutsos et al.), but the performance comparisons are entirely between quantum variants rather than against classical algorithms.
    [codes: C-003, C-010, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-045, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that choosing a fixed α in constant-CVaR is non-obvious and instance-dependent, and that using a fixed small α can lead to parameters that do not maximise the state’s overlap with the solution, motivating—but not fully resolving—the hyperparameter-tuning challenge. They observe that increasing α all the way to 1 is not necessary and suggest truncating at a threshold ε to reduce iterations, implicitly noting a trade-off between information and computational cost. For QAOA, they report that solving Max-Cut and number partitioning with small-depth circuits does not seem promising and that CVaRαt-QAOA tends to produce flat states and fails to achieve high overlap on larger instances, with all QAOA-based methods performing very poorly on portfolio optimisation; they also note that sigmoid schedules can be slower than linear ones. Finally, they explicitly leave open how to systematically fix schedule-related degrees of freedom according to problem and instance features.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-027, C-042, C-047, C-050, C-026, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose investigating more systematic rules for setting Ascending-CVaR hyperparameters, such as schedule shape and rate, tailored to problem classes and instance features. They also suggest that other dynamic objective functions beyond their specific Ascending-CVaR design are worth exploring, and speculate that with better tailoring the method might turn instances considered hard for other objectives into easier ones.
    [codes: C-052, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing an evolving, Ascending-CVaR objective function for variational quantum optimisation that starts from a CVaR tail and gradually becomes the full energy expectation, inspired by adiabatic quantum computing, and in formally analysing how changing α preserves the global minimum while potentially removing local minima. The authors highlight that this dynamic objective is fundamentally different from merely adaptively selecting a single optimal α, and they argue that increasing α adds information that can erase false local minima and improve convergence quality and speed compared to all fixed-α choices.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-029, C-030, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses QUBO mappings for all combinatorial problems and evaluates performance via overlap with the optimal solution and a 10% overlap success threshold, enabling clear quantitative comparisons across instances. Experiments are run on IBM’s noiseless Qiskit Aer simulator with a fixed shot budget scaled as K/α and a single gradient-free classical optimiser (COBYLA) across all settings, and include explicit expectation-value (α=1) baselines and several constant-α CVaR baselines, with regular vs non-regular Max-Cut and varying instance hardness for number partitioning carefully delineated.
    [codes: C-012, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-044]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that Max-Cut is NP-hard, number partitioning exhibits a hard–easy phase transition and is dubbed the 'easiest hard problem', and portfolio optimisation is NP-complete, situating the benchmarks within computational complexity theory. It also observes that even small instances can have highly nontrivial energy landscapes filled with sub-optimal local minima, which motivates the need for heuristics like dynamic objectives and provides an illustrative example where local minima vanish as the objective evolves.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-032, C-031]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets large combinatorial optimisation tasks, including a portfolio optimisation problem, and frames them as searching a discrete solution space for (near-)optimal solutions using a restricted-depth quantum circuit suitable for near-term devices. Problems are expressed via a quality (objective) function over candidate solutions, with the goal of maximising the probability of sampling the highest-quality (or low-risk/high-return in the portfolio case) states from the quantum superposition.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-020, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce the Maximum Amplification Optimisation Algorithm (MAOA), which first prepares a quantum state in which solutions above a quality threshold are maximally amplified given a fixed rotation count r, then repeatedly prepares and measures this state to sample high-quality solutions efficiently. Technically, MAOA uses a complete-graph quantum walk / Grover-like amplitude amplification with binary marking, leveraging analytically derived parameters γ = π and t = π/N that make each pair of QWOA unitaries equivalent to a Grover iteration, and they also define a restricted Grover Adaptive Search (RGAS) as a comparison method. The method incorporates graph reduction by degeneracy, a two-part strategy (threshold-finding then repeated sampling), and a structured threshold search that doubles rotation counts to stay in a high-convergence regime before applying an adaptive search at fixed depth.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-041]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the paper shows that in the low-convergence regime MAOA attains a marked-solution probability scaling PLC(r,ρ) ≈ ρ(2r+1)², yielding an amplification factor of (2r+1)² over the initial marked probability and a linear upper bound on speedup over classical random sampling of lim_{μ→0} e_C/e_Q = 2r+1. They prove that a binary marking function maximises amplification of a marked solution, with the complete graph giving the largest amplification among investigated graphs, and they demonstrate numerically that MAOA’s performance converges to this theoretical upper bound. Across simulations on vehicle routing, portfolio optimisation, and an arbitrarily large normally distributed test problem, both MAOA and RGAS achieve substantial speedup over classical random sampling in finding optimal solutions, with MAOA consistently outperforming RGAS and efficiently generating large sets of near-optimal solutions.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-017, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare MAOA and RGAS to classical random sampling, modelling computational effort as the number of calls to the quality function f(x). They show that both quantum algorithms provide substantial speedup over classical random sampling in all tested problems, and they derive an analytical expression indicating that MAOA achieves a linear speedup factor of 2r+1 over classical random sampling in the small-target-ratio limit, with numerical results reported as converging to this bound. RGAS is found to be an effective speedup method relative to random sampling, but MAOA consistently outperforms RGAS because RGAS must randomise its rotation count.
    [codes: C-007, C-020, C-021, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-033, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper notes that expectation-value-based optimisation, as used in QAOA, does not provide maximum speedup for actually finding optimal solutions, especially under restricted circuit depth where limited amplification allows suboptimal states to dominate, implying MAOA’s advantage is specific to this success-probability objective. The authors acknowledge that a threshold chosen to maximise expectation value will not maximise amplification of the highest quality solutions, motivating their alternative threshold search but also indicating sensitivity to threshold selection. They further concede that the amplitude-amplification framework may not be depth-optimal: other circuit ansätze outside amplitude amplification could project into high-quality states with significantly less depth, though the overall speedup of such variational methods remains undemonstrated due to their computational expense. More broadly, they imply that their claimed performance is contingent on the low-convergence regime assumptions and on the ability to implement the required amplification unitaries at the prescribed depth.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-022, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that exploring circuit ansätze beyond amplitude-amplification-based approaches could potentially achieve high-quality state projection with much shallower circuits, but emphasize that such methods would need careful analysis of overall runtime including variational overhead. They also allude to extending MAOA’s flexibility for multi-dimensional optimisation, where repeated sampling of the amplified state could support richer multi-criteria financial decision-making.
    [codes: C-041, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The primary novelty claim is the introduction of the Maximum Amplification Optimisation Algorithm (MAOA), a non-variational, restricted-depth quantum optimisation algorithm that directly maximises amplification of optimal solutions under circuit-depth constraints, avoiding the heavy parameter optimisation of QAOA-style methods. Methodologically, the paper also claims novelty in deriving analytic amplification parameters (γ = π, t = π/N) that recover Grover-equivalent iterations on a complete graph with a binary marking function, defining a restricted-depth variant of Grover Adaptive Search (RGAS) as a benchmark, and quantifying MAOA’s speedup via a theoretically derived upper bound that their numerics demonstrate convergence to.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-005, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper defines computational effort explicitly as the number of calls to the quality function f(x) and assigns a concrete cost of 2r+1 evaluations per preparation and measurement of an amplified state, enabling fair comparison across algorithms. It uses a structured two-part MAOA procedure with a detailed threshold search that doubles the rotation count to remain in a high-convergence regime, followed by an adaptive search at fixed depth, and applies graph reduction by degeneracy to simplify analysis while preserving amplitude amplification behaviour. The simulations span a vehicle routing problem with observed approximate normal quality distribution and multiple degenerate optima, a portfolio optimisation instance transformed into a one-dimensional low-risk subset, and a synthetic arbitrarily large normal-quality problem, providing diverse but stylised evaluation scenarios.
    [codes: C-006, C-013, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper highlights that repeated sampling from the MAOA amplified state naturally yields large sets of near-optimal solutions, which the authors argue provides additional flexibility for multi-dimensional optimisation and could be particularly relevant in financial contexts where portfolios along a near-optimal frontier are valuable.
    [codes: C-041, C-042]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets investment portfolio management, motivated by the promise of quantum finance to address NP-hard portfolio optimization problems where classical methods struggle with market complexity, dynamics, and local minima. It formulates portfolio optimization as balancing diversification and risk‑adjusted returns under real-world constraints, aiming to explore a large solution space via quantum algorithms. The problem is instantiated on a small, three‑asset stock universe using historical data and covariance information.

Within the system architecture, a quantum ensemble module forms the core computational component, combining QAOA’s combinatorial optimization capabilities with VQE’s flexibility to optimize under user-defined objectives and constraints; QAOA approximately explores the solution space while VQE estimates the ground state (minimum) of the corresponding Hamiltonian. The pipeline includes user-driven input, portfolio data collection, and a ‘reality check’ step comparing advised purchase prices with lower price ranges, using a buy‑low acceptance principle and allowing iterative refinement via feedback.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-032]

They further claim that the ensemble model has a significantly higher probability of sampling the optimal portfolio and thus better navigates the search space, and conclude that it outperforms individual QAOA and VQE in risk‑adjusted returns and solution-space exploration.
    [codes: C-004, C-026, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-005]

The explicit qualitative comparison highlights that the classical solution selects only SPOT and META, whereas the QAOA and ensemble solutions diversify across all three assets (SPOT, META, MSFT), which the authors frame as reduced reliance on any single stock and thus superior risk management.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that current quantum computers are still at an early developmental stage, constrained by limited qubit counts and high error rates, which restricts practical deployment of their approach. Specific algorithmic claims include faster inner‑product computation in QSVMs and theoretically exponential speedups for QPCA. The authors report VaR and TVaR estimates with much tighter confidence intervals than the classical baseline and claim that the resulting optimization recommends a non‑proportional treaty (10M attachment, 50M limit, two 100%‑premium reinstatements) that improves Capital Efficiency from 0.35 to 0.42 and allows reinsurers to free up capital by narrowing confidence bands around tail metrics.

The classical VaR estimate of $37.3M (±$4.1M) is contrasted with a hybrid VaR of $32.0M (±$0.8M), and the authors interpret the higher classical VaR as a variance‑induced upward bias that leads to over‑capitalization relative to the tighter hybrid estimates.

=== PAPER b10591681791 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets NP-hard financial portfolio allocation by reformulating classical Markowitz-style portfolio optimization into a binary knapsack problem, where each stock is either included or excluded and the task is to maximize expected return under a capacity constraint. Expected returns derived from the Markowitz model are used as knapsack values, with unit weights for each asset and a capacity set to half the number of available stocks, motivated by the need to move from percentage allocations to discrete share-selection decisions.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors employ a hybrid QAOA-based approach enhanced with a Quantum Walk Mixer (QWM) and a QFT-based feasibility oracle (QWM-QAOA) to solve the knapsack-formulated portfolio problem. Feasibility is enforced via an oracle implemented with QFT-based weight addition and an offset for capacity checking, while the quantum walk mixer approximates a constrained mixing operator using additional ancilla qubits and Trotterization; QAOA parameters are tuned classically using SHGO and executed in Qiskit on simulators and IBM hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-015, C-016, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the QWM-QAOA achieves high approximation ratios on small portfolio instances: under ideal (noise-free) simulation it attains 100–96% approximation ratios for 2–8 stocks, with best performance at circuit depth p=3 and Trotter steps m=3, and sensitivity analysis shows approximation ratios of roughly 100–95% once p≥3 and m≥3. When noise is included via a fake backend, performance declines, and on real IBM hardware the approximation ratio drops further, reported between about 96% (2 stocks) and 51% (6 stocks), though the authors emphasize that the method still enhances exploration of the solution space and can yield robust portfolios with high approximation ratios in some noisy settings.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-007, C-010, C-023, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Performance is evaluated using approximation ratio, defined as the QAOA solution value relative to the optimal classical knapsack solution, and the authors argue that with suitable configuration their QAOA-based method can outperform classical optimization approaches for these portfolio instances. The formulation and metric explicitly tie the quantum results to best-known classical solutions, though detailed runtime or large-scale comparative analyses are not reported.
    [codes: C-016, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: implementing the exact desired mixing operator is challenging due to its Hamiltonian structure, requiring non-commuting elements, ancilla qubits, and Trotter approximations, which increases circuit complexity. The feasibility oracle and mixer architecture cause qubit counts to grow (N + n_f + 3 qubits), constraining scalability on current hardware, and the discussion explicitly notes that scaling QWM-QAOA to larger datasets is difficult given qubit and coherence-time limits. Experimentally, real hardware noise leads to substantial fidelity loss, with approximation ratios dropping below 50% in some cases, and the evaluation is restricted to very small portfolios of 2–8 stocks, limiting practical validation. They further note that richer market realism (e.g., transaction costs and dynamics) is not yet incorporated, and that noise in real devices remains an unresolved issue.
    [codes: C-032, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is directed toward improving robustness on real quantum hardware by addressing device noise (e.g., via error mitigation or improved implementations) and extending the financial realism of the test cases by incorporating longer historical data, transaction costs, and market dynamics into the portfolio model.
    [codes: C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as a novel QWM-QAOA framework for knapsack-based portfolio optimization that integrates a Quantum Walk Mixer with QAOA and a QFT-based feasibility oracle, enabling the algorithm to target feasible states, reduce computational complexity via shallow circuits, and improve solution quality compared with prior quantum approaches to knapsack and portfolio problems. The authors position this within a context of prior work on binary-encoded portfolio optimization, hard-constraint mixing, and quantum walk optimization but claim their specific combination and application to financial portfolios as new.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the workflow starts from real historical stock prices, computes daily and expected returns via a Markowitz-based model, and constructs knapsack instances with unit weights and capacity equal to half the number of assets. Experiments are implemented in Qiskit and run on ideal simulators, a noisy FakeWashington backend, and real IBM hardware, with SHGO used to optimize QAOA parameters; performance is systematically probed via sensitivity analysis over circuit depth and Trotter steps, and approximation ratio is consistently used as the evaluation metric relative to classical optima. The authors also situate their design against prior quantum portfolio and knapsack work, indicating awareness of existing constraint-handling techniques and quantum-walk-based optimizers.
    [codes: C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-036, C-037, C-041, C-042, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all extracted codes map to the primary reporting dimensions.
    [codes: —]
