=== PAPER b155d83ad4b5 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses combinatorial portfolio selection in finance, treating it as an NP-hard binary optimization problem and motivating the use of quantum algorithms for portfolio optimization. The portfolio optimization task is formulated as a binary quadratic (QUBO) model with a budget constraint encoded into the objective via a penalty term, enabling mapping to a cost Hamiltonian suitable for quantum solvers.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-015]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study benchmarks two variational quantum approaches—QAOA and SamplingVQE—by mapping the QUBO portfolio model to a cost Hamiltonian and solving it on parameterized circuits. QAOA alternates evolution under cost and mixing Hamiltonians, while SamplingVQE uses a general parameterized circuit U(θ), and the authors test several ansatz architectures (TwoLocal, EfficientSU2, PauliTwoDesign, RealAmplitudes), analyzing convergence via cost differences between successive iterations.
    [codes: C-002, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Both QAOA and VQE-type methods effectively minimize the cost function, yet the portfolios they produce often violate financial criteria like diversification and realistic risk exposure, highlighting a disparity between algorithmic performance and financial applicability. In the 4-asset case, QAOA shows pronounced instability and variance, whereas the RealAmplitudes ansatz converges fastest, though deeper circuits require more evaluations and early convergence in shallow circuits may be misleading. For the 10-asset case, QAOA performance improves with depth while PauliTwoDesign remains stable; larger, more diversified asset sets yield stronger overall returns, with four of five 10-asset portfolios producing positive future-period returns. Nonetheless, the best-returning portfolio is not produced by any circuit, multiple high-probability bitstrings indicate selection uncertainty in correlated small sets, and experts consistently observe that portfolios containing Microsoft, Google, and Goldman Sachs perform well, while those including Tesla or Apple often underperform.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-022, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present explicit quantitative comparisons against classical optimization baselines; instead, it frames quantum computing as a potentially scalable alternative for generating candidate portfolios in an NP-hard setting. The claimed advantage is positioned at the level of enabling efficient exploration of candidate portfolios rather than demonstrated runtime or solution-quality superiority over classical methods.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress that good convergence of quantum optimizers does not guarantee financially suitable portfolios, underscoring a key limitation of using cost-function minimization as the primary success metric. They note that early convergence in shallow circuits may signal insufficient expressibility rather than true optimization, and that increasing circuit depth does not necessarily improve portfolio quality in small, highly correlated asset sets, with QAOA showing increasing variance and sensitivity to depth and initialization. On the data and modeling side, they acknowledge that relying solely on historical pricing data means the quantum models miss evolving market dynamics and external forward-looking factors, and that historical-only approaches cannot incorporate such variables. Additionally, they recognize that real quantum hardware will introduce noise and decoherence that may further degrade output quality, beyond what is observed in idealized simulations.

    [codes: C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in systematically benchmarking QAOA and SamplingVQE (with multiple ansatzes) for real-market portfolio optimization and, especially, in introducing an Expert Analysis Evaluation framework as a complementary post-processing stage. This expert layer is intended to ensure that quantum-generated portfolios are statistically sound, economically interpretable, practically feasible, and aligned with real-world conditions, positioning expert judgment as a necessary refinement mechanism in quantum-assisted decision pipelines.

=== PAPER b5820c538b42 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets solving linear systems arising from a mean–variance portfolio-optimization problem, formulated as a convex quadratic program and then converted into a linear system via Lagrange multipliers so it can be tackled with HHL-type algorithms. The authors frame this within a broader goal of enabling application-oriented benchmarking on today’s limited quantum hardware by adapting algorithms to device constraints rather than aiming at speedup.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work builds on the Hybrid HHL algorithm and proposes Hybrid HHL++, which introduces two key modifications: a spectral scaling algorithm to choose a scaling factor γ that makes the most effective use of the m ancilla qubits in quantum phase estimation, and a heuristic circuit compression scheme that leverages a semiclassical QPE with inverse QFT implemented via dynamic-circuit features such as mid-circuit measurement, reset, conditional logic, and qubit reuse. The hybridization also includes classically computing the matrix exponential used for Hamiltonian simulation and obtaining classical access to A’s eigenvalues, so that the number of controlled rotations in the eigenvalue inversion scales only with the number of distinct eigenvalues, and negative eigenvalues are handled via absolute values and two’s complement encoding.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim Hybrid HHL++ enables the largest-to-date experimental demonstrations of HHL for an application, including executions with two-qubit gate depth up to 291 on real hardware. They empirically validate their spectral scaling procedure by showing that certain γ choices (e.g., γ = 50, later refined to γ = 100) produce output distributions concentrated near zero and improve eigenvalue separation, while invalid choices (e.g., γ = 3200) are rejected. Benchmarking semiclassical QPE demonstrates that it uses fewer qubits and gates, with two-qubit gate savings growing quadratically with precision, and still yields very high fidelity distributions compared to noiseless simulations. End-to-end, the HHL-based portfolio optimization solutions on hardware exhibit high inner products with analytical solutions, with a median hardware–simulation gap of about 4.17%, and further noise-scaling studies indicate that reducing fault probabilities improves both fidelity and solution quality.
    [codes: C-005, C-022, C-026, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical computation appears in two roles: first, as a hybrid component where eigenvalues of A and the unitary e^{2πiγA} are computed classically, effectively replacing some quantum subroutines and thereby removing the asymptotic speedup associated with textbook HHL; second, as a benchmark reference, where the quality of the HHL solution is quantified by the inner product between the quantum state and the classically computed optimal portfolio solution using a controlled-SWAP test.
    [codes: C-007, C-011, C-012, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly state several limitations. They assume an exact-phase-estimation-friendly scaling γ such that all relevant eigenvalues lie in a discrete set, which simplifies analysis but is non-trivial in practice. They acknowledge that using semiclassical QPE for eigenvalue estimation collapses the ancilla state, so it cannot be used in the eigenvalue inversion step of HHL, and their circuit compression strategy is characterized as a heuristic rather than a rigorously optimal method. They further note that noise on current hardware significantly limits the size of linear systems that can be tackled and anticipate that larger systems will exhibit decreased solution quality. Crucially, they make no claim of any quantum speedup for Hybrid HHL++, presenting it instead as a step toward hardware evaluation rather than performance improvement.
    [codes: C-010, C-023, C-025, C-041, C-043, C-044]

    [codes: C-043, C-041]

They further highlight that their implementation avoids currently infeasible quantum arithmetic and exponentially deep uniformly controlled rotation gates, and that, to the best of their knowledge, this work provides both the largest-to-date application-oriented HHL experiments and the first benchmarking of semiclassical QPE performance on trapped-ion devices, which they position as a viable near-term benchmark for application-oriented evaluation.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-008, C-009, C-015, C-021, C-022, C-026]

The spectral scaling component includes a clear target (stretching the spectrum over the available discrete range) and concrete algorithms for choosing and validating γ, including handling of negative eigenvalues, which are then validated on small portfolio instances. For experimental evaluation, the authors use a fidelity metric to compare hardware probability distributions with noiseless simulations and employ controlled-SWAP tests to compare quantum and classical portfolio solutions. === PAPER b58f4a78e015 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies generic constrained combinatorial optimization problems that are hard for both classical and quantum methods, including a real-world financial use case of bond ETF basket optimization formulated with sector-exposure and other portfolio-style constraints. Constraints are modeled as Hamiltonian terms whose feasible subspace defines the allowed portfolios or discrete decisions, while the objective Hamiltonian encodes problem-specific goals such as maximizing value or minimizing mismatch to a benchmark.
    [codes: C-008, C-007, C-039, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce Q-CHOP, a quantum constrained Hamiltonian optimization algorithm that keeps a constraint Hamiltonian always on so that the system evolves entirely within the feasible subspace, while an objective Hamiltonian is slowly rotated to map a worst feasible state into a best feasible state along an adiabatic path. Q-CHOP relies on the insight that worst feasible states are often easy to prepare, uses a penalty-like scalar together with total runtime as its two free parameters, and includes variants that can start from any feasible state, handle odd and non-odd objectives via global or local rotations, and support inequality constraints through slack-variable encodings with bosonic or truncated finite-dimensional modes and specially engineered mixing terms that vanish at the endpoints.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-010, C-011, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-039, C-044]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across a wide range of benchmark problems—graph problems like maximum independent set and directed minimum dominating set, knapsack, combinatorial auctions, and a bond ETF basket optimization use case—the simulations indicate that Q-CHOP consistently achieves higher in-constraint approximation ratios and substantially higher probabilities of reaching optimal or near-optimal solutions than a standard penalty-based adiabatic annealing baseline. The authors derive a perturbative guarantee that, for small objective scaling, Q-CHOP outputs feasible states with probability 1−O(β²), show that on MIS its optimal-state probability remains roughly constant with system size at runtimes scaling as N² while the baseline decays, and observe that results on DMDS closely mirror MIS, that Q-CHOP dominates SQAA on all tested knapsack and ETF instances, and that it maintains an advantage on combinatorial auctions despite instance-to-instance variability and plateau behavior. They also note an equivalence between Q-CHOP and a prior non-Abelian adiabatic mixing algorithm on MIS, and interpret one additional term in their construction as an approximate counterdiabatic driving component that may help performance.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-017, C-020, C-021, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The primary comparison is to the standard quantum adiabatic algorithm (SQAA) that uses a large penalty factor λ added to the objective plus a separate driver Hamiltonian, where selecting λ is known to be difficult and runtime mis-specification can lead to infeasible outputs. The authors benchmark Q-CHOP directly against this penalty-based annealing approach and report that Q-CHOP consistently and significantly outperforms SQAA across MIS, DMDS, knapsack, combinatorial auctions, and the bond ETF basket optimization, both in terms of average in-constraint approximation ratio and in the probability of finding optimal or near-optimal solutions, with particularly favorable apparent scaling on MIS and mirrored advantages on DMDS and the other problem classes.
    [codes: C-005, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that Q-CHOP can struggle or fail on problem classes where the feasible subspace is weakly connected or disconnected under the objective-induced mixer, potentially making it impossible to reach good or optimal solutions if they lie in different connected components from the chosen worst feasible state. They also note that their generalization from requiring a worst feasible state to allowing any feasible initial state incurs costs: the modified objective can have quadratically larger norm, and energy degeneracy can suppress population transfer to the final ground state by 1/d*. For inequality constraints implemented via slack variables, they highlight that the induced fragmentation of Hilbert space into sectors labeled by slack values and the growth of the mixing term norm with slack dimension raise serious scalability concerns, and they stress that it is desirable to avoid costs that grow multiplicatively with the number of inequality constraints. In the experiments, they further caution that for real-valued objectives, demanding exact optima is too strict, motivating the use of near-optimal success criteria.
    [codes: C-009, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-031, C-035, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions include developing alternative strategies for enforcing inequality constraints and engineering better adiabatic paths within the feasible subspace, as the current slack-variable construction may not scale well. The authors also emphasize the need to test, validate, and refine their relaxed version of Q-CHOP that starts from arbitrary feasible states, and more generally to build a deeper theoretical understanding of Q-CHOP with quantitative performance guarantees or bounds. They further speculate that discretized variants of Q-CHOP, or related constructions, could improve the performance of QAOA and RQAOA, suggesting work on variational or gate-based adaptations.
    [codes: C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s central contribution is the proposal of Q-CHOP, a new quantum algorithmic framework for constrained optimization that enforces the constraint Hamiltonian throughout the evolution while using the objective solely as a mixer to rotate from easily prepared worst feasible states to high-quality feasible solutions, thereby separating and reinterpreting the roles of objective and penalty compared with standard approaches. They additionally claim novelty in providing a generalized construction that can start from any feasible state, extending the method to non-odd objectives and inequality constraints, and in showing that for MIS Q-CHOP recovers and unifies a previously specialized non-Abelian adiabatic mixing algorithm under a single general-purpose constrained optimization scheme.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: All results are obtained via exact classical numerical integration of the Schrödinger equation using a high-accuracy ODE solver, with clearly specified tolerances, and performance is evaluated using two metrics: an in-constraint approximation ratio defined solely over feasible states and a probability of finding optimal or near-optimal states, with a relaxed success criterion for real-valued objectives where exact optimality is deemed too strict. The experimental suite spans several textbook combinatorial problems and a structured financial benchmark, and the setup includes systematic parameter choices and explicit descriptions of inequality-constraint handling, but implementation is on simulators only and there is no mention of code release or hardware tests.
    [codes: C-007, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-041, C-043]

=== PAPER b97e7f0690c5 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses discrete portfolio optimization under Modern Portfolio Theory, aiming to balance expected return and risk via an objective that combines variance and expected return, subject to a budget constraint. The discrete formulation represents portfolios as binary selection vectors indicating whether each asset is included, with the budget simplified to a limit on the number of invested assets, and the constrained problem is recast as a QUBO using a penalty term to enable quantum treatment.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors build on quantum optimization approaches such as VQE and QAOA, which they state offer logarithmic complexity relative to classical methods, and formulate the portfolio problem as a QUBO/Ising Hamiltonian to be solved by these algorithms. They propose a specific quantum circuit design called QPO that uses amplitude encoding and quantum compiling, requires 2n+2 qubits to encode both the portfolio and return vectors, and employs a control qubit to switch between operating as VQE/QAOA and computing the return via an MCSWAP-TEST-based overlap estimation, where return is expressed as a normalized inner product and extracted from measurement probabilities.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In simulation, the quantum portfolios obtained with QPO are reported to be consistent with classical solutions, with an average Hamming distance of 0.092 to the target portfolios across tested instances. QAOA achieves near-zero Hamming distance over all tested asset counts, while VQE’s Hamming distance decreases as the number of assets increases. For the overlap-estimation branch, the mean squared error between the exact and MCSWAP-TEST-estimated overlap stays below an acceptance threshold of 10^-2, and the authors note that the MCSWAP-TEST subcircuit consumes less computational time than the optimization subcircuits.
    [codes: C-004, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical linear-programming-based portfolios are used as targets, and the quantum results are compared via average Hamming distance, with an overall average of 0.092 indicating close but not exact agreement. The authors also argue that for larger portfolios, classical computation of the optimal portfolio may become much more expensive than using QPO, contrasting classical scaling with their claimed logarithmic-complexity quantum methods, although this is presented as a prospective advantage rather than an empirically demonstrated one.
    [codes: C-004, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-002, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that the potential computational advantage of QPO for large portfolios is contingent and speculative, noting that when scaling to larger portfolios, classical computation might be much more expensive than using QPO but that any such quantum advantage comes at the cost of needing complete certainty of the outcome. They also note that practical implementation would require further development of encoding schemes and Hamiltonian simulation to reduce quantum resource requirements, implicitly limiting near-term deployability.
    [codes: C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is directed toward developing more efficient encoders and Hamiltonian simulation techniques to reduce quantum resources needed by QPO, and toward conducting experiments on portfolios with larger numbers of assets to better understand performance and scalability.
    [codes: C-040, C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is the QPO quantum circuit design, which extends standard VQE-style circuits by adding a switch mode controlled by a dedicated qubit, allowing the same circuit either to perform portfolio optimization (via VQE/QAOA) or to calculate the return value through overlap estimation; this dual functionality is presented as offering more functions than a normal VQE circuit.

Evaluation is based on small portfolio sizes (2 to 16 assets), uses average Hamming distance to classical linear-programming portfolios as a main metric, and separately assesses the MCSWAP-TEST via mean squared error to exact overlaps, with the paper also noting that MCSWAP-TEST is less time-consuming than the optimization routines, and that for small asset counts VQE runs faster than QAOA within the QPO framework.

=== PAPER bb0210fb8e67 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles portfolio optimization, i.e., finding asset allocations that balance risk and return, and notes that this task faces significant computational bottlenecks when formulated from real market data (large, ill‑conditioned linear systems) in Black’s equality‑constrained model. The authors position quantum computing as an alternative approach for solving this formulation, focusing on quantum linear solvers applied to the Lagrange system derived from Black’s model.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work extends the HHL quantum linear solver to a portfolio optimization setting, modifying the circuit design to incorporate mean‑variance/Black’s model structure and introducing equivalent scaling of the Lagrange equations via two factors s1 and s2 so as to reduce the condition number while preserving model structure. It adds a min–max eigenvalue model: the Lagrange matrix is standardized, Hamiltonian evolution time is set to π to obtain a more convenient mapping between QPE phases and eigenvalues, the normalization constant is set to the minimum eigenvalue, and a support vector regression model predicts only the minimum and maximum eigenvalues needed to set HHL hyperparameters; the overall SAPO system is implemented in Qiskit with SciPy and scikit‑learn on classical side. Complexity and accuracy are defined via custom metrics: a composite complexity metric combining qubit count, CNOT count and depth, and an accuracy metric based on cosine similarity between quantum and reference weight vectors.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-010, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that SAPO reduces their composite complexity metric by about 34.64–36.94% compared to basic HHL while maintaining specified error tolerances, with particularly large reductions in CNOT count (up to 99.996% in a 2‑asset case), largely attributed to a substantial decrease in the Lagrange matrix condition number by at least 98.59%. On accuracy, SAPO achieves on average 1.52× higher cosine‑similarity accuracy than Qiskit HHL and 1.46× higher than hybrid HHL under fixed 5‑qubit QPE or fixed asset settings; ablation analysis shows the scaling factor is the dominant contributor, improving accuracy by roughly 1.74–1.96×, while the eigenvalue predictor yields smaller but still positive gains (roughly 1.05–1.54×). The eigenvalue predictor itself typically attains relative errors within 50% on predicted eigenvalues, and the authors observe that static scaling factors optimized per dataset cluster in a small region, supporting the claim that a fixed factor can, on average, achieve strong condition‑number reduction.
    [codes: C-005, C-023, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Within the quantum‑algorithm landscape, SAPO is compared primarily to basic HHL, Qiskit’s HHL implementation, hybrid HHL and a quantum Ising‑model‑based solver: the Ising solver can only output binary buy/no‑buy decisions, whereas HHL‑based approaches including SAPO yield concrete portfolio weights. Basic HHL is described as offering these concrete weights but suffering from overwhelming circuit‑scale complexity, and hybrid HHL is said to reduce some numerical burden yet still require many qubits to resolve eigenvalues precisely; SAPO’s reported ~35% complexity reduction and 1.46–1.52× accuracy gains are measured relative to these HHL‑family baselines using the composite complexity and cosine‑similarity metrics. The work does not provide a detailed empirical comparison against a fully classical portfolio optimizer; rather, it focuses on improving quantum linear solvers that operate on a classical Black’s‑model formulation built from historical financial data.
    [codes: C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors identify that existing quantum methods for portfolio optimization face a fundamental trade‑off between scalability and accuracy, arising from either poor scalability (e.g., large condition numbers in realistic Lagrange matrices) or insufficient solution precision. They attribute several limitations of prior HHL and hybrid HHL approaches to their neglect of financial theory and historical financial information, which leaves numerical properties (such as ill‑conditioning) unaddressed and forces the use of many qubits for accurate eigenvalue estimation. For SAPO itself, the eigenvalue predictor exhibits notable challenges: some eigenvalues lie close to zero, making them difficult to predict and leading to relatively large percentage errors even when absolute errors are small, an issue the authors explicitly connect to the observed prediction‑error behavior.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-012, C-020, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The claimed contribution is a SAPO framework that integrates financial theory and historical data characteristics directly into the design of a quantum HHL‑based portfolio solver, thereby addressing both scalability and accuracy. Novel elements include: an equivalent scaling transformation of Black’s model using static, dataset‑level scaling factors that substantially reduce the condition number while preserving the model structure; a min–max eigenvalue model that uses standardized Lagrange matrices and historical data to refine HHL hyperparameters; and an SVR‑based eigenvalue predictor chosen to balance predictive performance with limited classical training cost so as to preserve the intended quantum advantages.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-031, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, SAPO is evaluated on portfolio instances built from real historical stock‑market data: the authors construct a dataset by collecting thousands of stocks over 251 days, computing returns, and deriving expected returns and covariance matrices to form Lagrange matrices, which are then padded to power‑of‑two size for HHL compatibility. They explicitly define evaluation metrics—a composite complexity metric based on qubits, CNOT count and depth, and an accuracy metric based on cosine similarity—and conduct ablation studies to isolate the contributions of the scaling factor and eigenvalue predictor, as well as an offline comparison of SVR against more complex models, ultimately selecting SVR to avoid heavy classical training that could undermine quantum advantage. However, the model is described as a static, dataset‑dependent construction grounded in historical financial data, which may limit its direct generalization beyond the studied datasets; the authors also emphasize that their complexity gains come from condition‑number reduction and are reported via the bespoke complexity metric rather than end‑to‑end wall‑clock benchmarks.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-024, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that SAPO’s resource savings, particularly in the number of QPE qubits and CNOT gates, arise from its scaling technique that shrinks the condition number, thereby reducing the minimum QPE qubits required to meet a given error tolerance; this links financial‑theory‑driven preprocessing directly to quantum resource estimates. It also highlights that leveraging both financial theory and historical data is central to the design philosophy of SAPO, in contrast to prior approaches that treat the Lagrange system purely as a numerical linear algebra object.
    [codes: C-014, C-019, C-029, C-040]

=== PAPER bbf0e3662d3c (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames its contribution as an accessible guide for practitioners interested in applying quantum computing to hard optimisation problems, with a primary focus on discrete optimisation tasks such as Max‑Cut and QUBO/Ising formulations, which are motivated by their classical intractability and straightforward mappings to quantum models. It emphasises that classical algorithms for problems like TSP rely on heuristics and approximations that can still be time‑consuming, and argues that the existence of simple mappings (e.g., Max‑Cut to Ising) is itself a reason to study certain problem classes. The work explicitly targets the near‑term NISQ era, focusing on problems that can be realistically attempted given current noisy hardware constraints.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-007, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-026, C-027, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper surveys optimisation approaches on both analog and digital quantum computers, including quantum annealing/adiabatic algorithms and gate‑based variational methods such as QAOA. For analog devices, it explains that quantum annealing performance depends on the adiabatic runtime governed by the minimum energy gap, and that the solvable problem class is tightly linked to the hardware Hamiltonian. For digital methods, it details universal gate‑based computation, superposition and measurement, and the structure of variational algorithms in which classical optimisers tune circuit parameters; specifically, QAOA is described as alternating cost and mixer unitaries, with the mixer ensuring non‑trivial dynamics. The paper further highlights standard mappings from QUBO to Ising Hamiltonians and notes strategies like parameter initialisation and divide‑and‑conquer schemes to reduce classical optimisation overhead and qubit requirements.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report and synthesise several results from the literature on QAOA and related optimisation methods: when realistic noise and compilation constraints are taken into account, cited studies find that QAOA at modest depths (p=4,8) can only handle graphs roughly 20 times smaller than the best classical solvers for a given time‑to‑solution, indicating limited practical advantage so far. They also highlight evidence that optimal QAOA parameters depend on topological features of the problem graph rather than specific instances or system sizes, and that divide‑and‑conquer strategies can on average reduce qubit requirements by about 42%. Hardware tests cited in the review suggest that planar graph instances show roughly size‑independent performance, while the paper notes that QAOA performance evidence overall remains mixed, with some hope for improvement at higher depths.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper consistently frames quantum optimisation methods in relation to classical heuristics and exact solvers. It underscores that classical approaches to NP‑hard problems like TSP and QUBO often rely on heuristics that trade optimality for efficiency, and that quantum algorithms for these problems are likewise typically approximate rather than exact. In benchmarking discussions, the authors cite studies where, under realistic noise and compilation overheads, QAOA at depths p=4 and p=8 only solved Max‑Cut instances on graphs about 20 times smaller than those handled by the best classical solver for the same time‑to‑solution, illustrating that current implementations do not yet outperform state‑of‑the‑art classical methods. They also discuss that stoquastic annealing may be classically easy to simulate, which further weakens the case for advantage over classical algorithms in that regime.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-017, C-028, C-029, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper is explicit about multiple limitations of current quantum optimisation approaches. At a high level, it stresses that true quantum advantage has not yet been demonstrated in practice and remains unclear for the techniques surveyed, especially in light of the approximate nature of quantum algorithms for NP‑hard problems. It notes hardware constraints in the NISQ era—limited qubit counts and allowable circuit depth—which restrict problem sizes that can be tackled, and observes that better hardware alone may not resolve core issues because finding good variational parameters can itself be NP‑hard and may not scale efficiently. On the algorithmic side, it highlights that superposition alone does not yield advantage, that entanglement is a poorly understood yet hypothesised key resource, and that analog quantum computers (e.g., annealers) are hardware‑specific, non‑universal, and potentially classically simulable when using stoquastic Hamiltonians. Furthermore, the adiabatic runtime is constrained by the minimum energy gap, so small gaps can render annealing impractically slow. For variational algorithms, the classical outer‑loop optimisation is NP‑hard and can dominate costs, and good solution quality appears to require hard constraints in the problem encoding, which increase circuit complexity and resource demands. The authors also emphasise that noise and compilation overhead can severely erode potential speedups and even drive quantum states toward maximally mixed, classically samplable regimes, further limiting practical advantage.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-022, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-029]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors argue that the field urgently needs more realistic and thorough benchmarking of quantum optimisation methods using noisy simulations and real hardware, to clarify their true performance relative to classical algorithms under practical conditions. They imply that such benchmarking should systematically explore the impact of noise, compilation constraints, and hardware topology on algorithmic performance and approximation quality.
    [codes: C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as a practitioner‑oriented guide that consolidates and explains the landscape of quantum algorithms for optimisation problems with a focus on NISQ‑era applicability, aiming to set clear expectations for the community regarding what current techniques can and cannot realistically achieve. It emphasises providing accessible information to newcomers, clarifying common misconceptions (e.g., about superposition and entanglement), and synthesising mixed empirical evidence on algorithms like QAOA rather than claiming new algorithmic breakthroughs or experimental results.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-028, C-029, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: As a conceptual and survey‑style paper, the work primarily synthesises existing results rather than presenting new experiments, and thus does not provide datasets or implementation details typical of empirical studies. Methodologically, the authors’ main emphasis is on the need for rigorous and realistic benchmarking—including noisy simulations and tests on actual hardware—to properly assess algorithmic performance; this implies their view that much of the current evidence base is limited by idealised assumptions and insufficiently thorough comparisons. They also adopt standard evaluation metrics such as approximation ratios when discussing QAOA case studies, reflecting alignment with common benchmarking practices in the literature.
    [codes: C-025, C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several cross‑cutting conceptual points do not fit neatly into other dimensions but inform the general perspective of the paper. These include the idea that simple mappings between problem classes and quantum models are themselves a reason to study those problems, that measurement collapses superposition to a random bitstring and thus necessitates amplitude‑amplifying algorithm design, and that noise can push quantum states toward Gibbs‑like maximally mixed states, providing a framework for reasoning about when quantum advantage is likely to be lost. The paper also highlights structural observations, such as QUBO’s exponentially large search space and the dependence of approximation quality on enforcing hard constraints, which shape how practitioners should think about modelling optimisation problems for quantum devices.
    [codes: C-007, C-019, C-026, C-033, C-035]

=== PAPER c0d24cf1b7ed (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the challenge that reinforcement-learning trading agents often overfit to specific stocks and fail to transfer to new but similar assets, framing this as a need for fast adaptation to changing portfolios in stock trading. It models stock trading as a Markov Decision Process where actions are portfolio weights and rewards are normalized logarithmic returns, with the explicit goal of using meta-reinforcement learning to train on multiple portfolios so that a model can quickly adapt to new portfolios using few samples. The stated aim is not to maximize profit per se, but to demonstrate how reinforcement learning, meta-learning, and quantum computing can learn to trade in a practical stock-market environment.
    [codes: C-010, C-014, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-001, C-003]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum approach uses continuous-variable quantum computing to build quantum neural networks (QNNs) that serve as function approximators within meta-reinforcement learning algorithms. The authors implement quantum adaptations of MAML and CAVIA (Q-MAML and Q-CAVIA), encoding stock closing prices into separate qumodes via displacement gates and, in some variants, using beamsplitter gates to couple wires; they stress that with an appropriate universal gate set, CV quantum circuits can approximate arbitrary functions. Quantum meta-learning models are trained on a simulated CV quantum computer with small portfolios containing two Consumer Cyclical stocks and a limited number of model parameters and epochs.
    [codes: C-002, C-012, C-020, C-021, C-005, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-053]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For the classical meta-learning models (MAML and CAVIA), the authors report that after meta-training, both can adapt to a new portfolio using only about 0.01% of the original training samples (20 epochs vs. 2500) while achieving performance within 0.1% ROI of a buy‑and‑hold benchmark. Quantitatively, the benchmark portfolio grows to $10,085.50 (0.86% ROI), while MAML and CAVIA respectively achieve $10,075.89 (0.76% ROI) and $10,016.01 (0.16% ROI), with MAML additionally showing lower return variability than CAVIA. For the quantum models on a different, smaller 2‑stock problem, all variants underperform the (loss‑making) market benchmark but the authors highlight that quantum meta-learned models with only about 60–65 parameters and 25 training epochs display learning patterns similar to much larger classical models, and that beamsplitter-equipped circuits systematically improve ROI over their non‑beamsplitter counterparts. They conclude that their quantum meta-learning algorithms Q-MAML and Q-CAVIA are able to learn to trade stock portfolios, albeit with limited performance.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-008, C-055, C-058, C-059, C-060]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Within the classical meta-learning family, MAML outperforms CAVIA on the test portfolio by 0.60% ROI and exhibits substantially lower standard deviation of returns (11.25 less), indicating more stable performance. Both classical meta-learned models can reach a trading performance comparable to the buy‑and‑hold benchmark, remaining within 0.1% ROI of the market value while reducing adaptation training from 2500 to 20 epochs, which the authors interpret as a practical efficiency gain. In comparing classical and quantum models, they emphasize that the quantum models, despite having orders of magnitude fewer parameters and fewer training epochs, show a similar qualitative learning pattern to the much larger classical meta-learned networks, but the quantum portfolios’ realized ROIs remain worse than the benchmarks and no quantitative quantum advantage is demonstrated.
    [codes: C-007, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-054, C-053, C-008, C-055, C-058, C-059]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The study’s trading environment is restricted to backtesting only, explicitly excluding live trading and associated execution complexities. The authors assume zero slippage, zero market impact, and no transaction costs, all of which simplify trading but limit financial realism. On the quantum side, hardware constraints mean they can simulate only up to 5 qumodes, which forces them to use 2‑stock portfolios and to halve the dataset from 360 to 180 days versus the classical experiments; they also limit quantum training to 25 epochs and use very small models (up to 65 parameters), noting that these constraints prevent the quantum models from sufficiently learning distinct trading strategies between Q‑MAML and Q‑CAVIA. Collectively, these limitations constrain both the economic realism and the scalability or expressiveness of the quantum experiments.
    [codes: C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-052, C-053]

They propose exploring larger, deeper quantum neural networks, training for more epochs, and extending to portfolios with more stocks to better assess the potential of their approach at more realistic scales.
    [codes: C-056, C-057]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to be the first to apply both classical meta-learning and quantum meta-learning techniques to enhance stock trading. More specifically, the authors assert that, to the best of their knowledge, they are the first to develop quantum meta-learning algorithms, instantiated as Q-MAML and Q-CAVIA for stock trading tasks, and they reiterate in the abstract that they are the first to apply these ideas to stock trading.
    [codes: C-009, C-013, C-060]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper combines reinforcement learning, meta-learning (MAML and CAVIA), and evolution strategies (ES/NES) as the optimizer, motivated by the claim that ES is effective and scales well in parallel across many CPUs. MAML is implemented using the standard two-loop structure with saved gradients for meta-parameter updates, whereas CAVIA introduces context parameters φ to avoid higher-order derivatives, with one context parameter per stock in the classical experiments. The classical network architecture is relatively large (two hidden layers of size 50×100 and 500×500, totalling around 257,500 parameters), with NES hyperparameters (learning rate 0.03, σ=0.1, population size 15) and a meta-training schedule of 2500 epochs, chosen because training progress slowed significantly by then. Actions are encoded as portfolio weights and rewards are normalized logarithmic returns to aid learning, and the stock-market environment is framed explicitly as an MDP. On the quantum side, the authors use continuous-variable quantum neural networks with carefully designed input encoding via displacement gates and design their quantum experiments so that Q‑MAML and Q‑CAVIA receive the same inputs for fair comparison. The authors repeatedly stress that their goal is to demonstrate learning behavior on a practical stock-market environment, not to construct an immediately profitable trading system, and they couch their claims about ES scalability and CV universality as supporting rationale rather than empirically validated within this paper.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also articulates broader conceptual goals and framing: it emphasizes meta-learning as a solution to portfolio changes in financial markets and portrays recent developments in quantum computing as a promising route to training algorithms quickly on large volumes of market data. It reiterates the general aim of meta-learning to obtain models that generalize or adapt to new tasks and environments without having seen them during training, and frames the overall contribution as a practical demonstration of these ideas on the stock market rather than a profit-maximizing system.

=== PAPER c0da85ef2954 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies a portfolio diversification task that is discretized and formulated as a Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on correlation graphs derived from SP500 stock data, where vertices represent assets and edges connect pairs whose absolute correlation exceeds a threshold. MIS is written as a binary quadratically constrained problem with an independent-set constraint (no adjacent selected vertices), which is then encoded into a cost/constraint Hamiltonian suitable for QAOA. The broader framing is that such MIS-based portfolio diversification is a hard optimization problem where QAOA may offer a route to quantum advantage over classical methods.
    [codes: C-005, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a QAOA/Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz specifically tailored to MIS, with a cost Hamiltonian over single-qubit terms and a constraint operator encoding edge penalties, together with a mixer that irreducibly commutes with the constraint so that evolution remains within the independent-set subspace. The mixer is built from vertex–neighborhood generators, which are grouped via a randomized partitioning strategy to reduce implementation depth, and its exponential is simplified using the projection property of the generators; the full QAOA circuit alternates these mixer and phase-separation unitaries starting from the all-zero state. Parameters are trained using gradient-based optimization with the parameter-shift rule, and the Train-and-Scale procedure warm-starts larger instances from smaller ones while growing circuit depth by inserting new layers—implemented as identity layers in the middle of the circuit—followed by retraining on families of subinstances.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-013, C-014, C-032, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On portfolio-diversification MIS instances generated from SP500 data, the Train-and-Scale QAOA achieves what the authors term high average-quality solutions, with average approximation (gap/ratio) values reported as below about 0.4–0.5 across tested settings and a small sampling complexity to obtain the best solution. Empirically, maintaining approximately linear growth in depth p with instance size n (e.g., p = 54 for n = 30) preserves good approximation quality and only modestly increases sampling complexity for the hardest instances with n ≤ 30. The authors also claim that a modest increase in p-depth can be sufficient to solve increasingly complex hard optimization instances and assert that, to their knowledge, this work reports scaling to the largest instance sizes used so far for QAOA-p on such problems.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-033, C-046, C-048, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares the sampling complexity scaling of Train-and-Scale QAOA to simulated annealing on the same portfolio-diversification MIS instances and reports a lower empirical scaling exponent for QAOA (0.044 versus 0.057), which they describe as demonstrating good transferability and more favorable scaling in terms of samples needed to find high-quality solutions.
    [codes: C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that low-depth quantum circuits have well-known limitations for solving optimization problems, while high-depth variational circuits trained from identity or random initialization are likely to suffer from vanishing gradients, motivating the need for alternative training strategies. They point out that if circuit depth is not increased, solving larger instances would rely entirely on sampling from a fixed-depth circuit, which they argue would likely scale exponentially. In their MIS-specific construction, they note that finding optimal groupings of mixer generators to minimize implementation depth is itself NP-hard, forcing them to adopt a simple randomized heuristic. On the data side, they explicitly state that the SP500 historical dataset used for benchmarking has survivorship bias, which affects the realism of the financial setting.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-012, C-024, C-031, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that if the empirically observed polynomial scaling in depth and sampling complexity persists for larger portfolios with hundreds of variables, their QAOA approach could become extremely useful for solving hard optimization problems of this scale. They further argue that Train-and-Scale could, in the near future, provide high-quality parameters at intermediate depths on intermediate-sized quantum systems to tackle hard graph problems—including portfolio-diversification MIS instances—with hundreds of variables.
    [codes: C-034, C-051]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main claimed contribution is the Train-and-Scale strategy for QAOA, which learns high-quality parameters on smaller, size-parameterized instances and then scales both instance size and circuit depth via warm-starting and layer insertion, with repeated retraining on families of subinstances. They position this as enabling high-quality parameters for intermediate or larger-depth QAOA circuits while keeping depth growth modest, and they claim to report, to the best of their knowledge, the largest-size hard optimization instances on which QAOA-p scaling has been studied to date.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-012, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is based on classical statevector simulations of QAOA-p, with extensive gradient-based training using the parameter-shift rule and a sizable training budget (about 130,000 gradient updates over 64 exponentially decayed learning-rate epochs). Training is conducted on large families of subgraphs generated by breadth-first search from SP500 correlation graphs, with 500 graphs per size for n between 6 and 100 and multiple correlation thresholds λ ∈ {0.1,…,0.5}; instances are further weighted during training according to the variability of their energy gaps. The authors also describe practical circuit-engineering choices, such as randomized grouping of mixer generators to reduce depth and insertion of identity layers in the middle of the circuit during depth growth, and they explicitly disclose a key dataset caveat—survivorship bias in the SP500 data—relevant to financial realism and reproducibility.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes could be assigned to one of the other reporting dimensions.

=== PAPER c50cff63fd9e (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses portfolio optimization with discrete asset selection in a derivatives universe, arguing that traditional mean-variance models with continuous decision variables are ill-suited when binary inclusion and limited-budget–type constraints are needed. It reformulates the problem as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) that uses binary asset inclusion variables to encode the asset set and embeds the portfolio risk–return trade-off using expected returns and the covariance matrix, applied to NSE-traded derivatives (Index/Stock Futures and Options).
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-007, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study employs the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), highlighted for its hybrid nature combining classical parameter optimization with quantum state evolution and its suitability for QUBO-type combinatorial binary problems. QAOA is implemented via Qiskit on a simulator, where a hybrid loop iteratively adjusts circuit parameters to minimize the QUBO objective derived from the portfolio’s risk–return structure.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the analysis shows that portfolios including Index Futures and Index Options provide the best risk-adjusted performance, with the combination of these two assets achieving the lowest QUBO objective (~19.03) and a Sharpe ratio around 0.286. The underlying asset statistics indicate Stock Options have the highest expected return but also the highest variance and substantial covariance with Stock Futures, while Index Options display the lowest variance, and portfolios with Stock Futures and Stock Options attain the highest expected return but also the greatest risk. The authors note that top Sharpe-ratio portfolios tend to include Index Options and emphasize that the optimal portfolios manage the risk–return trade-off rather than simply maximizing expected returns.
    [codes: C-005, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036]

Classical brute-force search confirms the portfolio identified by the quantum-inspired solver (e.g., the Index Futures–Index Options combination) as optimal under the given QUBO objective and Sharpe-ratio metrics, thereby serving primarily as a correctness and alignment check rather than a speed comparison.
    [codes: C-004, C-011, C-022, C-029, C-031, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge current quantum hardware constraints as a limiting factor, noting that the binary decision encoding is chosen in part because it fits within these hardware limits and implicitly constrains the scale of problems that can be realistically addressed at present. They also frame their work as an exploratory, simulator-based study rather than a demonstration on real quantum devices, underscoring that meaningful investigation currently relies on quantum-classical hybrid models and simulation rather than large-scale hardware execution.
    [codes: C-018, C-035]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions include scaling the QUBO–QAOA framework to larger asset universes and enriching the optimization with multi-objective criteria such as transaction costs, sectoral diversification, and regulatory constraints. The authors also propose investigating dynamic portfolio rebalancing through time-evolving QUBO matrices, experimenting with real-time implementations on quantum simulators or hardware, and exploring quantum machine learning to develop more adaptive and self-improving portfolio models.
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040]

By applying this framework to NSE-traded derivatives and validating the quantum-inspired solutions against classical brute-force and convex solvers, the authors claim to illustrate the promising role of quantum-inspired models for improving financial decision-making under uncertainty, especially where binary constraints challenge standard mean-variance approaches.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study bases its formulation on the classical mean-variance framework, computing monthly returns from NSE derivatives data to obtain expected returns and a covariance matrix as inputs to the QUBO. The QUBO matrix explicitly integrates risk via the covariance matrix and expected returns via the return vector, modulated by a specified risk-aversion parameter (λ, set to 0.5), and solutions are evaluated using standard portfolio metrics, including expected return, variance, QUBO objective, and Sharpe ratio. The work relies on quantum simulation via Qiskit for QAOA, with clearly described binary asset encoding and an exhaustive classical benchmark, but it does not discuss code release or detailed hyperparameter tuning, indicating moderate but not full reproducibility.

=== PAPER c5fa20e739f7 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets binary integer portfolio optimization, explicitly modeling the problem in a quadratic objective with a hard budget constraint that is then mapped to a quantum Hamiltonian suitable for VQE. The authors motivate this by arguing that limited trainability and scalability of current VQAs could obstruct solving large-scale financial optimization tasks. They also briefly extend the same combinatorial framing to graph bisection to illustrate generality beyond portfolio selection.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-032]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a VQE-based hybrid algorithm that uses a CCC Dicke-state ansatz where the budget constraint is hard-encoded into the circuit, and whose trainability is improved via a convex interpolation heuristic that predicts where the optimal solution lies in Hamming space. Building on the Dicke state's clustering property and the relation between Hamming distance and energy, the authors propose close-to-solution parameter initialization, expected-return-based reordering to regularize the cost landscape, and a recursive ansatz partition into hard-constraint subspaces, combined with CVaR as the objective, COBYLA optimization, and a parameter-correlation schedule. The method is further hybridized with a classical greedy algorithm and includes a sub-ansatz decomposition strategy that, according to the authors, requires exponentially fewer samples than standard circuit cutting.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-039, C-013, C-010]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors report that their close-to-solution initialization strategy outperforms random initialization in terms of optimization performance and convergence behavior. Using the proposed hard-constraint subspace and recursive partitioning, they demonstrate a 40-asset portfolio case corresponding to a 40-qubit Dicke state implemented on only 10 superconducting qubits, with the second experiment explicitly described as solving |D40_20⟩ via the hard-constraint method. Across experiments, they observe an overall descending trend in expectation values and an ascending trend in ground-state probability, and they note that expected-return-based reordering biases the ground state toward specific sub-ansatze near the “right” interpolation points. They also claim that sub-ansatz decomposition offers an exponential sampling reduction compared to circuit cutting and briefly show that convex interpolation scales to a graph bisection example.
    [codes: C-008, C-013, C-018, C-021, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: On the classical side, the authors design a prototype greedy algorithm inspired by their quantum heuristic and use it to verify and refine the VQE-derived solutions. They argue that the hybridization of VQE with greedy search yields mutual complementarity by combining the global exploration tendencies of the quantum variational search with the local refinement strengths of the greedy method.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-024, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. First, they state that the effectiveness of their approach is fundamentally constrained by the interpolation accuracy of the convex curve, implying that poor interpolation directly degrades performance. They note that their reordering strategy for graph bisection, based on the Laplacian’s diagonal elements, cannot always guarantee a regular cost-function landscape. They further report that hardware noise and crosstalk, particularly from parallel execution of multiple circuit blocks, cause severe fluctuations in convergence curves on real devices. Methodologically, they identify an “initialization-induced barren plateau” scenario where overly concentrated principal components trap the optimization in local minima, and thus their own initialization strategy can introduce new convergence pathologies. Collectively, these caveats indicate that both algorithmic heuristics and NISQ hardware effects currently limit the robustness and scalability of the method.
    [codes: C-031, C-033, C-034, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: To address interpolation-related weaknesses, the authors suggest increasing the number of interpolation points as a basic remedy and propose exploring machine learning models to better predict the shape and distribution of the convex energy curve. They also point to local expressibility enhancement—or local overparametrization—as a strategy to mitigate barren-plateau effects, reduce sensitivity to hardware noise, and smooth out a bumpy cost landscape, positioning these ideas as future algorithmic refinements to their current framework.
    [codes: C-035, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core claimed contribution is the use of convex interpolation, grounded in Dicke-state clustering and energy–Hamming-distance structure, as a quantum heuristic to systematically improve VQE trainability via close-to-solution initialization, landscape regularization, and recursive ansatz partitioning for large constrained combinatorial problems such as portfolio optimization. They further claim that their convex-interpolation framework offers a universal solution strategy for combinatorial optimization and that their sub-ansatz decomposition achieves exponentially fewer samples than circuit cutting while enabling a 40-qubit portfolio instance to be solved on 10-qubit hardware. The authors also highlight the hybrid global–local search workflow combining VQE with a greedy algorithm as part of the novelty.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-007, C-013, C-022, C-024, C-028, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper encodes the portfolio’s budget constraint directly into the CCC ansatz as a hard constraint, and introduces principal-component-based metrics—the ratio and variance—to evaluate the quality of probability distributions produced by different initializations. They observe a trade-off between concentration and smoothness in these distributions, implying a tuning challenge between sharp localization and a smoother landscape. The experiments employ CVaR as the cost function and an iterative COBYLA optimizer, with a parameter-correlation schedule that gradually decreases the number of correlated parameters to balance fast expectation descent with good ground-state convergence. The authors define and use hard-constraint subspaces via sub-ansatze, along with expected-return-based reordering to regularize the energy landscape; they also explicitly reflect on hardware noise and crosstalk effects in their convergence curves, indicating an awareness of NISQ-specific methodological constraints.
    [codes: C-012, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-031]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors emphasize that their convex interpolation idea should be understood as a quantum heuristic rather than a fully rigorous guarantee of optimality, framing it conceptually within the broader landscape of heuristic quantum optimization methods.
    [codes: C-039]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames credit risk assessment as a core input to contemporary financial decision-making and argues that existing classical machine learning approaches, while improving predictiveness, are increasingly constrained by scalability when applied to high-dimensional financial datasets with thousands of features and millions of entities that generate exponential computational loads. They emphasize hybrid quantum–classical architectures, where computationally intensive subroutines (e.g., variational quantum circuits, quantum kernels) are executed on quantum hardware while data preparation and optimization remain classical, and they note that quantum kernels and feature maps may enhance credit analysis once classical data are encoded into quantum states.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-028]

The authors further claim that quantum machine learning could improve credit scoring by extracting subtle patterns from diverse data and that quantum kernels may enhance credit analysis and, potentially, more inclusive credit provision.

They further state that quantum risk analysis and portfolio optimization, via amplitude estimation and related methods, have been theoretically shown to scale better than classical Monte Carlo-based techniques in terms of precision-dependent complexity.

On the data and algorithmic side, encoding classical credit data into quantum states is identified as a fundamental challenge, and the O(n) gate cost of loading n features can become a preprocessing bottleneck that may negate putative quantum speedups. The authors also point out that widely used quantum software frameworks such as Qiskit and PennyLane, while helpful, impose significant constraints on financial applications. They suggest that quantum kernels and alternative credit scoring methods could support more inclusive lending by better discriminating risk among previously marginalized borrowers and that modular adoption strategies, starting with quantum solutions for specific computational bottlenecks in risk processes, can gradually expand to more holistic applications. In the long run, they envision risk assessment systems that are potentially real-time, explainable, and more inclusive, contingent on advances in hardware and methods.

=== PAPER c6422717f546 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses an enterprise portfolio optimization problem, framed as rational allocation of investment resources given target returns and allowable risk, and characterized as a complex nonlinear, high-dimensional NP problem that is hard to solve with traditional methods. It builds a mathematical model based on mean-variance theory but replaces the pure return–variance objective with a comprehensive index that jointly evaluates income and risk, with risk given higher weight to reflect investor risk tolerance. The model is positioned for practical enterprise investment decision-making under varying risk levels.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid solution method that combines Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), representing each individual in a quantum population as a quantum state wave function and using quantum-inspired population updates. They specify that the population contains N individuals over M risky securities, introduce local and global attractors and a mean-best solution to guide convergence, and solve the portfolio model via iterative population update and elite selection. The implementation includes preprocessing historical returns into average returns and a covariance matrix, repairing infeasible portfolios to satisfy constraints, and then applying the PSO–QAOA procedure to output a global optimum.
    [codes: C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that the average performance metric of the proposed hybrid algorithm is below 0.06 and that its mean fitness values (0.0209, 0.0309, 0.0446, 0.0583) and corresponding variances (down to 3.7313E-06) are smaller than those of comparison algorithms, which the authors interpret as indicating lower risk for a given return. They find that as the preset risk level increases, the maximum, minimum, and average portfolio returns all rise, with reported increases of 10.99%, 19.80%, and 7.98% respectively, while the algorithm’s stability remains basically unchanged and returns tend to stabilize at higher risk levels. The authors conclude from these experiments that their algorithm is effective in solving the enterprise portfolio optimization problem for practical investment decision-making.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-005]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The proposed PSO–QAOA hybrid is empirically compared against three classical metaheuristics: Differential Evolution (DE), Genetic Algorithm (GA), and traditional PSO on the same portfolio optimization task. Across several experimental settings, the research algorithm is reported to have smaller mean objective values (0.0209, 0.0309, 0.0446, 0.0583) and smaller variances than these baselines, which the authors interpret as achieving less risk for a given return and better stability without degradation at higher risk levels.
    [codes: C-003, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that classical portfolio optimization research, including the mean-variance model they build on, is limited by the rational person hypothesis and risk attitude assumptions, which restrict how well such models capture real investor behavior. They further note a key limitation of the mean-variance foundation: it assumes asset returns follow a normal distribution, an assumption they state is difficult to uphold in real market operations.
    [codes: C-014, C-016]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper indicates that future research will focus on extending the proposed PSO–QAOA-based portfolio optimization algorithm to other economic models beyond the specific enterprise portfolio setting studied here.
    [codes: C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is the proposal of a hybrid PSO–QAOA algorithm tailored to enterprise portfolio optimization, together with a customized return–risk evaluation criterion (PRC) that asymmetrically penalizes risk beyond investor tolerance and amplifies returns within a preset risk level. The authors present this combination of a refined risk–return criterion and a PSO–QAOA hybrid solver as an effective tool for enterprise investment decision-making compared with existing methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-005]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study formulates the portfolio optimization model by importing historical yields of M risky securities over n trading days and computing average returns and the covariance matrix; the empirical application uses 20 stocks from different sectors and 50 trading days of return data. The algorithm encodes portfolios in a quantum-inspired population, applies feasibility repair to enforce total allocation constraints, and uses elite selection based on fitness comparisons between generations. However, the experiments are limited to this single small dataset and focus on optimization quality metrics without explicit analysis of scalability or robustness across different market conditions.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors situate their work within prior research, noting that quantum computing methods, including QAOA and quantum annealing, have increasingly been applied to portfolio optimization and have shown improved success probabilities or more powerful solutions in earlier studies, while classical metaheuristics such as PSO have also demonstrated good performance. They describe that, within their results, the optimal allocation pattern shifts toward higher-return stocks as the risk level increases, with lower-return stocks’ weights tending toward zero and higher-return stocks’ weights increasing.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets combinatorial optimization problems with a focus on real-world financial portfolio optimization, motivated by the difficulty of scaling classical methods as the solution space grows. It frames portfolio selection (choose stocks from a 30‑asset TSX universe) as a binary combinatorial problem and argues that quantum-inspired superposition can better handle larger search spaces, optimizing a trend ratio defined as expected return over risk. Portfolio optimization is positioned as a realistic and complex industrial COP that requires effective, fast solutions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-012, C-013, C-016, C-019, C-025]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum-inspired Jaguar Algorithm (QJA), a hybrid quantum-classical metaheuristic that simulates quantum superposition on a classical computer. QJA initializes each asset as an equal superposition state, measures |1⟩ as selecting a stock for the portfolio, and updates superposition probabilities using a rule based on global best and local worst solutions. It embeds a hunting-based adaptive update mechanism from the classical Jaguar Algorithm and inherits the best-versus-worst update concept from quantum-inspired tabu search (QTS), adaptively adjusting a parameter θ by doubling or halving it depending on historical state transitions to control convergence magnitude in the superposition state.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-009, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-042, C-044]

Across 831 sliding training–testing windows, it shows superior average solution quality and robustness compared to QTS and GQTS, including an average 13.26% improvement in trend ratio over QTS and large gains in the number of optimal solutions identified. The authors conclude that QJA can better and more efficiently address real-world financial portfolio optimization than the other evaluated QIO methods.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-043]

Within this QIO family, QJA is reported to outperform QTS and GQTS in most training–testing windows in average solution quality, robustness, convergence speed, and optimization counts for the portfolio optimization task.
    [codes: C-011, C-020, C-021, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly note that current universal quantum computers suffer from limitations in scaling size, gate fidelity, and quantum structure, preventing realization of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, which motivates their use of quantum-inspired optimization on classical hardware.
